title: Write Python Like It Ships
objective: Set up and structure a Python project the way production teams do, with types, validation, config, errors and logging.
narrative: You already write Python that works. This week is about Python that ships: the difference is structure, types, and boundaries. Everything you build all quarter sits on this base, so every hour here compounds.
whatYouCanBuild: A properly structured, typed, configured, logged Python package with a CLI — the skeleton every later service reuses.
whyProfessionally: Interviewers and clients judge you in the first 5 minutes of reading your repo. Production structure is the tell that you've shipped, not just studied.

days.title: Project bootstrap: uv, pyproject, src layout

items.title: Your toolchain — uv, virtualenvs and pyproject.toml
items.concept:
uv is one fast tool that replaces the pip + virtualenv + pip-tools stack (and most of what poetry does). Three reasons teams switched: it is 10-100x faster than pip, it writes a lockfile (uv.lock) so every machine installs identical versions, and it manages the virtualenv for you so you stop thinking about activation.

The daily verbs: **uv init** scaffolds a project, **uv add httpx** declares a dependency in pyproject.toml and locks it, **uv add --dev pytest** puts tooling in a dev dependency group, **uv run x** executes x inside the project's environment (creating/syncing it on demand), **uv sync** makes the environment match the lockfile exactly, **uv lock** re-resolves.

pyproject.toml is the single manifest for a modern Python project. [project] holds name, version, requires-python and dependencies (what your code needs to run). [dependency-groups] holds dev-only tools like pytest — installed for contributors, never shipped to users. Later you'll meet [project.scripts] (CLI entry points) and [build-system] (how the package is built).

Mental model shift from pip: you never 'pip install' into whatever environment happens to be active. You declare dependencies in pyproject.toml, the lockfile pins them, and uv run guarantees the code runs against exactly that set.
items.why: Every project this quarter — CLIs, FastAPI services, LLM clients — starts with uv init. Reproducible environments are also the first thing a reviewer checks: a repo with a lockfile says 'this will run on your machine too'.

learn.focus: Read: the landing page's Highlights, then Getting started → Installation and First steps. Skip: the pip interface docs and the standalone script (PEP 723) section for now.
Read the whole guide: Creating a new project, Managing dependencies (uv add / uv remove), Running commands (uv run), and the uv.lock + uv sync explanation. Skip: Building distributions at the bottom.
Read: the [project] table basics — name, version, requires-python, dependencies — and skim [build-system]. Skip: dynamic metadata, licence file details and classifiers.

build.task: Scaffold the aie-lab project with uv, declare runtime and dev dependencies, and prove the environment works.
steps: Install uv (official installer or pipx) and check: uv --version
uv init aie-lab, cd in, look at what was generated: pyproject.toml, main.py, .python-version, .gitignore
uv add httpx pydantic — then open pyproject.toml and find them under [project] dependencies
uv add --dev pytest — find it under [dependency-groups] dev, not in [project]
Open uv.lock briefly: pinned versions + hashes for the full transitive tree. You never edit this file by hand
Edit main.py to import httpx and print httpx.__version__, then run it with: uv run main.py
Run uv sync, then ls .venv/bin (or .venv\Scripts) to see where the interpreter actually lives
build.hint: If uv run complains it cannot find the project, you are not in the directory containing pyproject.toml — uv walks up from the cwd to find it.
build.code:
# pyproject.toml — what yours should roughly look like after the adds
[project]
name = 'aie-lab'
version = '0.1.0'
description = 'AI engineering lab projects'
requires-python = '>=3.12'
dependencies = [
  'httpx>=0.27',
  'pydantic>=2.7',
]

[dependency-groups]
dev = [
  'pytest>=8.2',
]

items.challenge: Run uv python list, then pin the project to a specific interpreter with uv python pin 3.12 and confirm .python-version changed. Explain to yourself why committing that file helps a teammate.

debugMission.scenario: A colleague 'installed' rich but imports fail when the script runs under uv. Their terminal transcript is below. Diagnose why the package is invisible.
debugMission.artifact:
$ pip install rich
Successfully installed rich-13.7.1
$ uv run python -c 'import rich; print(rich.__version__)'
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File '<string>', line 1, in <module>
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'rich'
$ python -c 'import rich; print(rich.__version__)'
13.7.1
hints: Two different interpreters are in play. Run: which python — then: uv run which python
uv run executes inside .venv, which only contains what pyproject.toml declares. Where did pip install rich?
Compare pip list against: uv pip list
debugMission.solution: pip installed rich into the system (or whatever env the shell had active), while uv run uses the project's .venv, which is built strictly from pyproject.toml + uv.lock — rich was never declared there. The fix is uv add rich, not pip install. General lesson: with uv there is one source of truth (pyproject.toml); if a package is not declared, it does not exist for your project, and 'which python' is your first diagnostic whenever imports behave impossibly.

reflection: What problem does uv.lock solve that a dependencies list in pyproject.toml alone cannot?
When would you still reach for pip inside a uv project — if ever?
done: aie-lab exists with httpx + pydantic under [project] and pytest under [dependency-groups] dev
uv run main.py prints the httpx version
uv.lock is present and you can say in one sentence what it pins
You reproduced the debug mission diagnosis with which python vs uv run which python

keyConcepts.def: A machine-written file (uv.lock) pinning exact versions and hashes of every transitive dependency so installs are reproducible.
A named set of dev-only dependencies (like pytest) in pyproject.toml, installed for development but not required by the shipped package.
Runs a command inside the project's virtualenv, creating and syncing it from the lockfile on demand.

items.title: src layout, packages and imports
items.concept:
Flat layout puts your package next to pyproject.toml; src layout puts it under src/. The difference matters because Python puts the current directory on sys.path: with flat layout, 'import aie_lab' can silently resolve to the folder on disk rather than the installed package. Your tests then pass locally while the built package is broken — the exact bug src layout makes impossible, because the package is only importable once properly installed.

A directory becomes a package via __init__.py. Inside your package, use absolute imports (from aie_lab.core.market import parse_price) — they survive file moves and are unambiguous. Relative imports (from .market import ...) are legal but save them for tight sibling modules.

[project.scripts] maps a command name to a function: aie-lab = 'aie_lab.cli:main' means 'run main() from aie_lab/cli.py'. For uv to install your project as an importable package (rather than just manage its dependencies), pyproject.toml needs a [build-system] table — then uv sync installs it in editable mode and the console script appears in .venv/bin.
items.why: Every service and client library you build this quarter uses this exact skeleton. It is also the first structural signal in a portfolio repo: src layout plus entry points reads as 'has shipped a package', flat main.py reads as 'tutorial'.

learn.focus: Read the whole discussion (it is short). Pay attention to the section explaining how the flat layout lets the cwd shadow the installed package — that is the core argument.

build.task: Restructure aie-lab into src layout with a real package and a console-script entry point.
steps: Create src/aie_lab/__init__.py and src/aie_lab/core/__init__.py; delete the scaffold main.py
Add src/aie_lab/core/market.py with one function: mid_price(bid: float, ask: float) -> float
Add src/aie_lab/cli.py with main() that prints mid_price(101.5, 102.5) using an absolute import
In pyproject.toml add the [build-system] table (see code) and [project.scripts] with: aie-lab = 'aie_lab.cli:main'
uv sync — watch it install aie-lab itself as an editable package
Run it both ways: uv run aie-lab, and uv run python -m aie_lab.cli
build.hint: Package folder is aie_lab (underscore, importable); project and command names use hyphens. Mixing those up is the classic five-minute time sink.
build.code:
# add to pyproject.toml
[build-system]
requires = ['hatchling']
build-backend = 'hatchling.build'

[project.scripts]
aie-lab = 'aie_lab.cli:main'

# src/aie_lab/cli.py
from aie_lab.core.market import mid_price

def main() -> None:
    print('mid:', mid_price(101.5, 102.5))

items.challenge: Add a second module src/aie_lab/core/fx.py and import it from market.py two ways: absolutely, then relatively (from .fx import ...). Decide which you'll standardise on and write the rule as a comment in __init__.py.

debugMission.scenario: Running the CLI module as a plain file explodes, but uv run python -m aie_lab.cli works. Explain the difference precisely — 'it just does' is not accepted.
debugMission.artifact:
$ uv run python src/aie_lab/cli.py
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File 'src/aie_lab/cli.py', line 1, in <module>
    from aie_lab.core.market import mid_price
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'aie_lab'
$ uv run python -m aie_lab.cli
mid: 102.0
hints: Print sys.path at the top of the file and run it both ways. What is entry zero in each case?
Running a file puts that file's directory (src/aie_lab/) on sys.path — can 'import aie_lab' resolve from inside itself?
python -m resolves the module via the installed package in .venv; the file path route never consults it.
debugMission.solution: python path/to/file.py puts the file's own directory on sys.path — here src/aie_lab/ — so the interpreter looks for an aie_lab package inside the package and fails. python -m aie_lab.cli (and the console script) resolve through site-packages, where uv installed your project editable. Lesson: in a src-layout project you always execute via the entry point, python -m, or tests — never by file path — and any ModuleNotFoundError for your own package is a sys.path question, not a code question.

reflection: In one sentence: what class of bug does src layout convert from 'discovered by users' to 'impossible'?
done: Tree shows src/aie_lab/ with __init__.py files and core/market.py
uv run aie-lab prints the mid price via the console script
uv run python -m aie_lab.cli works and you can explain why the file-path invocation cannot
All imports inside the package are absolute

keyConcepts.def: Project structure with the package under src/, ensuring code is only importable via the installed package — packaging bugs surface immediately.
A [project.scripts] mapping from a command name to package.module:function, installed as an executable in the venv.
The list of directories Python searches for imports; script invocation prepends the script's directory, python -m uses the installed environment.

items.title: Repo zero — git init, .gitignore, first push
items.concept:
You know basic git; this is about what a professional Python repo excludes and includes. Excluded: .venv/ (rebuildable from the lockfile), __pycache__/ and *.pyc (bytecode), .pytest_cache/, .mypy_cache/, .ruff_cache/ (tool scratch), dist/ (build output), and .env (secrets — the one that ends careers if committed).

Included, and this surprises people: **uv.lock is committed**. For an application, the lockfile IS the reproducibility guarantee — a teammate or CI runs uv sync and gets your exact environment. (Libraries published to PyPI sometimes choose otherwise; your projects this quarter are applications.)

First commit: make it meaningful ('Scaffold aie-lab: uv project, src layout, CLI entry point'), not 'initial commit blah'. Commit messages are the changelog your future self reads.
items.why: Recruiters and clients read repos top-down: .gitignore and lockfile hygiene are visible in the first screenful. A committed .venv or missing lockfile is an instant credibility hit.

learn.focus: Skim: Create a repository and the commit-and-push steps to mirror the flow with your own repo. Skip: the branching and pull request sections — that is Week 2's material.

build.task: Put aie-lab on GitHub with a professional .gitignore and a meaningful first commit.
steps: Check the .gitignore uv generated; ensure it covers .venv/, __pycache__/, *.pyc, .pytest_cache/, .mypy_cache/, .ruff_cache/, dist/, .env — add any missing lines
Confirm uv.lock is NOT ignored — git status should list it
git init (if needed), git add -A, then review exactly what is staged with git status — nothing from .venv should appear
Commit with a message that says what and why: Scaffold aie-lab: uv project, src layout, CLI entry point
Create the GitHub repo and push (gh repo create aie-lab --private --source . --push, or the manual remote route)
build.hint: If .venv shows up in git status, your .gitignore entry is probably venv/ without the dot. Ignore patterns are literal.

items.challenge: Add a .env file locally with FAKE_KEY=abc, confirm git status does not show it, then write one sentence in the README about where secrets live. Cheap insurance.
reflection: Why is committing uv.lock correct for an application but debatable for a published library?
done: Repo is on GitHub; git status is clean
uv.lock is tracked; .venv, caches and .env are ignored
First commit message describes the scaffold meaningfully

keyConcepts.def: Applications commit their lockfile so every environment (dev, CI, prod) resolves to identical dependency versions.

items.title: Type hints as design tools
items.concept:
Type hints are not bureaucracy; they are executable design notes. A signature like fetch_quotes(tickers: list[str], since: date | None = None) -> dict[str, float] tells the reader the whole contract before they read a line of the body — and a type checker enforces it on every call site, forever.

The practical toolkit, Python 3.12 flavour: builtin generics (list[str], dict[str, float], tuple[int, ...]) — never import List from typing; unions with the pipe (str | None, not Optional[str]); defaults are orthogonal to optionality (param: str | None = None is 'may be absent', param: str = 'GBP' is 'has a sensible default').

Choosing a shape for structured data: **TypedDict** when data genuinely is a dict (JSON you pass straight through), **dataclass** when it is an internal object with behaviour (tomorrow's topic), **Pydantic** at trust boundaries (Day 3). And **Any** is an honest admission that a value is dynamically shaped — but it switches the checker off for everything it touches, so quarantine it at the edges.

Run a checker, read its output slowly once: mypy and pyright report the same class of truths. When the checker fights you, it is usually reporting a design smell — a function returning str or None or list depending on mood is bad API, not bad annotation.
items.why: Typed code is the entry bar for professional Python teams, and LLM-adjacent code especially: request/response shapes, tool schemas and model outputs are all types. Interviewers read your signatures before your logic.

learn.focus: Read the whole cheat sheet top to bottom — variables, functions, classes, the standard-duck-types section. Keep it open in a tab all week; it answers 90% of 'how do I annotate this'.
Skim: the intro paragraphs and the 'Type aliases' + 'NewType' sections; use the rest strictly as a lookup reference. Skip: Protocols, TypeVar and anything under Generics — not needed yet.

build.task: Write five fully typed functions for a mini market-data domain and make mypy pass with zero errors.
steps: uv add --dev mypy, then create src/aie_lab/core/market.py (extend the Day-1 file)
Implement with full annotations: parse_price(raw: str) -> float | None — handles '101.5', ' 101.5 ', returns None for junk
filter_tickers(tickers: list[str], prefix: str) -> list[str] and latest_quote(quotes: dict[str, float], ticker: str) -> float | None
mid_price(bid: float, ask: float) -> float and spread_bps(bid: float, ask: float) -> float (basis points, 4 decimal places)
Run: uv run mypy src — fix every complaint without a single type: ignore
Deliberately call latest_quote(q, 42) somewhere and watch mypy catch it; then delete the call
build.hint: For parse_price, try/except ValueError around float(raw.strip()) is enough — the interesting part is that the return type forces every caller to handle None.

items.challenge: Add a TypedDict RawQuote (ticker: str, price: str, ts: str) and a function to_quotes(rows: list[RawQuote]) -> dict[str, float] that uses parse_price and skips unparseable rows. Notice how the TypedDict documents the wire format without inventing a class.

debugMission.scenario: mypy flags matching_tickers and the author wants to 'fix' it by changing the annotation to list[str] | None. Persuade them (and yourself) that the design is the bug.
debugMission.artifact:
def matching_tickers(tickers: list[str], prefix: str) -> list[str]:
    if not tickers:
        return None  # signal 'no data'
    return [t for t in tickers if t.startswith(prefix)]

# mypy:
# market.py:3: error: Incompatible return value type
#   (got 'None', expected 'list[str]')  [return-value]
hints: What would every caller have to write if this returned list[str] | None? Is 'no matches' actually exceptional?
An empty list already means 'nothing matched'. What extra information would None carry here? None.
debugMission.solution: The honest fix is return [] — an empty list is the natural 'nothing matched' value, and callers can iterate it without a None-check. Widening the annotation to list[str] | None would make the signature match a bad design and tax every caller forever. General lesson: when the checker complains, first ask whether the TYPE is wrong or the DESIGN is wrong; reserve None for 'unknown/absent', never for 'empty'.

reflection: Which of your five functions changed design (not just annotation) once you thought about its return type?
Where in an LLM app would Any be an honest annotation?
done: Five typed functions exist and uv run mypy src exits clean
No type: ignore comments anywhere
You watched mypy catch one deliberately wrong call before deleting it
parse_price returns None for junk input and callers must handle it

keyConcepts.def: A static tool (mypy/pyright) that verifies every call site against declared signatures without running the code.
Python 3.10+ union syntax for optional values; forces callers to handle absence explicitly.
A typed description of a dict's exact keys and value types — ideal for JSON-shaped data you don't want to convert to objects.
An escape hatch that disables checking for a value; honest at dynamic edges, corrosive everywhere else.

items.title: Dataclasses vs dict-passing
items.why: LLM pipelines shuttle structured records everywhere — requests, tool calls, extracted entities. Teams that pass dicts around ship key-error bugs to production weekly; typed objects make those bugs unrepresentable.

learn.focus: Read: the module intro and the field() section (default_factory especially), plus the frozen paragraph. Skim __post_init__. Skip: InitVar, KW_ONLY details and the descriptor notes.

build.task: Refactor the provided dict-passing snippet into frozen dataclasses and feel the difference in your editor.
steps: Copy the snippet in code into src/aie_lab/core/positions.py — run it once as-is to see it work
Define @dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True) Quote (ticker: str, price: float, currency: str = 'GBP')
Define @dataclass Position (quote: Quote, units: int) with a value property (price * units)
Rewrite position_value and describe to take these types; delete the dict versions
Type quote. in your editor and enjoy real autocomplete; run uv run mypy src again
build.hint: frozen=True means you build corrected quotes with dataclasses.replace(quote, price=...) instead of mutating — that is a feature, not friction.

items.challenge: Add a total_value(positions: list[Position]) -> dict[str, float] grouped by currency. Notice you never once wondered what keys exist — that is the disease cured.

debugMission.scenario: A teammate added a currency field to Quote and now the module will not even import. The traceback fires at class-definition time, before any instance is created.
debugMission.artifact:
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Quote:
    ticker: str
    price: float = 0.0
    currency: str

# Traceback (most recent call last):
#   File 'positions.py', line 4, in <module>
#     class Quote:
# TypeError: non-default argument 'currency'
#   follows default argument 'price'
hints: dataclass generates __init__(ticker, price=0.0, currency) — is that a legal Python signature?
Two fixes exist: reorder the fields, or make the ordering irrelevant with a dataclass flag.
debugMission.solution: Dataclass fields become positional __init__ parameters in declaration order, and Python forbids a required parameter after a defaulted one — so the class fails to build. Fix: move currency above price, or declare @dataclass(kw_only=True) (or field(kw_only=True) on the tail fields) so everything is keyword-only and order stops mattering. Lesson: dataclasses are code generators; when one misbehaves, mentally expand the __init__ it would write.

reflection: Say the boundary rule aloud: where do Pydantic models live, where do dataclasses live, and why?
done: positions.py uses frozen dataclasses; the dict versions are deleted
mypy passes and autocomplete works on quote fields
You can state the field-ordering rule and the kw_only escape hatch
The boundary rule (validate at edges, trust inside) is written as a module docstring

keyConcepts.def: Dataclass mechanism for mutable defaults — field(default_factory=list) builds a fresh list per instance.
Immutable instances; changes require dataclasses.replace, which prevents aliasing surprises.
Validate untrusted data with Pydantic at system edges; use lightweight dataclasses for trusted internal data.

items.title: Type an untyped module
items.concept:
This is the real skill: taking a working-but-untyped module and letting types interrogate it. The module below runs fine on the happy path — and hides three design flaws that annotations will drag into the light: a function that returns float or str depending on input, an implicit None escaping from a lookup, and a total that silently mixes currencies.

Method: annotate one function at a time, run uv run mypy --strict src after each, and treat every error as a question about the design, not an obstacle. --strict adds disallow-untyped-defs and friends, so nothing slips through unannotated.

You are allowed — encouraged — to change behaviour where the types reveal it was wrong: make return types honest, raise instead of returning sentinel strings, and force callers to handle absence.
items.why: You will inherit untyped code constantly — client codebases, notebook-grown pipelines, LLM-generated snippets. Typing-as-audit is how consultants earn trust in week one of an engagement.

build.task: Fully type the provided module under mypy --strict, refactoring where the types expose design flaws.
steps: Copy the code below into src/aie_lab/core/legacy_portfolio.py verbatim; run mypy --strict and count the errors
Annotate load_positions — decide what rows really is (hint: TypedDict from yesterday) and what the function returns
Fix position_value: it returns float OR the string 'N/A'. Make it float | None, or raise — pick one and justify in a comment
Fix find_position: the implicit None return must appear in the signature; update the caller in total_value to handle it
total_value adds values across currencies as if they were one number — restructure to return dict[str, float] by currency
Finish when uv run mypy --strict src is clean and the module still produces sensible output for the sample data at the bottom
build.hint: When a function can return two unrelated types, the type checker is telling you callers cannot safely use the result. That is a redesign signal, not an annotation puzzle.

items.challenge: Run mypy --strict with warn_unreachable = true in pyproject.toml [tool.mypy] — does it find any code your refactor made dead?
reflection: Which of the three flaws would have reached production without types, and what would the incident have looked like?
done: uv run mypy --strict src exits clean
position_value no longer returns a string sentinel; callers handle absence explicitly
total_value returns per-currency totals and a comment explains why
Sample data at the bottom still produces correct output

keyConcepts.def: Strict preset that forbids untyped functions and implicit Any, making the checker's guarantees total across a module.

items.title: Pydantic v2 — validate at the boundary
items.concept:
Pydantic turns 'I hope this JSON is shaped right' into 'it is this shape or it is a ValidationError'. A BaseModel declares fields with types; construction validates and coerces ('2024-03-01' becomes a date, '42' becomes 42 in lax mode). Entry points: Model.model_validate(obj) for Python objects, Model.model_validate_json(raw) for JSON text (faster — parses and validates in one pass). Export with model_dump() / model_dump_json().

A ValidationError is a report, not just a crash: e.errors() yields one entry per problem with loc (field path), msg, and type. Read it like a checklist — it names every bad field at once, which is exactly what you want at a boundary.

Custom rules use @field_validator('field') on a classmethod. mode='after' (default) runs after type coercion — you receive a real date, not a string; mode='before' runs on raw input when you must pre-clean. Validators must return the value (transformed or untouched) or raise ValueError.

The philosophy that makes this scale: **validate once at the edge, then trust types inside**. Endless re-checking mid-pipeline means you never established a boundary in the first place.
items.why: Every external thing you touch this quarter — API payloads, LLM outputs, files, env vars — arrives untrusted. Pydantic at the boundary is THE core pattern of AI engineering; Week 4's structured LLM outputs are literally these models.

learn.focus: Read: Basic model usage, Nested models, and the model_validate / model_validate_json part of Helper functions. Skip: generic models, dynamic model creation, RootModel and everything below Faux immutability.
Read: Field validators (decorator syntax, mode='before' vs 'after') and skim Model validators. Skip: Annotated-pattern validators and validation context.

build.task: Model a filings feed with validated fields, a normalising validator, and a future-date rejection rule.
steps: Create src/aie_lab/core/filings.py; define FilingType as an Enum with TEN_K='10-K', TEN_Q='10-Q', EIGHT_K='8-K'
Company(ticker: str, name: str, exchange: str); Filing(ticker: str, filing_type: FilingType, filed: date, currency: Literal['USD','GBP','EUR'], amount: float)
Add @field_validator('ticker') on both models: strip whitespace and uppercase (so ' azn ' becomes 'AZN')
Add a Filing validator rejecting future dates: if v > date.today(): raise ValueError('filed date is in the future')
In a scratch block, feed one good dict and two bad ones (currency 'JPY', filed '2031-01-01'); print e.errors() and read loc/msg/type for each
model_dump_json(indent=2) the good filing and eyeball the output
build.hint: Literal['USD','GBP','EUR'] gives you an enum-strength constraint without an Enum class — perfect for small closed sets.

items.challenge: Make amount reject negatives using Field(gt=0) instead of a validator, and add model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True). Which constraints belong in Field() vs a validator? Write your rule of thumb as a comment.

debugMission.scenario: The ticker normaliser 'stopped working' — Filing accepts ' azn ' untouched, no error anywhere. The code below is what shipped. Find why the validator never runs.
hints: Which class is the validator defined inside? Which class is being instantiated?
Validators are per-model, not global by field name. Company validating ticker says nothing about Filing.ticker

Bonus check: if the validator had named a field that does not exist on its class, pydantic would have raised PydanticUserError at class-definition time — silence here means it IS attached, just elsewhere.
debugMission.solution: The validator lives on Company, but the code instantiates Filing — validators belong to the model they are defined in, so Filing.ticker was never touched, silently. Fix: move (or duplicate) the validator onto Filing, or better, define a reusable Annotated ticker type once and share it. Lesson: 'validator never ran' bugs are location bugs; also note the contrast — a misspelt field name fails loudly at import, the wrong-class version fails silently, which is why it reaches production.

reflection: Where exactly is 'the boundary' in a FastAPI service? Name the line of code where untrusted becomes trusted.
Why is model_validate_json preferable to json.loads followed by model_validate?
done: Filing rejects bad currency and future dates with readable ValidationErrors
Ticker normalisation proven with a ' azn ' input on the right model
You printed e.errors() and can name loc, msg, type from memory
One good filing round-trips through model_dump_json

keyConcepts.def: Pydantic v2 entry point that validates a Python object against a model, raising ValidationError on failure.
Decorator attaching custom per-field validation/normalisation to a model; runs after coercion by default.
Structured list of every failure with loc/msg/type — a machine-readable boundary report.
Validate untrusted data exactly once at the system edge, then rely on types internally.

items.title: Settings and environment variables done right
items.concept:
Config belongs in the environment, not in code — the 12-factor 'Config' rule. Anything that varies between deploys (URLs, keys, timeouts, log level) is an env var; code is identical everywhere. Secrets in git are forever: a key committed once lives in history even after deletion.

pydantic-settings makes this typed: a BaseSettings subclass reads fields from environment variables (and a local .env file for development) and validates them like any model. SecretStr masks values in repr and logs — you must call .get_secret_value() to use one, which makes accidental leakage grep-able.

The fail-fast property is the point: if AIE_API_KEY is missing or AIE_TIMEOUT_S is 'ten', the app dies at startup with a ValidationError naming the exact field — not at 3am when the first request needs the key. Instantiate Settings once at startup; pass it down (Week 3 wires this into FastAPI dependencies).

Hygiene: .env is gitignored (Day 1 already did this); commit a .env.example with dummy values so teammates know what to set.
items.why: Leaked keys are the most common — and most career-limiting — junior mistake in LLM work, where every call costs money. Typed fail-fast settings are also what stops the classic 'worked locally, crashed in prod with a KeyError' deploy.

learn.focus: Read: Installation, Usage, Dotenv (.env) support, and the Field value priority list (env beats .env — know this order). Skip: secrets directories, Azure/AWS sources and CLI support.
Read the Config page only (3 minutes). The litmus test paragraph — could you open-source the repo right now without leaking credentials — is the takeaway.

build.task: Add a typed Settings class that loads from .env, masks the API key, and dies loudly when config is missing.
steps: uv add pydantic-settings; create src/aie_lab/settings.py
Settings(BaseSettings): api_base_url: str, api_key: SecretStr, timeout_s: float = 10.0, log_level: str = 'INFO'
model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file='.env', env_prefix='AIE_')
Write .env with AIE_API_BASE_URL and AIE_API_KEY=dev-secret-123; write .env.example with dummy values and commit only the example
Prove masking: print(Settings()) must show api_key=SecretStr('**********')
Prove fail-fast: temporarily rename the AIE_API_KEY line and run again — read the ValidationError naming api_key as missing; restore it
build.hint: env_prefix='AIE_' means the field api_key maps to AIE_API_KEY. Prefixes stop your app hoovering up unrelated vars like PATH-adjacent junk.
build.code:
from pydantic import SecretStr
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
        env_file='.env', env_prefix='AIE_')

    api_base_url: str
    api_key: SecretStr
    timeout_s: float = 10.0
    log_level: str = 'INFO'

items.challenge: Support dev/prod profiles: read APP_ENV and pass env_file='.env.' + profile into Settings(_env_file=...), or use SettingsConfigDict(env_file=('.env', '.env.prod')) layering. Prove prod overrides one value and document the precedence you observed.

debugMission.scenario: A teammate swears the key is 'right there in the .env file' but the app refuses to start. Both artefacts below are exactly as on their machine.
debugMission.artifact:
# .env
API_BASE_URL=https-example-endpoint
API_KEY=dev-secret-123

# crash on startup:
# pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError:
#   2 validation errors for Settings
# api_base_url
#   Field required [type=missing]
# api_key
#   Field required [type=missing]
hints: The error says missing, not invalid — pydantic-settings never saw those vars at all. What name is it actually looking for?
Check model_config. What does env_prefix='AIE_' do to the expected variable names?
debugMission.solution: Settings declares env_prefix='AIE_', so the fields map to AIE_API_BASE_URL and AIE_API_KEY — the .env provides unprefixed names, which are simply invisible. Fix the .env (and .env.example) to use the prefixed names. Lesson: 'Field required but it is right there' is almost always a name-mapping problem — prefix, case, or wrong .env path — and the .env.example you commit is where the correct names get documented for the next person.

reflection: Why is crashing at startup on bad config strictly better than defaulting quietly?
What is the 12-factor litmus test for whether config is done right?
done: Settings loads from .env with the AIE_ prefix; .env.example is committed, .env is not
repr shows the masked SecretStr, and .get_secret_value() is the only way to read the key
Removing AIE_API_KEY produces a startup ValidationError naming the field
You can state the env-beats-dotenv precedence order

keyConcepts.def: Everything that varies between deploys lives in environment variables; code stays identical across environments.
Pydantic type that masks secrets in repr/logs; the value is only accessible via get_secret_value().
Validate all config at startup so missing/invalid values kill the process immediately with a named error.

items.title: Design your failure modes
items.concept:
Professional code designs its failures like it designs its API. Start with a hierarchy: class AppError(Exception) as the root, then DataFetchError and DataParseError as branches. Callers can then catch exactly the layer they can handle — except DataFetchError for network trouble, except AppError at the top of the CLI — and let genuine bugs (TypeError, KeyError) crash loudly.

**raise ... from err** is the habit that separates seniors from juniors. When you translate a low-level error into a domain error, chaining preserves the true cause: the traceback prints the original, then 'The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception', then yours. Raise without from inside an except block and Python prints the vaguer 'During handling... another exception occurred'; raise from None and you have amputated the evidence entirely.

Classify failures at design time: **retryable** (timeouts, 5xx, connection resets — transient, worth another attempt) vs **fatal** (bad credentials, malformed data, 404 — retrying is pure waste). Encode it in the hierarchy (RetryableFetchError) so Week 2's retry logic can make the decision mechanically.

EAFP — easier to ask forgiveness than permission — is idiomatic Python: try the operation and catch the specific failure, rather than pre-checking conditions that can race or lie.
items.why: LLM apps live on flaky networks and rate-limited APIs; the retryable/fatal split you encode today literally becomes your Week 2 tenacity policy and your Week 4 LLM client. Muddled error handling is also the #1 code-review red flag.

learn.focus: Read: Raising Exceptions, Exception Chaining, and User-defined Exceptions. Skim Handling Exceptions if rusty. Skip: the sys.exc_info notes and Enriching Exceptions with Notes.

build.task: Create the aie-lab exception module and a fetch_filings() that wraps low-level errors into domain errors with context.
steps: Create src/aie_lab/core/errors.py: AppError(Exception) root; DataFetchError(AppError); DataParseError(AppError); RetryableFetchError(DataFetchError)
Give AppError an __init__(message, **context) that stores a context dict and includes it in __str__
In filings.py write fetch_filings(ticker: str) — for now it reads a local JSON file named after the ticker (network arrives Week 2)
Wrap FileNotFoundError/OSError as DataFetchError('could not read filings', ticker=ticker) using raise ... from err
Wrap json.JSONDecodeError and pydantic ValidationError as DataParseError, again with from err and the ticker in context
Trigger each failure (missing file, junk JSON, bad fields) and read all three chained tracebacks bottom-to-top
build.hint: Wrap at the boundary of meaning, not around every line: one try per 'operation the caller cares about' (read the file; parse the payload), not one per statement.
build.code:
class AppError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, message: str, **context: object) -> None:
        super().__init__(message)
        self.context = context

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        base = super().__str__()
        if self.context:
            pairs = ', '.join(
                k + '=' + repr(v) for k, v in self.context.items())
            return base + ' (' + pairs + ')'
        return base

class DataFetchError(AppError): ...
class DataParseError(AppError): ...
class RetryableFetchError(DataFetchError): ...

items.challenge: Add a retryable: bool class attribute (True only on RetryableFetchError) and a tiny should_retry(err: Exception) -> bool helper. Week 2's tenacity policy will call it unchanged.

debugMission.scenario: Production traceback below blames JSON parsing, but the on-call engineer wasted an hour because the REAL root cause is invisible. What was destroyed, and by which line?
hints: The traceback is suspiciously short. Where is the KeyError that triggered the except block?
What does from None do to __cause__ and the printed chain?
Which key was missing? The current error cannot tell you — that is the complaint.
debugMission.solution: from None suppresses exception chaining, discarding the KeyError that would have shown exactly which key was absent and on which line. Change it to except KeyError as err: raise DataParseError(...) from err and the traceback prints the original KeyError followed by 'the direct cause of' your domain error — root cause preserved. Lesson: from err when translating errors, bare raise when passing through, and from None only when deliberately hiding an internal detail you have already logged.

reflection: Which failures in fetch_filings are retryable and which are fatal? Say why in one sentence each.
Why catch narrow low-level exceptions but raise wide domain ones?
done: errors.py hierarchy exists with context support
fetch_filings raises DataFetchError/DataParseError with ticker context, always via from err
You triggered and read all three chained tracebacks
should_retry (or the retryable attribute) classifies the hierarchy

keyConcepts.def: raise NewError(...) from err links the original cause into the traceback; from None severs it.
App-specific error tree (AppError -> fetch/parse) letting callers catch at the layer they can handle.
Design-time classification of failures: transient ones deserve retries, permanent ones must fail fast.
Idiomatic Python: attempt the operation and catch specific failures rather than pre-checking state.

items.title: Debug mission — the silent except
items.concept:
Standalone mission. The report below prints a portfolio total that is quietly wrong — no crash, no warning, just a number smaller than reality. Somewhere, an except Exception: pass is eating the evidence.

Bare (or overly broad) except-and-ignore is a bug factory for three compounding reasons: it catches everything including typos (NameError, AttributeError) you absolutely wanted to see; it destroys the signal at the exact moment you had full context; and the damage surfaces far away — as a wrong total in a report, not an error at the bad row.

Your job: find the swallowed exception, name its type and the offending rows, then rebuild the loop the professional way — catch the NARROW exception you expect, log it with row context, count rejects, and let anything unexpected crash.
items.why: Silently-wrong numbers are the most expensive failure class in data and AI work — a crashed pipeline gets fixed today, a wrong total ships to a client deck. You will meet this exact pattern in real codebases within your first month.
items.challenge: After fixing, add the invariant assert len(valid_rows) + len(rejects) == len(rows) at the end of the loop. Yesterday's quarantine thinking, applied.

debugMission.scenario: Finance says the portfolio report undercounts by roughly the value of the US positions. The script exits 0 every time. Find out why the total is silently wrong and fix the loop properly.
debugMission.artifact:
rows = [
  {'ticker': 'AZN', 'units': 50, 'price': 118.4},
  {'ticker': 'MSFT', 'units': 10, 'value': 4152.0},
  {'ticker': 'SHEL', 'units': 20, 'price': 27.8},
  {'ticker': 'AAPL', 'units': 5, 'value': 1140.0},
]

total = 0.0
for row in rows:
    try:
        total += row['units'] * row['price']
    except Exception:
        pass  # some rows are dodgy, skip them

print('portfolio total:', total)
# prints 2924.0 — finance expected ~8216
hints: Which rows lack a 'price' key? What exception does row['price'] raise for them?
Replace pass with raise for one run — what do you see, and on which rows?
The US rows use a different schema ('value' = units * price already). Skipping them was never the right behaviour — surfacing them was.
debugMission.solution: Rows 2 and 4 carry 'value' instead of 'price'; row['price'] raises KeyError, and except Exception: pass discards both the rows and the evidence, so the total silently excludes the US positions. Fix: catch KeyError only, log the ticker and reason, collect the row into a rejects list, and report both totals and reject count — or better, normalise the two schemas explicitly before summing. General lesson: never swallow; catch the narrowest exception you can name, keep context, and make skipped work visible — an except that ends in pass with no log is a bug by definition.

reflection: Why did this bug surface as a wrong number rather than an error, and which of the two is worse in a client setting?
What is your personal rule now for the width of an except clause?
done: You named the exact exception type and the two offending rows before reading the solution
Fixed loop catches KeyError narrowly, logs context, and counts rejects
Unexpected exception types now crash the script (proven by injecting one)
The count invariant from the challenge holds

keyConcepts.def: except-and-ignore that discards both work and evidence, converting loud failures into quiet data corruption.

items.title: Defensive parsing — junk in, structure out
items.concept:
Real feeds are filthy: blank rows, 'N/A', dates as 2024-03-01 in one row and 01/03/2024 in the next, prices with thousands separators. The professional pattern is **parse -> validate -> quarantine**: normalise what you can, validate with Pydantic, and route failures into a rejects list with a reason — never crash the batch on row 3 of 10,000, and never silently drop (yesterday's lesson).

The shape: robust_parse(rows) returns (valid, rejects). Each reject records the row index, the offending input, and a human-readable reason harvested from the ValidationError. The loop's try covers exactly one row's parse+validate — tight enough that a failure cannot corrupt bookkeeping.

The invariant that makes this trustworthy: every input row lands in exactly one bucket, so len(valid) + len(rejects) == len(input), always. Cheap to assert, priceless in production.
items.why: Every ingestion pipeline you build — filings, tickets, LLM batch outputs — needs this exact function shape. 'How do you handle bad records without losing good ones?' is a stock interview question; this is the answer.

build.task: Build robust_parse(rows) returning (valid, rejects) with per-row rejection reasons over deliberately messy fixture rows.
steps: In filings.py add a Reject dataclass: index: int, row: dict, reason: str — a dataclass, not Pydantic (it is internal; boundary rule)
Write normalise_row(row) handling: strip whitespace, '' and 'N/A' to None, '1,250.50' to '1250.50', and both date formats to ISO
robust_parse(rows: list[dict]) -> tuple[list[Filing], list[Reject]]: per row, try normalise + Filing.model_validate; on ValidationError, build a reason from the first error's loc and msg
Use the messy fixture in code; expect 3 valid, 3 rejected with distinct reasons
Assert the count invariant at the end of the function and log a one-line summary: parsed=3 rejected=3 total=6
build.hint: For mixed dates: try date.fromisoformat first, fall back to datetime.strptime(v, '%d/%m/%Y').date(). Two formats, two attempts, no cleverness.
build.code:
MESSY_ROWS = [
  {'ticker': ' azn ', 'filing_type': '10-K',
   'filed': '2024-03-01', 'currency': 'GBP',
   'amount': '1,250.50'},
  {'ticker': 'MSFT', 'filing_type': '10-Q',
   'filed': '01/03/2024', 'currency': 'USD',
   'amount': '900'},
  {'ticker': '', 'filing_type': '10-K',
   'filed': '2024-01-15', 'currency': 'USD',
   'amount': '10'},
  {'ticker': 'SHEL', 'filing_type': '8-K',
   'filed': '2024-02-20', 'currency': 'EUR',
   'amount': '77.1'},
  {'ticker': 'BP', 'filing_type': '10-K',
   'filed': '2031-12-01', 'currency': 'GBP',
   'amount': '55'},
  {'ticker': 'RIO', 'filing_type': '10-Q',
   'filed': '2024-04-02', 'currency': 'JPY',
   'amount': 'N/A'},
]

items.challenge: Prove the invariant property-style: loop 50 random shuffles and corruptions of MESSY_ROWS (delete keys, inject junk) and assert count(valid) + count(rejects) == count(input) survives every one.

debugMission.scenario: A previous attempt at robust_parse sometimes loses rows entirely — with certain inputs the invariant fails and neither bucket contains the row. Find the structural flaw.
hints: The try block does more than parse and validate. What else can raise in there?
row['note'] raises KeyError for rows without a note — which except clause catches KeyError? None of them.
Wait — a KeyError would crash the function... unless a caller wraps it. Either way, the row never reaches valid.append. What is the minimal try body that makes this impossible?
debugMission.solution: The try body includes the summary line, which raises KeyError on rows lacking 'note' — that is not a ValidationError, so it escapes the except, aborting the loop mid-row (and if some caller swallows it, the row lands in neither bucket). Fix: the try must cover exactly normalise + model_validate; move any post-processing after valid.append, outside the try, and let it operate on the validated model only. General lesson: a quarantine loop is only sound if the guarded region is minimal — every extra statement inside try is a new way to break the invariant.

reflection: Why is Reject a dataclass while Filing is a Pydantic model? Point at the boundary.
done: robust_parse returns 3 valid and 3 rejects on MESSY_ROWS with distinct, human-readable reasons
The count invariant is asserted and holds under the challenge's random corruption
The try block covers only normalise + validate — nothing else
Summary log line prints parsed/rejected/total

keyConcepts.def: Route unparseable records into a rejects collection with reasons instead of crashing the batch or dropping silently.
len(valid) + len(rejects) == len(input) — the cheap assertion proving no record was lost or double-counted.

days.title: Logging and seeing inside your code

items.title: Logging that answers questions
items.concept:
print tells you something happened on your screen, once. Logging records what happened, when, at what severity, from which module — to any destination — and can be filtered after the fact. The levels are a contract: DEBUG (diagnostic detail, off in prod), INFO (normal operations worth an audit trail), WARNING (survivable oddity — a quarantined row), ERROR (an operation failed), CRITICAL (the process cannot continue).

Architecture in two rules. Rule one: modules call logging.getLogger(__name__) and just log — the name gives you per-module filtering for free. Rule two: exactly ONE place configures handlers/format/level — the entrypoint. Records propagate up the dotted-name hierarchy to root, where configuration catches them; that is why libraries never call basicConfig.

Structured logging emits key=value or JSON lines instead of prose, because machines read production logs: duration_ms=182 ticker=AZN is queryable, 'fetched AZN quite fast' is not. Log at boundaries: an input summary on entry, duration and outcome on exit, full context on error (logger.exception inside an except block captures the traceback). Never log secrets, API keys, or full payloads containing PII — SecretStr already helps.
items.why: In every ops incident this quarter — and in every job — logs are the only witness. AI services add cost: Week 4 logs tokens and spend per call through exactly the setup you build today.

learn.focus: Read: Basic Logging Tutorial through the 'Logging from multiple modules' example, plus the level table. Skim 'Configuring Logging'. Skip: the Advanced Tutorial, handler zoo and logging cookbook links.
Read the 'Why structured logging' page for the argument (5 minutes) — you are stealing the philosophy, not adopting the library today.

build.task: Add a configure-once logging module to aie-lab, convert stray prints, and log a timed fetch as structured key=value lines.
steps: Create src/aie_lab/logging_setup.py with configure_logging(level: str = 'INFO', json_mode: bool = False)
Plain mode format: timestamp, level, logger name, message. JSON mode: a JSON object per line (json.dumps in a custom Formatter is fine)
Call configure_logging(settings.log_level) at the top of cli.py main() — and nowhere else
In filings.py: logger = logging.getLogger(__name__); replace any prints; robust_parse logs one WARNING per reject with index and reason
Time fetch_filings with time.perf_counter() and log INFO: fetch complete ticker=AZN rows=6 duration_ms=42
Run once with AIE_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG and once with WARNING — observe what disappears
build.hint: In an except block, logger.exception('fetch failed ticker=%s', ticker) logs at ERROR and appends the traceback automatically — no need to pass the exception object around.

items.challenge: Add duration logging as a context manager: with log_duration(logger, 'fetch', ticker='AZN'): — it logs duration_ms on exit even when the body raises. You will reuse this in the Week 4 LLM client.

debugMission.scenario: Every log line prints twice, and after touching another module it briefly printed three times. The team blames 'a logging bug in Python'. It is not.
debugMission.artifact:
# filings.py
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
handler = logging.StreamHandler()
handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter(
    '%(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s'))
logger.addHandler(handler)

# cli.py main()
logging.basicConfig(
    format='%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s',
    level='INFO')

# output:
# INFO aie_lab.core.filings fetch complete ticker=AZN
# 2026-01-12 09:14:02 INFO fetch complete ticker=AZN
hints: Count the handlers: how many exist, and on which loggers?
A record logged on aie_lab.core.filings is handled by ITS handler, then propagates to root — what happens there?
Note the two lines have different formats — that is the fingerprint telling you two different handlers fired.
debugMission.solution: The module attached its own StreamHandler AND basicConfig attached one to root; every record is emitted by the module handler, then propagates up and is emitted again by root's. The differing formats betray the two sources. Fix: delete all handler setup from filings.py — modules only getLogger(__name__) and log; the entrypoint configures once. Lesson: duplicate log lines always mean duplicate handlers on the propagation path; configure at exactly one place and the problem class disappears.

reflection: Which three fields would you need in every log line to debug a slow fetch six months from now?
Why do libraries never configure logging themselves?
done: configure_logging exists with plain and JSON modes; called only from the entrypoint
No print calls remain in src/ (grep proves it)
A timed fetch logs duration_ms and rejects log as WARNINGs with context
Level switch via AIE_LOG_LEVEL demonstrably filters output

keyConcepts.def: DEBUG/INFO/WARNING/ERROR/CRITICAL — a severity contract that lets one codebase serve dev verbosity and prod signal.
getLogger(__name__) creates dotted-name loggers whose records propagate to root, where the single configuration lives.
key=value or JSON log lines designed for machine querying, not human prose.

items.title: pdb and breakpoint() — stop print-debugging
items.concept:
breakpoint() drops you into pdb at that exact line, with every variable live. The vocabulary that covers 95% of sessions: **n** (next line), **s** (step INTO the call), **c** (continue to next breakpoint), **p expr** (print), **pp** (pretty-print), **w** (where am I — full stack), **u**/**d** (walk up/down frames), **q** (quit). Because you can inspect and even mutate state mid-flight, one session replaces ten edit-add-print-rerun cycles.

Post-mortem is the power move: pytest --pdb opens the debugger at the moment a test fails, frames intact — you interrogate the corpse instead of reproducing the crime. (python -m pdb script.py, then c, does the same for scripts.)

Triage rule you'll refine in reflection: debugger for 'why is THIS run wrong here and now'; logs for 'what happened in prod while I wasn't looking'; tests for 'stop this regressing ever again'. Ship the environment variable knowledge too: PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0 disables stray breakpoint() calls — but grep them out before committing anyway.
items.why: Engineers who can drive a debugger diagnose in minutes what print-debuggers circle for hours — and pytest --pdb plus a stack walk is often the fastest route through unfamiliar client code.

learn.focus: Read: 'Getting Started', 'Printing Expressions', 'Stepping Through Code' and 'Moving Up and Down the Stack' (the u/d section). Skip: breakpoint-condition syntax and the .pdbrc customisation at the end.

build.task: Find the bug in the provided function using ONLY the debugger — adding a print disqualifies the run.
steps: Copy the code below into scratch/debug_me.py; run it and note the wrong output (first window average is off)
Insert breakpoint() at the top of the loop body and run with uv run python scratch/debug_me.py
First iteration: p i, p window, p len(window) — compare what is IN the window against what SHOULD be
Step with n through two iterations watching pp averages grow; state the off-by-one aloud before touching code
Fix, delete breakpoint(), verify the output is [15.0, 25.0, 35.0] for the sample input with window=2
build.hint: The slice prices[i - window:i] for i=0 is prices[-2:0] — an empty-by-way-of-negative-index slice. Watch p prices[i - window:i] say [] while the code believes otherwise.
build.code:
def moving_average(prices: list[float],
                   window: int) -> list[float]:
    averages = []
    for i in range(len(prices) - window + 1):
        chunk = prices[i - window:i]
        averages.append(sum(chunk) / window)
    return averages

print(moving_average([10.0, 20.0, 30.0, 40.0], 2))
# expected [15.0, 25.0, 35.0]
# actual   [0.0, 0.0, 15.0]  — zeros, then one late value

items.challenge: Re-break the function differently (window=0) and use post-mortem instead: let it crash under python -m pdb, then w and p your way to the ZeroDivisionError's context without any breakpoint() call.

debugMission.scenario: A pytest failure's traceback points at a line that is obviously correct — the assert inside spread_bps. Use pytest --pdb and frame-walking to find the real culprit one frame up.
hints: Run pytest --pdb; you land in spread_bps. p bid, p ask — which is bigger, and is that sane?
Type u to move up into quote_report's frame; p ticker, then look hard at the tuple unpacking in the for line.
The fixture stores (ask, bid)... or does it store (bid, ask)? Someone's convention slipped.
debugMission.solution: The debugger shows bid=118.6, ask=118.4 inside spread_bps — swapped. One frame up, the unpacking reads for ticker, (ask, bid) while the test data is written as (bid, ask); the values cross on the way in, and the innocent assert catches it. Fix the unpacking (and encode the lesson properly: a frozen dataclass Quote with named fields instead of a bare tuple — Day 2 already gave you the tool). General lesson: when a traceback points at correct code, the bug is upstream in the arguments; u and p are how you climb to it.

reflection: Debugger, logs, tests: name the last real bug you had and which of the three would have caught it cheapest.
done: Found the moving-average bug without adding a single print; fix verified
Used u/d to diagnose the swapped-arguments failure via pytest --pdb
Can list n/s/c/p/pp/w/u/d from memory with one-line meanings
No breakpoint() calls left anywhere (grep proves it)

keyConcepts.def: Built-in that opens pdb at that line; disable stray ones with PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0.
Opening the debugger on the frames of an already-raised exception, e.g. pytest --pdb at a failure.
u/d movement through the call stack to inspect the arguments and locals of callers when the crash site looks innocent.

items.title: Mini-project — Market Snapshot CLI
items.concept:
Assembly day. Everything from the week becomes one coherent tool: a typer CLI command snapshot that reads a JSON fixture of instruments, validates each with Pydantic, quarantines the corrupt ones, filters by exchange/currency flags, computes summary statistics, and writes both a human-readable report and a machine-readable JSON file — with Settings for paths, your exception hierarchy for failures, and logging throughout.

typer is FastAPI's CLI sibling: you write a typed function, decorate it, and flags fall out of the signature — snapshot(exchange: str | None = None) gives you --exchange for free. Same type-driven philosophy you have used all week.

The fixture below is deliberately 20% corrupt (a negative price, a bad currency, a missing field, a price as 'N/A'). Your quarantine pattern means the tool reports them and carries on — corrupt data is a WARNING and a rejects section, never a crash.
items.why: This repo section is the first thing you can show a hiring manager: structure, types, validation, errors, logging, CLI — one artefact proving all of it. Every later project (LLM clients, RAG tools) is this skeleton with a different core.

learn.focus: Read: First Steps, then follow the links to the CLI Arguments and CLI Options pages — enough for one command with optional flags. Skip: subcommands, callbacks, colours and shell completion.

build.task: Ship the snapshot CLI end-to-end: validated fixture in, filtered stats and two report files out, corrupt rows quarantined.
steps: Milestone 1 — data: save the fixture below as data/instruments.json; uv add typer; extend Settings with data_path and output_dir (env-overridable, sensible defaults)

Milestone 2 — model: Instrument(ticker, name, exchange Literal['LSE','NYSE','XETRA'], currency Literal['GBP','USD','EUR'], price float gt=0) plus robust_load(path) -> (valid, rejects) reusing the Day-4 quarantine shape; wrap file errors in DataFetchError
Milestone 3 — CLI: typer command snapshot(exchange: str | None = None, currency: str | None = None); wire the console script snapshot = 'aie_lab.cli:app'; configure logging first thing
Milestone 4 — stats: for the filtered set compute count, min/max/mean price, and per-exchange counts; log duration_ms for load+parse
Milestone 5 — output: write report.txt (aligned columns, stats footer, rejects section with reasons) and snapshot.json (model_dump of instruments + stats + rejects) into output_dir

Milestone 6 — resilience: run against a copy of the fixture with 2 rows mangled further — exit code 0, rejects reported; then point data_path at a missing file — clean DataFetchError message, no raw traceback
Milestone 7 — quality gate: uv run mypy src clean; no prints; commit

items.title: Ship it — README and tag v0.1.0
items.concept:
A README is the interface to your work; most readers never open src/. Minimum professional shape: one-sentence what-it-is, install (two commands: clone, uv sync), usage (a real command and its real output, pasted), and — the habit that marks seniority — a short **Design decisions** paragraph: why src layout, why quarantine instead of crash, why Settings over hardcoded paths.

Tags mark releases: git tag -a v0.1.0 -m 'Market Snapshot CLI' creates an annotated tag; git push --tags publishes it. From now on, every mini-project ends with a tag — it turns 'a repo I poked at' into 'a thing I shipped, versioned'.
items.why: Consultants and interviewers read READMEs, not code, first. A design-decisions paragraph signals judgement — the thing they are actually hiring.

items.title: Extension — cache layer and output formats
items.concept:
Two small-but-real features. First, a file cache: hash the query (the filter flags that define it) into a key, store the computed snapshot as .cache/<key>.json with a saved_at timestamp, and serve from cache when a fresh-enough entry exists. The two eternal cache problems appear immediately in miniature: **key design** (the key must include EVERYTHING that changes the result — forget currency in the key and --currency USD serves GBP data from cache) and **invalidation** (TTL answers 'how stale is acceptable', here ttl_s=300).

Second, output formats: --format json|table|md via an Enum flag. Same data, three renderers — which forces the healthy separation of computing a snapshot from presenting one. The md renderer is a markdown table you can paste straight into a client doc.
items.why: Caching LLM responses is a Week 5 cost lever worth real money; the key-design and TTL instincts transfer unchanged. Renderer separation is the same discipline as API response models in Week 3.

build.task: Add a TTL file cache keyed on the query and a --format flag with json, table and md renderers.
steps: cache.py: cache_key(exchange, currency, min_price, max_price) -> sha256 hex of a canonical 'exchange=LSE|currency=None|...' string — canonical means identical queries hash identically
cache_get(key, ttl_s=300) -> Snapshot | None checking saved_at age; cache_put(key, snapshot) writing atomically (write .tmp, then os.replace)
Wire into build_snapshot: on hit log cache=hit and skip load+parse; on miss compute and store; add --no-cache to bypass
OutputFormat(str, Enum) with json/table/md; snapshot(--format) selects render_json / render_table / render_md — three pure functions taking the same Snapshot
Prove the cache: run twice with identical flags (second logs cache=hit, visibly faster), then change one flag and confirm a miss
Prove the key: temporarily drop currency from cache_key, demonstrate the wrong-data bug with --currency USD after a GBP run, then restore it — now you have SEEN a cache-key bug
build.hint: Serialise Snapshot with model_dump_json for the cache; on read, Snapshot.model_validate_json — your boundary tools work on your own files too.

items.title: Week 1 review — explain it aloud
items.concept:
Thirty minutes, spoken aloud, every tab and resource closed. Walking about while you talk is not optional decoration — it is what keeps this from becoming silent rereading, which feels like revision and is not.

- **Re-read Monday's code first.** Open src/aie_lab/ and read w1d1's scaffolding with six days of hindsight. Say out loud what you would now do differently. Five minutes, no editing.
- **Explain Pydantic to an imaginary PM** in two sentences with no jargon. If you hear the word 'serialisation', start again from 'the data arriving from outside is a rumour until something checks it'.
- **Re-explain raise ... from err.** Say what the traceback shows with it, what it shows with from None, and which of your own errors in errors.py would be undebuggable if you got this wrong.
- **Recite the boundary rule**: Pydantic at the edges, dataclasses inside. Then name one place in the Market Snapshot CLI where you had to decide, and defend the call you made.
- **Narrate the snapshot run end to end**: Settings loads, logging configures once, the fixture parses, three rows get quarantined with reasons, the stats compute, two files are written. Where does each week-1 topic appear in that sentence?
- **Mark two need-revision items** in your notes — the two explanations that came out worst. They become next Monday's warm-up.
items.why: Everything you get paid to do with this material is spoken: standups, client calls, interviews, whiteboards. An explanation that only works with the file open is recognition, not knowledge.
reflection: Which explanation collapsed without notes — and was that a gap in understanding or just a gap in fluency?
If a client handed you a new Python repo tomorrow, which two week-1 checks would you run before reading any logic?
done: Monday's code re-read and one concrete would-do-differently stated aloud
Pydantic explained to a hypothetical PM in two jargon-free sentences

Two weakest concepts written down as need-revision

items.title: Week 1 quiz
items.concept: Take the Week 1 quiz. It tests judgement rather than syntax recall: which tool to reach for, which structure catches which class of bug, and what each failure mode looks like from the outside. Treat a wrong answer as a debugging lead — trace it back to the day it came from, re-explain that idea aloud, and only then move on.
items.why: The quiz converts a week of doing into a week of retrieval, which is what actually survives to Week 5 when this scaffolding has to hold an LLM service up.
reflection: Which wrong answer surprised you most, and which file are you going to reopen because of it?
done: Quiz completed in one sitting without looking anything up
Score at or above 70%, or every miss re-explained aloud after reading the explanation

questions.q: A teammate asks what actually changes when you swap pip + venv for uv. Which answer describes the mental model rather than the marketing?
options: uv is a faster pip, so the same install-into-the-active-environment habits carry over unchanged
You stop installing into whatever environment is active and instead declare dependencies in pyproject.toml, pin them in uv.lock, and let uv run guarantee the environment matches
uv replaces pyproject.toml with its own manifest format, so packaging metadata lives in uv.lock
uv installs packages globally and isolates them at import time
questions.explain: Speed is the smallest part. The shift is declarative: pyproject.toml states intent, uv.lock pins the whole transitive tree, and uv run syncs before executing — so 'works on my machine' stops being a sentence anyone needs to say. pyproject.toml stays the manifest; uv.lock sits beside it and is committed.

questions.q: You move aie_lab from the repo root into src/aie_lab/. What class of bug does that actually catch?
options: Circular imports between submodules
Type errors that mypy would otherwise miss
Packaging bugs — with a flat layout the repo root is on sys.path, so tests import your source tree directly and never notice a module missing from the built distribution
Name collisions between your package and installed third-party packages
questions.explain: src layout makes the installed package the only importable copy, so your tests exercise what users will actually get. A file you forgot to include in the distribution fails immediately instead of at someone else's install.

questions.q: Inside the snapshot pipeline you need a small internal record type to carry a rejected row and its reason between two of your own functions. Dataclass or Pydantic model?
options: Pydantic — validation is always safer, at any layer
Dataclass — the data has already crossed the boundary and been checked; re-validating internal objects costs runtime for no new guarantee
Dataclass, but only because Pydantic cannot express a reason string
Neither — a plain dict keeps it flexible
questions.explain: Validate once at the edge, then trust your types inside. Pydantic earns its cost where untrusted data arrives (files, HTTP, LLM output); internal structs want a dataclass, which is free and gives you the same autocomplete and repr.

questions.q: You added a field_validator to normalise ticker case, but tickers still arrive lowercase and no error is ever raised. Most likely cause?
options: Pydantic v2 removed field_validator, so the decorator silently does nothing
The validator is attached to a field name that does not exist on the model (or sits on the wrong class), so it never runs at all
model_validate skips validators; only model_validate_json runs them
Validators only fire when a field is missing from the input
questions.explain: A validator naming a field the model does not define is the classic silent no-op — Pydantic raises at class definition for genuinely unknown fields, but a validator sitting on a sibling class or shadowed by an inherited definition simply never fires. Also remember field_validator wants @classmethod under it. Confirm quickly by raising inside the validator: if nothing blows up, it is not wired to that field.

questions.q: The snapshot run quarantines three corrupt fixture rows and completes successfully. What level do those three log lines belong at?
options: DEBUG — they are diagnostic detail, not operational news
INFO — the run succeeded, so nothing is wrong
WARNING — the batch survived, but a human should know some input was unusable
ERROR — data was lost
questions.explain: WARNING is exactly the survivable-oddity level: the operation completed, but a person reading logs at INFO-and-above should still see it. ERROR is reserved for an operation that failed; a spike in quarantine WARNINGs is your early signal that an upstream feed changed.

questions.q: Which combination handles the API key correctly for a repo that will be pushed to GitHub?
options: A default value in the Settings class so the app runs out of the box, with the real key committed to a config.py that is gitignored
api_key: SecretStr with no default, loaded from a .env file that is gitignored, so a missing key fails fast at startup with a clear message
os.environ.get('AIE_API_KEY', '') read at each call site, defaulting to empty so nothing crashes
The key in .env, .env committed so teammates can run it, and the key rotated weekly
questions.explain: No default means the process refuses to start rather than failing mysteriously three layers down at the first call; SecretStr keeps the value out of logs and reprs; .env stays local and gitignored. A silently-empty default is the worst of the four — it turns a config error into an authentication error at runtime.

questions.q: Someone translates a KeyError into your DataParseError using raise DataParseError('bad payload shape') from None. Why is the reviewer unhappy, and what should the line be?
questions.answer: from None suppresses the chain, so the traceback shows only the domain error and throws away the KeyError that named the exact missing key and line — the one fact you need at 2am. Use except KeyError as err: raise DataParseError('bad payload shape', ticker=ticker) from err, which keeps the original as the direct cause while still giving callers a domain error to catch. Rule of thumb: from err when translating, bare raise when passing through, from None only to hide an internal detail you have already logged.

questions.q: A nightly batch job reports success every night, but the totals it produces are quietly about 8% low. The only suspicious code is try: ... except Exception: pass wrapped around the per-row loop body. Explain the failure mechanism and the fix.
questions.answer: The bare except swallows a real bug — a KeyError on rows whose shape changed upstream — so those rows are skipped without a trace and the totals silently shrink; the job exits 0 because nothing ever propagated. Silent failure is worse than a crash: a crash gets fixed the same day, this gets discovered a quarter later by a client. Fix by catching narrowly (only the exception you can actually handle), logging every skipped row with its index and reason, routing it into a rejects list, and re-raising anything unexpected as a domain error. The count invariant, valid plus rejects equals input, is what makes the loss impossible to hide.

title: Prove It Works
objective: Test code properly (including HTTP), understand async, and use a resilient HTTP client — with a professional git workflow.
narrative: Week 1 gave you structure; week 2 gives you confidence. Tests are how you refactor without fear, and async plus retries are how Python talks to the network like a grown-up. Every LLM app you build later is 'just' HTTP + async + validation, so the muscle you build this week is the one you use every remaining week.
whatYouCanBuild: A tested, retrying, concurrent HTTP data fetcher — the exact skeleton of every LLM client you'll ever write.
whyProfessionally: AI engineering interviews probe testing and async more than ML math. 'How would you test this?' is a guaranteed question.

items.title: pytest fundamentals and fixtures
items.concept:
pytest finds tests by convention: files matching test_*.py, functions starting with test_, classes named Test* (no __init__). Put them in a tests/ directory that mirrors src/ — tests/core/test_market.py tests src/aie_lab/core/market.py — so 'where is the test for this?' is never a question.

You write plain assert statements. pytest rewrites them at import time so a failure prints both sides of the comparison, including diffs for dicts and lists. That means no assertEquals vocabulary to memorise: **assert parse_price('N/A') is None** is the whole API. For expected failures, use **with pytest.raises(DataParseError) as exc:** and then assert on the message or context.

**Fixtures are dependency injection for tests.** A function decorated with @pytest.fixture returns (or yields) a value; any test that names it as a parameter receives it. Built-ins you get free: **tmp_path** (a fresh Path per test — never write to the repo), **capsys** (captures stdout/stderr), **monkeypatch** (tomorrow's topic). Shared fixtures live in tests/conftest.py, which pytest imports automatically for everything below it — no imports needed.

**Scope is where the danger lives.** Default scope is 'function': a new object per test, total isolation. scope='module' or 'session' builds the object once and shares it — fast, and a trap the moment the object is mutable. Yield fixtures give you teardown: everything after the yield runs when the scope ends.

Test behaviours, not lines. For the Week-1 CLI that means: a valid row parses to the right model, a corrupt row lands in rejects with a reason, filtering by exchange excludes others, stats over a known set produce known numbers. Coverage percentage is a weak proxy; a test per behaviour you'd hate to break is the real target.
items.why: You cannot refactor an LLM pipeline you're afraid of, and everything after Week 4 is refactoring under uncertainty. Tests are also the fastest way for a reviewer to judge you: they show what you think the contract is.

learn.focus: Read all of it: Install, Create your first test, Run multiple tests, 'Assert that a certain exception is raised', Group multiple tests in a class, and 'Request a unique temporary directory'. It is 15 minutes.

Read: 'What fixtures are', 'Requesting fixtures', 'Fixtures can request other fixtures', conftest.py, 'Fixture scopes', and 'Teardown/Cleanup (yield fixtures)'. Skip: fixture-availability internals, factories-as-fixtures and parametrized fixtures for now.

build.task: Write a real test suite for the Week-1 snapshot CLI core: parsing, filtering, quarantine and stats.
steps: Create tests/ mirroring src/aie_lab/ (tests/core/test_market.py, tests/core/test_snapshot.py); confirm discovery with: uv run pytest --collect-only
conftest.py: a fixture sample_rows returning 4 dicts (3 valid, 1 with price 'N/A') and a fixture written_fixture(tmp_path) that writes them to a JSON file and returns the path
Behaviour tests for robust_load: valid rows become Instrument models; the bad row lands in rejects with a reason mentioning price
Behaviour test for filtering: build_snapshot(..., exchange='LSE') returns only LSE instruments — assert on tickers, not counts alone
Stats test: over a known 3-row set assert mean/min/max exactly (use pytest.approx for floats)
Error test: point the loader at tmp_path / 'missing.json' and assert pytest.raises(DataFetchError) with the ticker or path in the message
Run uv run pytest -q, then uv run pytest -x -vv on a deliberately broken assertion to see the diff output pytest gives you
build.hint: If pytest cannot import aie_lab, you did not need to add sys.path hacks — uv sync installed the package, so run tests with uv run pytest and let the src layout do its job.
build.code:
# tests/conftest.py
import json
import pytest

@pytest.fixture
def sample_rows() -> list[dict]:
    return [
        {'ticker': 'AZN', 'name': 'AstraZeneca', 'exchange': 'LSE',
         'currency': 'GBP', 'price': 118.42},
        {'ticker': 'SHEL', 'name': 'Shell', 'exchange': 'LSE',
         'currency': 'GBP', 'price': 27.85},
        {'ticker': 'MSFT', 'name': 'Microsoft', 'exchange': 'NYSE',
         'currency': 'USD', 'price': 415.2},
        {'ticker': 'NOPE', 'name': 'Missing Price plc', 'exchange': 'LSE',
         'currency': 'GBP', 'price': 'N/A'},
    ]

@pytest.fixture
def written_fixture(tmp_path, sample_rows):
    path = tmp_path / 'instruments.json'
    path.write_text(json.dumps(sample_rows), encoding='utf-8')
    return path

# tests/core/test_snapshot.py
def test_bad_row_is_quarantined(written_fixture):
    valid, rejects = robust_load(written_fixture)
    assert [i.ticker for i in valid] == ['AZN', 'SHEL', 'MSFT']
    assert len(rejects) == 1
    assert 'price' in rejects[0].reason

items.challenge: Add an invariant test: for any sample file, len(valid) + len(rejects) == len(rows). Then break robust_load deliberately (drop a row on a parse error) and watch the invariant catch it — that is what a good test feels like.

debugMission.scenario: A new test passes when run alone and fails when the suite runs. The engineer has re-run it six times and started muttering about 'flaky pytest'. It is not flaky; it is shared state.
debugMission.artifact:
# tests/conftest.py
@pytest.fixture(scope='module')
def loaded():
    valid, rejects = robust_load(FIXTURE)
