    return valid

# tests/core/test_filters.py
def test_lse_filter(loaded):
    lse = [i for i in loaded if i.exchange == 'LSE']
    assert len(lse) == 2

def test_sorting_is_in_place(loaded):
    loaded.sort(key=lambda i: i.price)
    assert loaded[0].ticker == 'SHEL'

$ uv run pytest tests/core/test_filters.py::test_lse_filter -q
1 passed
$ uv run pytest -q
.F                                              [100%]
E  assert 'MSFT' == 'SHEL'   (test_sorting_is_in_place)
# ... and on a re-ordered run, test_lse_filter fails instead
hints: Run the suite with -p no:randomly (or reverse the file order) and see which test fails change. Order dependence means shared state.
The fixture is scope='module': how many times does robust_load actually run for these two tests?
Which test mutates the object it was handed?
debugMission.solution: The module-scoped fixture builds the list once and hands the SAME object to every test in the file; test_sorting_is_in_place sorts it in place, so whichever test runs afterwards sees a re-ordered list. Fix: drop to the default function scope (cheap here), or keep the scope and have the test copy — sorted(loaded) rather than loaded.sort(). General lesson: a wide fixture scope is a performance optimisation that trades away isolation. Only widen scope for genuinely immutable or externally-managed resources (a started container, a read-only file), and treat 'passes alone, fails in suite' as proof of shared mutable state until disproved.

reflection: Which three behaviours of your Week-1 CLI would you be most upset to break silently? Do they each have a test?
When is a session-scoped fixture the right call rather than a landmine?
done: tests/ mirrors src/ and uv run pytest -q passes with at least 8 tests
A quarantine test asserts both the valid tickers and the rejection reason
One test uses tmp_path and one uses pytest.raises with a domain exception
You reproduced the pass-alone/fail-in-suite bug and fixed it via scope or copying

keyConcepts.def: A pytest function whose return value is injected into any test that names it as a parameter; yield fixtures also run teardown.
How long a fixture's value is reused (function/class/module/session); wider scope trades isolation for speed.
Auto-imported file holding fixtures shared by every test in its directory and below — no import statement needed.
pytest rewrites plain assert statements so failures show both sides of the comparison with a diff.

items.title: Parametrize the edges
items.concept:
Copy-pasting a test five times with different inputs is how edge cases get skipped. **@pytest.mark.parametrize('raw,expected', [...])** turns one test body into N independent test cases: each gets its own pass/fail, its own traceback, and its own line in the report.

The value is not brevity, it is that the parameter list becomes a visible **edge table** you can review like a spec. Force yourself down the standard axes for every input: empty, whitespace-only, huge, unicode and accents, negative, zero, boundary-minus-one and boundary, wrong type, and the sentinel junk your domain actually emits ('N/A', 'null', '-', '')

**ids=** gives each case a readable name so failures read as test_parse[whitespace] rather than test_parse[raw3-None]. Stacking two parametrize decorators multiplies the cases (3 x 4 = 12 runs) — occasionally useful, frequently a way to produce 200 slow tests nobody reads.

For cases that must raise, either add a separate parametrized test using pytest.raises, or put the expectation in the table with pytest.param(..., marks=pytest.mark.xfail) — but a plain second test is usually clearer.

The habit worth building: when a bug is reported, add the failing input as a new row in the table FIRST, watch it fail, then fix the code. That is test-first without the ceremony.
items.why: Data and LLM pipelines fail at the edges — the empty string, the 40k-token document, the unicode dash from a client's Word export. A parametrized edge table is the cheapest insurance you can write.

learn.focus: Read the whole page: the basic decorator, 'Mark a test as expected to fail', stacking parametrize marks, and the ids section. Skip: pytest_generate_tests and the indirect-parametrization hook at the end.

build.task: Write a parametrized test table of 8 nasty inputs for the Week-1 robust_parse/price parsing, with readable ids.
steps: Build the table for parse_price: '101.5', ' 101.5 ', '', '   ', 'N/A', '-', '1e3', '1,234.50' — decide the correct expected value for each BEFORE running anything
Add ids=['plain','padded','empty','whitespace','na','dash','scientific','thousands-separator']
Run uv run pytest -q and read which cases fail — the thousands separator almost certainly does
Decide deliberately: is '1,234.50' valid input for your domain? Write the answer as a comment, then make code and table agree
Add a second parametrized test for whole rows: missing key, price as a bool, unicode ticker 'AZN\u00a0' (non-breaking space), 40k-character name
Run uv run pytest -q -k parse to see the id list, and confirm every case name reads as English
build.hint: float('1e3') is 1000.0 and float(' 101.5 ') works because float() strips whitespace — surprises like these are exactly why the table exists rather than your intuition.
build.code:
import pytest
from aie_lab.core.market import parse_price

@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    'raw,expected',
    [
        ('101.5', 101.5),
        (' 101.5 ', 101.5),
        ('', None),
        ('   ', None),
        ('N/A', None),
        ('-', None),
        ('1e3', 1000.0),
        ('1,234.50', None),
    ],
    ids=['plain', 'padded', 'empty', 'whitespace',
         'na', 'dash', 'scientific', 'thousands-separator'],
)
def test_parse_price(raw: str, expected: float | None) -> None:
    assert parse_price(raw) == expected

@pytest.mark.parametrize('bad', [None, True, 42, ['101.5']])
def test_parse_price_rejects_non_strings(bad: object) -> None:
    with pytest.raises((TypeError, AttributeError)):
        parse_price(bad)  # type: ignore[arg-type]

items.challenge: Add one case that reveals a genuine bug in your parser (the non-breaking space in a ticker is a good candidate — .strip() does not remove \u00a0 in every context you think it does). Watch it fail, fix the code, keep the row forever.

debugMission.scenario: A parametrized suite of 6 cases passes on the developer's machine and fails on CI with case 5 red. Re-running only case 5 passes. The team blames CI.
debugMission.artifact:
ROWS = [
    {'ticker': 'AZN', 'price': 118.42},
    {'ticker': 'SHEL', 'price': 27.85},
]

def normalise(rows: list[dict]) -> list[dict]:
    for row in rows:
        row['ticker'] = row['ticker'].upper()
        row['price'] = round(row['price'], 1)  # in-place
    return rows

@pytest.mark.parametrize('precision', [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])
def test_precision_preserved(precision: int) -> None:
    out = normalise(ROWS)
    assert out[0]['price'] == round(118.42, precision)

# CI output
# test_precision_preserved[1] PASSED
# test_precision_preserved[2] FAILED  assert 118.4 == 118.42
# test_precision_preserved[3] FAILED  assert 118.4 == 118.42
hints: Print ROWS at the start and end of the first case. Is it the same data the second case receives?
normalise says 'in-place' in a comment. What does that do to a module-level list shared by every case?
Why does running case 5 alone pass?
debugMission.solution: ROWS is a single module-level list of dicts, and normalise mutates it in place, so case 1 rounds the price to 118.4 permanently and every later case sees corrupted input. Running one case alone re-imports fresh data, which is why it 'passes on my machine'. Fix either end: build the input inside a function-scoped fixture (or a factory) so each case gets fresh data, and make normalise return new dicts instead of mutating its argument. General lesson: parametrized cases share module state, so shared mutable literals plus in-place functions produce order-dependent failures — the same class of bug as yesterday's fixture scope, wearing a different hat.

reflection: Which edge axis (empty, huge, unicode, boundary, wrong type) do you skip most often, and what did it cost you last time?
done: A parametrized test with 8 cases and readable ids runs green
At least one case initially failed and was resolved by a deliberate decision recorded in code or comment
A second parametrized test covers non-string input via pytest.raises
You can explain why the shared-mutable-ROWS suite failed only in order

keyConcepts.def: Decorator that expands one test body into independent cases from a table of inputs and expected values.
The deliberate list of boundary inputs (empty, huge, unicode, negative, sentinel junk) a function must survive.
Human-readable names for parametrized cases so failure output names the scenario, not an index.

items.title: Mocking and monkeypatch
items.concept:
Tests must be deterministic, fast and offline. Three things break that: the clock, the environment, and the network. Test doubles replace them with something you control.

**monkeypatch** is pytest's built-in, and its superpower is automatic undo at the end of the test. The four verbs you need: **monkeypatch.setattr(target, value)** replaces an attribute (a function, a constant, a method), **monkeypatch.setenv / delenv** control environment variables, **monkeypatch.setitem** patches dict entries, and **monkeypatch.chdir** moves the working directory. Nothing leaks into the next test.

**unittest.mock.Mock** is for when you need to record calls, not just replace behaviour. A Mock returns a new Mock for any attribute you touch — convenient and dangerous, because a typo like mock.assert_call_once() silently passes (it just creates an attribute). Two defences: **spec=RealClass** so unknown attributes raise AttributeError, and **autospec** when patching. Use **return_value** for a fixed answer and **side_effect** for a sequence of answers or an exception to raise.

**The over-mocking trap.** If you mock every collaborator, your test asserts that your code calls the mocks you told it to call — a tautology that passes while production burns. Rule of thumb: mock at the process boundary (clock, network, filesystem, randomness, third-party SDK), never your own pure functions. If mocking feels unavoidable in the middle of your code, that is a design signal: extract the impure part and pass it in.

**The patch-path rule, which you will get wrong at least once: patch where the name is looked up, not where it is defined.** If report.py does 'from market import fetch_price', it binds its own reference at import time, so patching market.fetch_price changes nothing report can see. Patch report.fetch_price. The alternative that sidesteps the whole issue: import the module ('from aie_lab.core import market') and call market.fetch_price() so the lookup happens at call time.
items.why: Every LLM test you write from Week 4 onwards is a mocked SDK call plus a fixture response. Getting doubles right today is why your Week 4 suite runs offline in two seconds instead of costing money per run.

learn.focus: Read: 'Simple example: monkeypatching functions', 'Monkeypatching returned objects: building mock classes', 'Global patch example: preventing requests from remote operations', and 'Monkeypatching environment variables'. Skip: the dictionary-patching section on first pass.

build.task: Test time-dependent and environment-dependent code with a fake clock and patched env vars.
steps: Take the Week-1 cache: cache_get(key, ttl_s=300) decides freshness from saved_at versus time.time()
Write a fake_clock fixture: a small class with .now attribute and a .tick(seconds) method; monkeypatch time.time to fake_clock.now
Test 1: write an entry, advance 299 seconds, assert a cache hit. Test 2: advance 301 seconds, assert a miss. No sleeping, no flakiness
Use monkeypatch.setenv('AIE_LOG_LEVEL', 'DEBUG') and assert Settings() picks it up; then monkeypatch.delenv('AIE_API_KEY', raising=False) and assert the ValidationError fires
Replace one collaborator with Mock(spec=FilingsClient) and assert client.get_company.assert_called_once_with('AZN')
Deliberately mistype it as assert_called_once_wtih and confirm it still 'passes' — then add spec= and watch the typo raise
build.hint: Patch the name your code actually calls: if your cache module does 'import time' and calls time.time(), patch 'time.time'; if it does 'from time import time', patch 'aie_lab.core.cache.time'.

items.challenge: Write a no_network fixture in conftest.py that monkeypatches httpx.Client.send to raise RuntimeError('network access in a unit test'), and apply it with autouse=True. Any test that accidentally reaches the internet now fails loudly rather than slowly.

debugMission.scenario: The suite is green and has been for weeks, but the daily report has been printing stale prices in production since Tuesday. Someone notices the unit test takes 3.4 seconds. Find why the mock never took effect.
debugMission.artifact:
# src/aie_lab/core/report.py
from aie_lab.core.market import fetch_price

def daily_line(ticker: str) -> str:
    return ticker + ' @ ' + str(fetch_price(ticker))

# tests/core/test_report.py
from aie_lab.core.report import daily_line

def test_daily_line(monkeypatch):
    calls = []

    def fake_fetch(ticker: str) -> float:
        calls.append(ticker)
        return 100.0

    monkeypatch.setattr(
        'aie_lab.core.market.fetch_price', fake_fetch)
    line = daily_line('AZN')
    assert 'AZN' in line

$ uv run pytest tests/core/test_report.py -q
.                                        [100%]
1 passed in 3.41s
hints: 3.41 seconds for one string-formatting test. What is it actually doing during those seconds?
Add a call-count assertion to the end of the test: assert calls == ['AZN']. Does the fake ever run?
report.py did 'from ... import fetch_price' at import time. Which module's namespace holds the name that daily_line calls?
debugMission.solution: The from-import copied fetch_price into report.py's namespace when report was first imported, so report.fetch_price and market.fetch_price are two independent references to the same function object. Patching market.fetch_price rebinds only the market module's name; daily_line still calls its own copy — the real one, over the network, which is where the 3.4 seconds and the stale production data came from. The assertion 'AZN' in line was weak enough to pass either way. Fix: monkeypatch.setattr('aie_lab.core.report.fetch_price', fake_fetch), or change report.py to 'from aie_lab.core import market' and call market.fetch_price(ticker) so the lookup resolves at call time. General lesson: patch where the name is looked up, not where it is defined — and always assert the double was actually used (call count), so a mis-patched test fails instead of quietly hitting production.

reflection: Where is the boundary in your own code between 'worth mocking' and 'testing the mock'?
How would you have caught the mis-patched test before it reached production?
done: A fake-clock fixture makes two TTL tests deterministic with no sleeps
Env-var tests cover both a set value and a missing required value
You reproduced the wrong-patch-path bug, saw the call-count assertion fail, and fixed the patch target
At least one Mock uses spec= and you demonstrated the typo-assertion trap

keyConcepts.def: pytest fixture that sets attributes, env vars or dict items for the duration of one test and undoes them automatically.
Patch the name in the module that calls it, because from-imports bind their own reference at import time.
Constrains a Mock to a real object's attributes so typos and non-existent methods raise instead of silently passing.
Mocking your own logic until the test only verifies that mocks were called — green tests, broken production.

items.title: Testing HTTP without the internet
items.concept:
Hand-rolled mocks for HTTP are miserable: you end up faking response objects, status codes, headers and json() methods. **respx** replaces httpx's transport layer instead, so your code makes an ordinary httpx call and respx decides what comes back. Your client code is not modified or aware.

Usage has two shapes: the **@respx.mock** decorator (or 'with respx.mock:' block) around a test, and routes registered inside it. A route is matched by method plus patterns — respx.get(host='api.example.dev', path='/companies/AZN') — and mocked with **.mock(return_value=httpx.Response(200, json={...}))**. Matching by host and path rather than a full URL string keeps tests readable when the base URL comes from Settings.

**Failures are the point.** side_effect=httpx.TimeoutException('read timeout') makes the call raise as a real timeout would; side_effect=[Response(500), Response(500), Response(200)] returns a different response per call, which is exactly how you will prove tomorrow's retry policy works. Errors you want to cover for any fetch function: 200 happy path, 404 (fatal), 500 (retryable), timeout (retryable), and malformed JSON body (parse failure, not network failure).

**Assert on the request, not just the response.** route.called, route.call_count, and route.calls.last.request let you check the URL, headers and body your client actually sent — including whether the API key header went out. A test that only asserts the parsed result cannot tell you that your client silently dropped authentication.

Finally: respx.mock(assert_all_called=True) fails a test whose registered routes were never hit, which catches 'my client called a different endpoint than I thought'.
items.why: Every network-dependent test you write for the rest of the quarter — filings APIs in Week 2, LLM endpoints in Week 4, vector stores later — uses this pattern. Offline, deterministic, sub-second tests are what make a CI pipeline usable.

learn.focus: Read: Getting Started (decorator vs context manager), 'Mock HTTPX' router basics, Routing (method/host/path patterns and route.calls), and Mocking Responses (return_value, side_effect). Skip: the pass-through and ASGI/WSGI app sections.

build.task: Write a respx test suite covering 200, 404, 500 and timeout paths for a small filings fetch function.
steps: uv add --dev respx; write fetch_company(client: httpx.Client, ticker: str) -> Company that GETs /companies/{ticker}, calls raise_for_status(), and validates the JSON with your Week-1 Pydantic model
Map failures to your Week-1 taxonomy: 404 -> DataFetchError (fatal), 5xx/timeout -> RetryableFetchError, bad JSON or schema -> DataParseError, all with raise ... from err
Test 200: route returns a valid company payload; assert the model fields and that route.call_count == 1
Test 404: assert pytest.raises(DataFetchError) and that RetryableFetchError is NOT what comes out (the distinction matters tomorrow)
Test 500 and timeout: side_effect=httpx.TimeoutException for the latter; assert RetryableFetchError both times
Test the request: assert route.calls.last.request.headers['x-api-key'] carries the key from Settings
Add one malformed-payload test (JSON missing 'ticker') asserting DataParseError, and run the suite with the network cable metaphorically cut: uv run pytest -q should take under a second
build.hint: respx matches on what your client actually sends. If a route never fires, print route.calls or set assert_all_called=True — nine times in ten the base_url has a trailing slash and the path has a leading one, producing a double slash.
build.code:
import httpx
import pytest
import respx

HOST = 'api.example.dev'

@respx.mock
def test_fetch_company_ok(client: httpx.Client) -> None:
    route = respx.get(host=HOST, path='/companies/AZN').mock(
        return_value=httpx.Response(
            200, json={'ticker': 'AZN', 'name': 'AstraZeneca',
                       'exchange': 'LSE'}))
    company = fetch_company(client, 'AZN')
    assert company.name == 'AstraZeneca'
    assert route.call_count == 1

@respx.mock
def test_fetch_company_404_is_fatal(client: httpx.Client) -> None:
    respx.get(host=HOST, path='/companies/NOPE').mock(
        return_value=httpx.Response(404, json={'detail': 'not found'}))
    with pytest.raises(DataFetchError) as err:
        fetch_company(client, 'NOPE')
    assert not isinstance(err.value, RetryableFetchError)

@respx.mock
def test_fetch_company_timeout_is_retryable(client: httpx.Client) -> None:
    respx.get(host=HOST, path='/companies/AZN').mock(
        side_effect=httpx.TimeoutException('read timeout'))
    with pytest.raises(RetryableFetchError):
        fetch_company(client, 'AZN')

items.challenge: Add a test proving your client sends no Authorization header when Settings has no key, and one proving a 429 response is classified retryable while a 400 is not. Two lines each; they encode a policy you would otherwise only have in your head.

debugMission.scenario: A respx test fails with httpx.ConnectError even though a route is registered for exactly the endpoint under test. The engineer is convinced respx is broken.
debugMission.artifact:
@respx.mock
def test_list_filings():
    route = respx.get(
        host='api.example.dev', path='/filings').mock(
        return_value=httpx.Response(200, json={'items': []}))
    with httpx.Client(base_url=SETTINGS.api_base_url) as client:
        filings = list_filings(client, exchange='LSE')
    assert filings == []
    assert route.called

# E  httpx.ConnectError: All connection attempts failed
# E  assert route.called
# E   +  where False = <Route get //api.example.dev/filings>.called
#
# captured log: sending GET //api.example.dev/filings?exchange=LSE
hints: The route says .called is False, so respx never matched — respx did not block the call, it simply did not recognise it.
Compare the registered pattern with the logged request line character by character. What does list_filings add?
respx patterns are exact by default: a path pattern does not match a query string unless you say so.
debugMission.solution: The client sent /filings?exchange=LSE, and the route was registered with path='/filings' only — respx matched neither, so the request fell through to the real transport and failed to connect. Fix: register the query too (respx.get(host=..., path='/filings', params={'exchange': 'LSE'})) or match the path pattern loosely with respx.get(url__regex=...) if the query is genuinely irrelevant to the test. General lesson: an unmatched respx route does not fail loudly by itself — it lets the real network attempt happen, so assert route.called (or set assert_all_called=True) in every HTTP test, and read the logged request line rather than trusting the pattern you meant to write.

reflection: Which of the five failure paths (200/404/500/timeout/bad payload) would break your Week-1 CLI worst if it happened silently?
What does asserting on the outgoing request catch that asserting on the parsed result cannot?
done: respx suite covers 200, 404, 500, timeout and malformed-payload paths
404 maps to a fatal error and 5xx/timeout to RetryableFetchError, asserted in tests
At least one test asserts on the outgoing request headers or params
Full suite runs offline in under a second

keyConcepts.def: Mock transport for httpx: routes match outgoing requests and return responses you define, with no code changes in the client.
A sequence of responses or an exception to raise per call — how you simulate a flaky endpoint or a timeout.
Checking route.calls.last.request (URL, headers, body) to verify what your client actually sent, not just what it parsed.

items.title: httpx — the client, configured
items.concept:
httpx.get(...) at module level opens a connection, does a TLS handshake, sends one request and throws the connection away. **httpx.Client** keeps a connection pool alive, so the second request to the same host skips the handshake entirely — on a fetch loop over 20 tickers that is the difference between 4 seconds and 0.6. It also gives you one place to set **base_url**, default **headers**, **auth** and **timeout** so every call inherits the same policy.

Use it as a context manager ('with httpx.Client(...) as client:') or, in a long-lived service, build one at startup and close it at shutdown. Never construct a client per request — that is a pool leak wearing a convenience costume.

**Timeouts, always.** httpx is unusual in defaulting to a 5-second timeout on everything (requests defaults to no timeout at all, which is how services hang forever). You still set them explicitly, because one number is rarely right: httpx.Timeout(connect=3.0, read=10.0, write=10.0, pool=5.0). connect is 'can I reach you', read is 'time between bytes' — a streaming LLM response needs a generous read timeout, a health check needs a mean one. The one value you must never write is timeout=None.

**raise_for_status()** converts a 4xx/5xx into httpx.HTTPStatusError, which carries .response so you can classify by status code. Do it explicitly at the boundary and translate into your Week-1 taxonomy: 404 to DataFetchError, 429/5xx/timeouts to RetryableFetchError.

**response.json() lies to you eventually.** A proxy error page, an empty 204 body or an HTML login redirect all produce a JSONDecodeError from a call you assumed was safe. Catch it and raise DataParseError with the status code and the first 200 characters of the body in context — that single habit turns 'the pipeline broke' into 'the API returned an HTML captcha page'.
items.why: Every remote system you touch for the rest of this course — filings APIs, model providers, vector databases — is an httpx call underneath. A client with sane timeouts and honest error translation is the difference between an outage that pages you and one that self-heals.

learn.focus: Read: Sending requests, Response content, JSON response content, Custom headers, Errors and exceptions, and 'Client instances' at the end (that last section is the point of the lesson). Skip: streaming responses and multipart uploads.

Read the whole page — it is short: the default 5-second timeout, the four timeout kinds (connect/read/write/pool), setting them per-client and per-request, and the section on disabling timeouts (so you know exactly what you are choosing when you do).

build.task: Build FilingsClient: an httpx.Client wrapper with explicit timeouts, auth headers and a typed get_company(ticker) returning a Pydantic model.
steps: src/aie_lab/core/client.py: FilingsClient(settings: Settings) building httpx.Client(base_url=settings.api_base_url, timeout=httpx.Timeout(connect=3.0, read=10.0, write=10.0, pool=5.0), headers={'x-api-key': settings.api_key.get_secret_value()})
Implement __enter__/__exit__ (or a close() method) so the pool is closed deterministically; log at DEBUG when the client is created and closed
get_company(ticker: str) -> Company: GET /companies/{ticker}, raise_for_status(), Company.model_validate(response.json())

Write _translate(err) mapping httpx.HTTPStatusError by status (404 -> DataFetchError, 429 and 5xx -> RetryableFetchError) and httpx.TimeoutException/ConnectError -> RetryableFetchError, always with raise ... from err and ticker in context
Wrap the json()/model_validate step: catch json.JSONDecodeError and pydantic.ValidationError -> DataParseError with status and body[:200] in context
Log every request at INFO with method, path, status and duration_ms using the Week-1 log_duration helper
Port yesterday's respx tests onto the class; add one test asserting the client's timeout config is what you think it is
build.hint: Keep get_company free of retry logic today — tomorrow's tenacity policy wraps it from outside. A method that both retries and translates errors is a method you cannot test in isolation.

items.challenge: Add a per-request override for one slow endpoint (client.get(path, timeout=httpx.Timeout(read=30.0))) and write down in a comment which of the four timeout kinds you relaxed and why. Precision here is what separates a considered timeout from a superstitious one.

debugMission.scenario: A nightly job that used to finish in four minutes has been running for eleven hours. It is not crashed, not looping — it is waiting. Someone 'fixed the flaky timeouts' last week.
debugMission.artifact:
# commit 3f1c9ad — 'fix flaky timeouts in nightly fetch'
-  client = httpx.Client(base_url=BASE, timeout=10.0)
+  client = httpx.Client(base_url=BASE, timeout=None)

# nightly.log
2026-02-11 02:00:03 INFO  fetch start tickers=480
2026-02-11 02:00:03 DEBUG GET /companies/AZN status=200 duration_ms=143
2026-02-11 02:00:04 DEBUG GET /companies/SHEL status=200 duration_ms=155
2026-02-11 02:00:04 DEBUG GET /companies/HSBA ...
2026-02-11 13:07:41 WARN  job still running, 2 of 480 complete

$ ss -tnp | grep 443
ESTAB  0  0  10.2.4.19:51544  93.184.x.x:443  users:(('python',pid=8814))
hints: The third request never logged a status. What state is the process in — busy, crashed, or blocked?
Read the diff. What does timeout=None mean to httpx, as opposed to leaving the argument out?
Which of the four timeout kinds would have ended this wait, given the connection is ESTABLISHED and no bytes are arriving?
debugMission.solution: timeout=None disables all timeouts, so when the upstream accepted the connection and then stopped sending bytes, the read blocked forever — the socket is ESTABLISHED, the process is alive, and nothing will ever break the wait. httpx's default is 5 seconds; the 'fix' explicitly removed the only thing that would have failed fast. The correct fix for genuine slowness is a larger, per-kind timeout — httpx.Timeout(connect=3.0, read=30.0, write=10.0, pool=5.0) — plus retries on the timeout, never disabling it. General lesson: a hung request is worse than a failed one because nothing alerts on it; every client gets an explicit read timeout, and 'timeout=None' should not survive code review.

reflection: For your own fetcher, what read timeout would you set, and what evidence would you use to pick the number?
Why translate httpx exceptions into your own error types at the client boundary rather than letting callers catch httpx errors?
done: FilingsClient sets all four timeout kinds explicitly and closes its pool deterministically
get_company returns a validated Pydantic model and never leaks raw httpx exceptions
404, 429/5xx, timeout and malformed-JSON paths each map to the right Week-1 error type, proven by tests
Request logs show method, path, status and duration_ms

keyConcepts.def: A reused httpx.Client keeps TCP/TLS connections alive between requests, removing handshake cost from every call after the first.
connect (reach the host), read (gap between bytes), write (sending the body), pool (waiting for a free connection) — set individually, never None.
Converting transport exceptions into domain errors at the client boundary so callers depend on your taxonomy, not httpx's.

items.title: Retries with tenacity — but only when safe
items.concept:
A retry policy is four decisions: **what** to retry, **how many times**, **how long to wait between attempts**, and **what to do when attempts run out**. tenacity encodes all four in a decorator.

**@retry(retry=retry_if_exception_type(RetryableFetchError), stop=stop_after_attempt(4), wait=wait_exponential_jitter(initial=0.5, max=8.0), reraise=True, before_sleep=before_sleep_log(logger, logging.WARNING))**. Read it aloud: retry only the errors I classified as transient, up to four attempts, backing off 0.5s, 1s, 2s with random jitter added, and raise the original exception when exhausted rather than tenacity's RetryError wrapper.

**Jitter is not decoration.** Plain exponential backoff makes every client that failed at the same moment retry at the same moment — a synchronised stampede that keeps the struggling service down. Randomising the wait spreads the load; the AWS builders' library has the graphs.

**Retry only what can succeed on a second attempt.** Timeouts, connection resets, 429 and 5xx: yes. 400, 401, 403, 404 and validation failures: never — the same request will fail identically, three times slower, while burning your rate-limit budget. This is precisely why Week 1 made you split RetryableFetchError from DataFetchError: the classification lives in the exception hierarchy and the policy just reads it.

**Idempotency is the other half of the question.** Retrying a GET is free. Retrying a POST that creates something may create it twice, because the first attempt might have succeeded and lost only the response. You either need the server to offer an idempotency key or you need to accept duplicates — Week 3 builds the server side of exactly this.

One more rule: retries belong at ONE layer. If the client retries 4 times and the caller retries 3 times and the queue redelivers, one bad upstream minute becomes 12 attempts per message.
items.why: LLM providers rate-limit you and overload constantly; a correct retry policy is the difference between a 2% error rate and a 0.01% one. Retrying the wrong things is equally career-defining — in the wrong direction.

learn.focus: Read: Basic Retry, 'Stopping' (stop_after_attempt / stop_after_delay), 'Waiting before retrying' (wait_exponential and wait_exponential_jitter), 'Whether to retry' (retry_if_exception_type), 'Error handling' for reraise=True, and 'Before and after retry, and logging' for before_sleep_log. Skip: async retry, statistics, and custom callback classes.

build.task: Add a correct retry policy to FilingsClient and prove with respx that 500-500-200 succeeds while a 404 fails on the first attempt.
steps: uv add tenacity; create a module-level RETRY_POLICY = retry(...) so the same policy is applied consistently rather than re-typed per method
Decorate a thin wrapper (get_company_with_retry, or apply the decorator to get_company itself) — retry OUTSIDE error translation so tenacity sees your domain error types
Set retry=retry_if_exception_type(RetryableFetchError), stop=stop_after_attempt(4), wait=wait_exponential_jitter(initial=0.5, max=8.0), reraise=True
Add before_sleep=before_sleep_log(logger, logging.WARNING) so every retry logs attempt number and the exception
Test A: respx side_effect=[Response(500), Response(500), Response(200, json=...)] — assert the call succeeds and route.call_count == 3
Test B: respx returns 404 — assert DataFetchError is raised and route.call_count == 1 (fail fast, no waiting)
Test C: patch the wait to wait_none() in tests (or use a small initial) so the suite does not actually sleep 3.5 seconds — assert the policy, not the wall clock
build.hint: If your retry tests are slow, you are sleeping for real. Expose the wait strategy as a parameter or override it in tests; a retry suite should still finish in under a second.

items.challenge: Honour Retry-After: when a 429 arrives with that header, sleep for the value the server asked for instead of your exponential schedule. tenacity supports custom wait callables; a provider that tells you when to come back deserves to be obeyed.

debugMission.scenario: A retry policy was added a fortnight ago. During yesterday's 90-second upstream wobble the job failed anyway, and the logs show exactly one attempt per ticker. The decorator is definitely there.
hints: before_sleep logging would have printed a line per retry. There are none — so tenacity is not retrying, rather than retrying and failing.
What exception type actually leaves get_company? What type does the policy say to retry on?
Order matters: the try/except runs inside the decorated function, so tenacity only ever sees what escapes it.
debugMission.solution: The method catches httpx.HTTPStatusError and re-raises RetryableFetchError, so the only exception tenacity ever observes is RetryableFetchError — which is not an httpx.HTTPError, so retry_if_exception_type never matches and the call fails on the first attempt. Fix: retry on your own taxonomy (retry_if_exception_type(RetryableFetchError)), which is the whole reason the Week-1 hierarchy encodes retryable-vs-fatal. General lesson: a retry predicate must be written against the exception type that actually escapes the retried function — and a policy with before_sleep logging tells you instantly whether it is firing, which is why every retry policy should log.

reflection: Which of your endpoints are safe to retry blindly, and which would need an idempotency key first?
If both your client and its caller retry four times, what is the worst-case number of requests one user action produces?
done: RETRY_POLICY retries only RetryableFetchError, with jitter, reraise=True and before_sleep logging
The 500-500-200 test passes with call_count == 3
The 404 test proves a single attempt (fail fast)
Retry tests run in under a second because the wait is overridden in tests
You can state in one sentence why POST retries need server-side support

keyConcepts.def: Waits that double per attempt plus randomness, so retrying clients spread out instead of stampeding a recovering service.
The rule deciding which exceptions are worth retrying; it must match the exception type that actually escapes the function.
Retries at several layers multiplying (4 x 3 x redelivery), turning a brief upstream wobble into a self-inflicted load spike.

items.title: async is cooperative waiting
items.concept:
The café model, which the FastAPI docs tell better than anyone: a waiter taking ten orders does not stand at the first table until the food arrives. They take an order, go to the next table while the kitchen cooks, and come back when something is ready. One waiter, ten tables, no cloning. That waiter is the **event loop**; the cooking is your I/O; **await** is the moment the waiter walks away.

Precisely: **async def** creates a coroutine function; calling it returns a coroutine object that does nothing until awaited. **await** hands control back to the event loop, which runs other ready work and resumes you when your result lands. **asyncio.run(main())** starts the loop, usually once, at the top of your program.

Concurrency comes from launching work before awaiting it. **await asyncio.gather(*[fetch(t) for t in tickers])** starts all coroutines and waits for all results; gather(..., return_exceptions=True) collects failures as values instead of cancelling the lot at the first error. **asyncio.TaskGroup** (Python 3.11+) is the modern structured alternative: an 'async with' block where every task is guaranteed finished or cancelled at exit.

**Async only helps I/O-bound work.** Ten HTTP calls that each wait 200ms overlap beautifully: total time is roughly the slowest call, not the sum. Ten calls that each burn 200ms of CPU do not overlap at all — there is one thread, and a coroutine that never awaits never yields. CPU-bound work needs processes (or Rust/C libraries that release the GIL); async gives you nothing there.

Practically: **httpx.AsyncClient** mirrors the sync client with 'await client.get(...)' and 'async with' for lifecycle. Every function in the call chain from asyncio.run down to the await must be async — this is the 'function colouring' complaint, and it is why you decide sync-vs-async at the architecture level, not per function.
items.why: Concurrency is the single biggest lever on LLM application latency: five sequential model calls at 2 seconds each is 10 seconds of user-visible waiting, or 2 seconds if you gather them. Every serious FastAPI endpoint you write from Week 3 is async.

learn.focus: Read the narrative from 'Asynchronous Code' through the burger/waiter story to 'Concurrency + Parallelism: Web + Machine Learning' — the best plain-English async explanation in any documentation. Skip: 'Very Technical Details' at the end for now.

Read: Coroutines, Awaitables, 'Running an asyncio Program' (asyncio.run), Creating Tasks, 'Running Tasks Concurrently' (gather), and the Task Groups section. Skip: Futures, Introspection, and the low-level scheduling APIs.

Optional depth if the mental model has not landed: read 'The 10,000-Foot View of Async IO' and 'The asyncio Package and async/await'. Skip: the aiohttp web-scraping walkthrough and the queue example unless you have energy to spare.

build.task: Fetch ten endpoints sequentially and then with gather, measure both, and explain the ratio you observe.
steps: uv run python -c 'import httpx; print(httpx.__version__)' to confirm the client is present; write scratch/bench_async.py
Write fetch_one(client: httpx.AsyncClient, path: str) -> dict awaiting client.get(path) and returning response.json()
Sequential version: 'async with httpx.AsyncClient(base_url=..., timeout=TIMEOUT) as client:' then a for loop of awaits; time it with time.perf_counter()
Concurrent version: same client, results = await asyncio.gather(*[fetch_one(client, p) for p in paths]); time it
Run both against a public JSON API (api.github.com repository endpoints work well; ten different paths, not the same one ten times) and record the two numbers
Write the ratio down and explain it in one sentence: sequential is roughly the SUM of latencies, concurrent is roughly the MAX plus overhead
Now add a deliberately CPU-heavy variant (sum of squares to 20 million inside each coroutine) and confirm gather buys you nothing — this is the experiment that makes the rule stick
build.hint: Reuse ONE AsyncClient across the gather. Creating a client per coroutine gives you ten connection pools and destroys the benefit you are trying to measure.
build.code:
import asyncio
import time
import httpx

PATHS = ['/posts/' + str(i) for i in range(1, 11)]
TIMEOUT = httpx.Timeout(connect=3.0, read=10.0,
                        write=10.0, pool=5.0)

async def fetch_one(client: httpx.AsyncClient, path: str) -> dict:
    response = await client.get(path)
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.json()

async def sequential(client: httpx.AsyncClient) -> list[dict]:
    out = []
    for path in PATHS:
        out.append(await fetch_one(client, path))
    return out

async def concurrent(client: httpx.AsyncClient) -> list[dict]:
    return await asyncio.gather(
        *(fetch_one(client, path) for path in PATHS))

async def main() -> None:
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(base_url=BASE,
                                 timeout=TIMEOUT) as client:
        for name, runner in (('sequential', sequential),
                             ('concurrent', concurrent)):
            start = time.perf_counter()
            results = await runner(client)
            elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
            print(name, len(results), round(elapsed, 2), 's')

asyncio.run(main())

items.challenge: Rewrite the concurrent version with asyncio.TaskGroup instead of gather, then make one path 404. Observe how TaskGroup cancels siblings and raises an ExceptionGroup, versus gather(return_exceptions=True) handing you a list with an exception in it. Decide which failure semantics your fetcher wants.

debugMission.scenario: An async report function returns nonsense: printing the results shows a list of objects rather than data, and the terminal is full of RuntimeWarnings. The author insists 'it is async, so it runs in the background'.
debugMission.artifact:
async def fetch_one(client, path):
    response = await client.get(path)
    return response.json()

async def build_report(client, paths):
    results = []
    for path in paths:
        results.append(fetch_one(client, path))
    total = sum(r['value'] for r in results)
    return total

# output
# sys:1: RuntimeWarning: coroutine 'fetch_one' was never awaited
# Traceback (most recent call last):
#   File 'report.py', line 9, in build_report
#     total = sum(r['value'] for r in results)
# TypeError: 'coroutine' object is not subscriptable
hints: Read the warning literally: which call produced a coroutine that nobody awaited?
What does calling an async def function actually return before you await it?
You want all ten in flight at once, not ten sequential awaits — which asyncio call starts them together and collects results?
debugMission.solution: Calling fetch_one(...) creates a coroutine object; without await (or wrapping in a task) nothing runs, so the list holds ten inert coroutines and the sum fails on the first subscript. There is no 'background' in asyncio — work runs only while something awaits it. The fix that also gets the concurrency you wanted: results = await asyncio.gather(*(fetch_one(client, p) for p in paths)). Appending 'await fetch_one(...)' inside the loop would also be correct but serialises the calls. General lesson: 'coroutine was never awaited' means a coroutine was created and dropped — and the fix is a deliberate choice between awaiting in sequence and gathering concurrently, not sprinkling awaits until the warning disappears.

reflection: Explain to a colleague in three sentences why one thread can serve 500 waiting requests but not 500 calculating ones.
In your Week-1 CLI, which operations would actually benefit from async, and which are pure CPU?
done: Sequential and concurrent timings recorded for the same ten calls, with the ratio explained in writing
The CPU-bound variant demonstrably shows no speed-up from gather
One AsyncClient is shared across all coroutines
You can define coroutine, event loop, await point and gather without notes

keyConcepts.def: The single-threaded scheduler that runs ready coroutines and resumes each one when the I/O it awaited completes.
The place a coroutine yields control back to the loop; between await points nothing else in the loop can run.
Runs multiple coroutines concurrently and returns their results in order; return_exceptions=True collects failures instead of cancelling the rest.
Async overlaps waiting, not computing — CPU-heavy work needs processes, since one loop thread cannot parallelise it.

items.title: Debug mission — the blocking sleep
items.concept:
Standalone mission. A service that was rewritten to async runs at exactly the speed it did before — sometimes slightly worse. The tasks are launched with gather, the functions are all async def, and the author has read yesterday's lesson. Something inside a coroutine is refusing to yield.

This is the single most common async bug in production Python, and it has one root cause: **a blocking call inside a coroutine stops the entire event loop**, not just that coroutine. One thread runs everything, so any function that sleeps, computes or does synchronous I/O without awaiting holds the loop hostage — and every other task waits, including the ones that were ready to run.

The usual culprits, in order of frequency: **time.sleep()** instead of asyncio.sleep(), the **requests** library (or any sync SDK) instead of an async client, synchronous file I/O on large files, and heavy CPU work inline. The tell is always the same shape in the evidence: total wall time equals the SUM of the per-task durations, and the log timestamps march in single file rather than interleaving.

Your job: read the code and the timing evidence, name the exact line that blocks, predict the corrected wall time before you run anything, fix it, and be able to explain WHY the loop stalls — 'one thread, cooperative scheduling, no pre-emption' — to someone who has not read the docs.

The escape hatch worth knowing: when a library is only available in blocking form, **await asyncio.to_thread(blocking_call, arg)** moves it to a worker thread so the loop keeps turning. That is a bridge, not a licence — the right fix is an async client when one exists.
items.why: Every async service you deploy from Week 3 onwards can be crippled by one careless sync call in a dependency, and the symptom (slow, not broken) is exactly the kind that survives code review. Being able to spot it from a latency chart is a genuinely marketable skill.
items.challenge: After fixing it, add a guard: run the fetcher under asyncio.run(main(), debug=True) and set the slow-callback threshold (loop.slow_callback_duration = 0.1). The loop then logs a warning naming any callback that hogs it — a cheap detector you can leave switched on in development.

debugMission.scenario: The filings fetcher was converted to async last sprint. It fetches 10 tickers, each upstream call takes about 0.9s, and the team expected roughly 1 second total. It takes 12. The author has added a polite 0.2s pause between calls to respect the upstream rate limit, and gather is definitely being used.
debugMission.artifact:
import asyncio, time, httpx

async def fetch_ticker(client, ticker):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    response = await client.get('/companies/' + ticker)
    time.sleep(0.2)  # be polite to the rate limiter
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
    print(round(time.perf_counter() - T0, 2), ticker,
          'took', round(elapsed, 2))
    return response.json()

async def main():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(base_url=BASE) as client:
        return await asyncio.gather(
            *(fetch_ticker(client, t) for t in TICKERS))

T0 = time.perf_counter()
results = asyncio.run(main())
print('total', round(time.perf_counter() - T0, 2), 's')

# 1.12 AZN  took 1.12
# 2.24 SHEL took 1.11
# 3.35 HSBA took 1.11
# 4.47 BP   took 1.12
# ...
# total 11.98 s
hints: Ten tasks, each reporting 1.1s of its own, and a total of 12s. If they were genuinely overlapping, what would the total be — and what does a total equal to the sum tell you?
Look at the completion timestamps: 1.12, 2.24, 3.35 — evenly spaced by one full task duration. The tasks are queueing behind something.
One line in fetch_ticker does not have await in front of it. What does that function do to the thread it runs on?
debugMission.solution: time.sleep(0.2) blocks the single event-loop thread: while one coroutine sleeps, no other coroutine can run, not even one whose HTTP response has already arrived. Because every task takes its turn holding the loop for 0.2s (and the awaited request cannot be resumed during it), the tasks serialise and the total becomes the sum. The fix is await asyncio.sleep(0.2), which yields control so the other nine requests progress during the pause; wall time drops to roughly 1.1s. Timings confirm the diagnosis: evenly spaced completions equal to sum-of-durations mean serial execution, whereas true concurrency shows near-simultaneous completions. The general rule: inside async def, everything that waits must be awaited — asyncio.sleep instead of time.sleep, httpx.AsyncClient instead of requests, and asyncio.to_thread(...) for blocking libraries you cannot replace. And rate limiting belongs in a shared semaphore or limiter, not a per-task sleep that pretends to be polite while blocking everybody.

reflection: How would you detect this bug in a service you did not write, using only its latency metrics?
When is asyncio.to_thread the right answer, and when is it papering over a wrong library choice?
done: You named the blocking line and predicted the corrected wall time before running the fix
The fixed version completes 10 tasks in roughly one task's duration
You can explain in two sentences why one blocking call stalls unrelated tasks
You know the to_thread escape hatch and when it is legitimate

keyConcepts.def: A synchronous call inside a coroutine holds the single event-loop thread, stalling every other task until it returns.
Runs a blocking function in a worker thread and awaits its result, keeping the event loop responsive when no async library exists.
Total wall time equal to the sum of task durations, with evenly spaced completion timestamps — the signature of a blocked loop.

items.title: Branch, PR, review — even solo
items.concept:
GitHub flow is four moves: branch off main, commit small changes, open a pull request, merge after review. Working solo does not exempt you — it makes the discipline cheaper to practise and more visible when someone reads your repo later.

**Branch per change, not per day.** A branch named tests/pytest-suite or feat/async-fetcher describes one reviewable idea. When the branch does three unrelated things, the reviewer (you, in an hour) cannot hold it in their head, and the diff stops being a story.

**Commit messages: imperative subject, why in the body.** 'Add retry policy to FilingsClient' as the subject, then a paragraph explaining that 5xx and timeouts are retried while 4xx fails fast, and why. The diff already says what changed; only you can record why. Six months from now, git log is the only design document that stayed true.

**Self-review is the highest-yield habit in this lesson.** Open your own PR's Files Changed tab and read every line as if a stranger wrote it. You will find, reliably: a stray breakpoint(), a debug print, a hard-coded path, a note-to-self comment you never acted on, a test that asserts nothing. Reading a diff engages a different, more sceptical part of your brain than writing it does — this is why the tab exists.

**A PR description is practice for consulting writing.** Three headings: what changed, why, how to verify (the exact command a reviewer runs). Do this on your own repos and the habit is already automatic on your first client team.

Keep a rescue reference to hand for the moments git bites — committed on main, committed the wrong file, need the last commit undone. Knowing that these are all recoverable is what stops people from deleting the folder and re-cloning.
items.why: Your GitHub history is read before your CV in AI-engineering hiring: small, well-described PRs with self-review comments read as 'has worked on a team'. Clients also grant repo access based on how much they trust your process.

learn.focus: Read all six steps end to end (create a branch, make changes, create a pull request, address review comments, merge, delete the branch). It is five minutes and it is the exact loop you will follow every week from now on.
Optional practice, 20 minutes: Main levels 1-4 (commits, branching, merging, rebasing) in the interactive sandbox. Skip the Remote section for now unless you enjoy it.
Do not read end to end. Skim the headings once so you know what problems it covers, then bookmark it — it is the page you open at the moment of panic, not the page you study.

build.task: Put this week's work through a real branch-PR-self-review-merge cycle on the aie-lab repo.
steps: git switch -c tests/pytest-suite (or move existing work: commit on main by accident is fixable — that is the debug mission)
Commit in logical chunks: the test suite, then the httpx client, then retries — three commits with imperative subjects and a why-body each
Push and open a PR with three headings: What changed, Why, How to verify (paste the exact uv run pytest command)
Self-review the Files Changed tab line by line; leave at least three review comments on your OWN diff — including one that asks a real question
Act on your comments in follow-up commits, then merge (squash if the intermediate commits were noisy) and delete the branch
Run git log --oneline main and check the history reads as a sequence of intentions, not a diary of keystrokes
build.hint: If the PR diff is over about 400 lines, you did not make a branch, you made a release. Split it — reviewers (including future you) skim anything larger and approve it blindly.
build.code:
# the loop, as commands
git switch -c tests/pytest-suite
git add tests/ && git commit -m 'Add pytest suite for snapshot core'
git push -u origin tests/pytest-suite
gh pr create --fill --web

# a commit message worth reading
Add retry policy to FilingsClient

Upstream returns 503 during their nightly window; a single
attempt turns a 40-second blip into a failed job. Retries
cover RetryableFetchError only (timeouts, 429, 5xx) with
jittered backoff, four attempts max. 4xx still fails fast
so bad tickers are not retried into the rate limit.

# after merging
git switch main && git pull && git branch -d tests/pytest-suite

items.challenge: Add a .github/pull_request_template.md with your three headings. Every future PR then starts pre-structured — the cheapest process improvement in this course.

debugMission.scenario: An hour of work has vanished. The engineer checked out a commit by hash to look at an older version, kept working, committed twice, and now git switch main shows none of it. They are about to re-write the changes from memory.
debugMission.artifact:
$ git checkout 9c1f2ab
Note: switching to '9c1f2ab'.
You are in 'detached HEAD' state. You can look around, make
experimental changes and commit them...
HEAD is now at 9c1f2ab Add pytest suite for snapshot core

$ ... work, work ...
$ git commit -am 'Add respx tests'
[detached HEAD 4d77e10] Add respx tests
$ git commit -am 'Add retry policy'
[detached HEAD b02ca55] Add retry policy

$ git switch main
Warning: you are leaving 2 commits behind, not connected to
any of your branches:
  b02ca55 Add retry policy
  4d77e10 Add respx tests

$ git log --oneline -1
9c1f2ab Add pytest suite for snapshot core
hints: Nothing is deleted. Read the warning again: 'leaving 2 commits behind, not connected to any of your branches'.
The commits still have hashes (b02ca55 is right there in the terminal). What does a branch actually consist of?
If the hash had scrolled away, git reflog lists every position HEAD has held for the last 90 days.
debugMission.solution: Committing in detached HEAD state creates real commits that no branch name points at, so switching away leaves them unreachable-but-alive until garbage collection (about 90 days by default). Recover with git branch rescue b02ca55 (or git switch -c rescue b02ca55), then merge or cherry-pick into main; if the hash is gone from the screen, git reflog shows every HEAD position and you take the hash from there. General lesson: in git, work is lost only when it was never committed — commits, stashes and reflog entries survive nearly everything. Learn reflog once and 'I lost my work' becomes 'I misplaced a pointer for four minutes'.

reflection: What did self-reviewing your own diff catch that writing the code did not?
Write the one-sentence rule you will use to decide when a branch is 'one change'.
done: This week's work went through a branch and a PR, not straight to main
The PR description has What changed / Why / How to verify with a runnable command
At least three self-review comments exist on your own diff and were acted on
You recovered commits from a detached HEAD (or reproduced the recovery deliberately) and know git reflog

keyConcepts.def: Branch per change, small PR, review, merge, delete branch — the default workflow on nearly every team you will join.
Reading your own diff in the Files Changed view before merging; catches debug leftovers and unclear code that writing-mode misses.
Working directly on a commit rather than a branch; commits made there are real but unreferenced until you name them with a branch.
The local log of every position HEAD has held, and the recovery tool for commits that appear lost.

items.title: ruff + pre-commit — free code review
items.concept:
**ruff** is a linter and formatter in one binary, fast enough that running it on save is unnoticeable. Two commands: **ruff check .** (find problems, --fix applies the safe ones) and **ruff format .** (opinionated formatting, black-compatible, no debate).

Configure it in pyproject.toml under [tool.ruff]. A sensible starting rule set: **E** and **F** (pycodestyle errors, pyflakes — unused imports and variables, undefined names), **I** (import sorting, which ends a whole genre of merge conflicts), **UP** (pyupgrade — rewrites old idioms to modern Python), and **B** (flake8-bugbear, which catches genuine traps like mutable default arguments). Add rules gradually; adding 40 rule families to an existing codebase produces 900 errors and one demoralised engineer.

**noqa is a promise, not an escape.** '# noqa: F401' with no explanation is a code smell; '# noqa: F401 - imported for side effect, registers the handlers' is a decision. Same principle as type: ignore in Week 1.

**pre-commit** runs the tools on staged files before a commit is created, so junk cannot land. Install the framework, write .pre-commit-config.yaml with the ruff hooks (lint then format), run 'pre-commit install' once per clone, and the hook fires on every commit. When a hook reformats a file the commit is aborted with 'files were modified by this hook' — that is the system working: inspect the changes, git add them, commit again.

The pay-off is not tidiness for its own sake. Every trivial thing a machine catches — unsorted imports, an unused variable, a line at 140 characters — is attention a human reviewer gets to spend on your logic instead.
items.why: Consistent, lint-clean code is the baseline expectation on any professional Python team, and the diff noise from unformatted code makes real review impossible. It is also a 20-minute setup that pays off every day for the rest of the course.

learn.focus: Read: the Tutorial (both the linter and formatter halves), then Configuring Ruff — the pyproject.toml example, lint.select/ignore, and per-file-ignores. Skip: the full Rules reference; look up individual codes as ruff reports them.

build.task: Add ruff to aie-lab, fix everything it finds, and wire a pre-commit hook so unformatted code cannot be committed.
steps: uv add --dev ruff pre-commit; add the [tool.ruff] config below to pyproject.toml (line-length 88, target-version py312, select E, F, I, UP, B)
Run uv run ruff check . and read the full list before fixing anything — count the categories, they are a portrait of your habits
uv run ruff check --fix . then uv run ruff format . ; review the diff carefully (this is exactly the self-review skill from this morning)
Fix the remaining findings by hand; where you genuinely disagree, add a targeted noqa WITH a reason, or add the rule to the ignore list with a comment saying why
Write .pre-commit-config.yaml with the ruff hooks (ruff-check with --fix, then ruff-format), run: uv run pre-commit install
Test it: introduce an unused import and an over-long line, try to commit, watch the hook block you, then git add the fixes and commit successfully
Commit the config files themselves so a fresh clone is one 'pre-commit install' away from the same guarantees
build.hint: Run ruff check --fix and ruff format in that order. Formatting first means the linter's fixes can reintroduce formatting changes, and you end up with two passes anyway.
build.code:
# pyproject.toml
[tool.ruff]
line-length = 88
target-version = 'py312'
src = ['src', 'tests']

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = ['E', 'F', 'I', 'UP', 'B']
ignore = ['E501']  # formatter owns line length

[tool.ruff.lint.per-file-ignores]
'tests/**' = ['B011']

# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: ruff-check
        name: ruff check
        entry: uv run ruff check --fix
        language: system
        types: [python]
      - id: ruff-format
        name: ruff format
        entry: uv run ruff format
        language: system
        types: [python]
      - id: pytest
        name: pytest
        entry: uv run pytest -q
        language: system
        pass_filenames: false
        stages: [pre-push]

items.challenge: Add mypy to the pre-commit config as a pre-push stage alongside pytest. Slow checks belong at push time, fast ones at commit time — that split is what keeps the hook from being disabled in frustration.

debugMission.scenario: After a routine 'ruff check --fix' the test suite still passes, but the deployed CLI stops applying the custom JSON log format. Nothing about logging was edited — the diff only removed imports.
debugMission.artifact:
# diff of the autofix commit
--- a/src/aie_lab/cli.py
+++ b/src/aie_lab/cli.py
@@
 from aie_lab.core.config import Settings
-from aie_lab.core import log_handlers
 from aie_lab.core.snapshot import build_snapshot

# src/aie_lab/core/log_handlers.py
import logging

class JsonFormatter(logging.Formatter):
    ...

logging.getLogger('aie_lab').handlers[:] = [_json_handler()]

# ruff output before the fix
src/aie_lab/cli.py:4:1: F401 [*] 'aie_lab.core.log_handlers'
  imported but unused

# after deploy
2026-02-19 08:01:14 INFO snapshot complete count=7
# expected: {'ts': '2026-02-19T08:01:14', 'level': 'INFO', ...}
hints: The import was removed because nothing in cli.py references the name. Is 'referenced by name' the same as 'has no effect'?
Read log_handlers.py to the bottom. What runs at import time?
Why did the test suite not catch it — do the tests assert on log formatting at all?
debugMission.solution: log_handlers.py does its work as an import side effect: importing the module installs the JSON handler. ruff's F401 rule correctly saw that the name was never used and removed it, deleting the side effect and with it the log configuration. The tests never asserted on log output, so nothing failed. Two fixes, and the second is better: keep the import with '# noqa: F401 - imported for side effect, installs the JSON log handler', or eliminate the implicit magic by exporting configure_logging() and calling it explicitly from main() — an explicit call cannot be optimised away by a linter or a reader. General lesson: autofixes are safe only for code whose meaning is visible to the tool; import-time side effects are invisible to it. Review autofix diffs like any other diff, and prefer explicit initialisation over import magic.

reflection: Which ruff finding appeared most often in your code, and what habit does it reveal?
Where should slow checks (mypy, pytest) run — commit, push, or CI — and why?
done: ruff check and ruff format both run clean on the repo
[tool.ruff] config is committed with a deliberate rule selection
pre-commit is installed and demonstrably blocks a bad commit
Every noqa in the codebase carries a reason

keyConcepts.def: A single fast binary providing linting (check) and formatting (format) for Python, configured in pyproject.toml.
A check that runs on staged files before a commit is created, so lint or format violations never enter history.
Code that runs merely because a module is imported; invisible to linters, which is why unused-import autofixes can break behaviour.

items.title: Mini-project — Concurrent Filings Fetcher
items.concept:
Assembly day: everything from this week becomes one tool. An async fetcher takes a list of tickers, fetches them concurrently with bounded parallelism, retries transient failures, validates every payload, quarantines the ones that fail, and writes a JSON report — with a test suite that runs entirely offline.

**Bounded concurrency is the part most people skip.** gather over 200 tickers opens 200 connections at once and gets you rate-limited, or worse, silently throttled. An asyncio.Semaphore(5) wrapped around the fetch means at most five in flight: fast enough to matter, polite enough to survive. The semaphore lives around the whole fetch-with-retries, not just the HTTP call.

**Partial failure is the normal case.** Use gather(..., return_exceptions=True) so one dead ticker does not cancel the other nineteen, then split results into successes and failures — the Week-1 quarantine pattern, now concurrent. The report must state both: fetched 18, failed 2, with reasons. A fetcher that reports 18 without mentioning the 2 is how silent data loss starts.

**Data source.** Use a public JSON API as a stand-in: api.github.com repository endpoints (rate-limited but generous, and real JSON shapes with nested objects worth validating), or any free fake-JSON service you already know if you want no rate limits at all. Point AIE_API_BASE_URL at it in .env and keep the client generic, so swapping to a real filings vendor later changes one environment variable and one Pydantic model. Document that swap in the README — it is the difference between a toy and a design.

This repo is portfolio item number one. Write it as if a hiring engineer will read it, because that is precisely what it is for.
items.why: This is the exact skeleton of every LLM client you will build: concurrent calls to a flaky remote service, bounded, retried, validated, logged and tested offline. Week 4 swaps the endpoint for a model provider and reuses the structure unchanged.

build.task: Ship an async, bounded-concurrency, retrying filings fetcher with a full offline respx test suite and a JSON report.
steps: Milestone 1 — client: AsyncFilingsClient wrapping httpx.AsyncClient with explicit Timeout, base_url and headers from Settings; async context manager lifecycle; one client shared by all tasks

Milestone 2 — one fetch: async fetch_one(ticker) -> Filing doing GET, raise_for_status, model_validate, translating errors into the Week-1 taxonomy (404 fatal, 429/5xx/timeout retryable, bad payload DataParseError)

Milestone 3 — retries: apply the tenacity policy (retry_if_exception_type(RetryableFetchError), stop_after_attempt(4), wait_exponential_jitter, reraise=True) — use tenacity's AsyncRetrying or the decorator on the async function

Milestone 4 — concurrency: fetch_all(tickers, limit=5) using an asyncio.Semaphore around the retried fetch and gather(..., return_exceptions=True); log start/finish with duration_ms per ticker and for the batch

Milestone 5 — report: split results into ok and rejects (ticker, error type, message), write report.json with counts, duration_ms, the validated records and the rejects; assert ok + rejects == requested

Milestone 6 — tests: respx suite covering all-success, partial failure (one 404, one 500-then-200), a timeout, a malformed payload, and one flaky-simulation test where a route returns 500 twice then 200 and the report still shows success
Milestone 7 — concurrency test: assert bounded parallelism (a counting fixture that records max in-flight and asserts it never exceeded 5)
Milestone 8 — measure: run 20 tickers concurrently and again with limit=1, record both wall times in the README, and make sure the concurrent run is under 3 seconds
Milestone 9 — quality gate: ruff clean, mypy clean, pre-commit passing, all work merged via a PR
build.hint: Put the semaphore around the retried call, not inside it. Inside, a retrying task releases its slot between attempts and your concurrency ceiling quietly stops meaning anything.

items.challenge: Add a --limit flag and chart the trade-off: run 20 tickers at limit 1, 3, 5, 10, 20 and record wall time and any 429s. You now have a real concurrency-versus-politeness graph and an evidence-based default rather than a guess.
reflection: Where did partial failure force a design decision you had not anticipated?
If the upstream started returning 200 with an empty body, which layer of your fetcher would notice, and would the report be honest about it?
done: 20 tickers fetch concurrently in under 3 seconds; the same run with limit=1 takes roughly 20 seconds, both recorded in the README
The whole test suite passes offline in under 2 seconds, including a flaky-simulation test (500, 500, 200)
A test proves in-flight requests never exceed the semaphore limit
report.json shows counts, duration_ms, records and rejects with reasons; ok + rejects always equals the requested tickers
ruff, mypy and pre-commit are clean and the work was merged through a PR

keyConcepts.def: An asyncio.Semaphore capping simultaneous in-flight requests so you go fast without triggering rate limits or exhausting connections.
gather option that returns failures as values instead of cancelling siblings — the basis of partial-failure handling.
Tests that stub the transport (respx) so the whole suite runs deterministically in seconds with no network or credentials.

items.title: Portfolio checkpoint — repo public
items.concept:
Make the repo public and write the README a stranger needs. Four sections beyond the Week-1 shape: an **architecture sketch** (ASCII is completely fine — tickers into a semaphore-bounded fetch pool, through retries and validation, out to report.json), **how to run the tests** with the actual command and the actual runtime, **test honesty**, and **what I would do next**.

**Test honesty** means describing what is covered and what is not: 'respx-stubbed unit tests cover success, 404, 5xx-then-success, timeout and malformed payloads; there is no live integration test against the real API'. A badge claiming 96% coverage over untested error paths fools nobody who reads the code, and it costs you credibility that an honest paragraph would have earned.

**What I would do next** is the section interviewers actually quote back at you: 'persist rejects for reprocessing', 'add a live smoke test behind a marker', 'replace the in-process semaphore with a shared token bucket if this ran on multiple workers'. Naming your own limitations demonstrates the judgement they are hiring for.
items.why: This is your first public artefact of the course, and it is evidence of exactly the skills AI-engineering job descriptions list: async, HTTP resilience, testing. A README that explains the design decisions turns a code dump into a portfolio piece.

build.task: Publish the repo with a README containing an architecture sketch, verification commands, honest test coverage notes and next steps.
steps: Make the repository public; confirm no secrets in history (git log -p -- .env should show nothing; if it does, rotate the key and rewrite before publishing)
README: one-sentence what-it-is, then an ASCII diagram of tickers to semaphore to retry to validate to report
Add Run and Test sections with real commands and real pasted output, including the two wall times from the concurrency comparison
Design decisions paragraph: why bounded concurrency, why retry only transient errors, why the quarantine pattern instead of failing the batch
Test honesty paragraph plus a 'What I would do next' list of three specific items
Tag v0.2.0, push tags, and re-read the whole README as a stranger for 60 seconds
build.hint: Paste genuine terminal output, including the failure counts. A README showing 18 fetched and 2 quarantined with reasons is more persuasive than one showing a suspiciously perfect run.

items.challenge: Add a GitHub Actions workflow that runs ruff, mypy and pytest on every push. Ten lines of YAML, and the green tick on your PRs is the most-read piece of evidence in your repo.
reflection: Which sentence in your README would a hiring engineer quote in an interview, and is it the sentence you would choose?
done: Repo is public, secret-free, and tagged v0.2.0
README has an architecture sketch, real commands with real output, and both wall times
Test coverage is described honestly, including what is not tested
A 'What I would do next' list names three specific improvements

keyConcepts.def: Stating plainly what the suite covers and what it does not, rather than implying completeness with a coverage badge.

items.title: Week 2 review
items.concept:
Spoken review, 30 minutes, no reopening of docs or your notes. Recall is the exercise; re-reading only feels productive.

**Explain aloud, timed at 2 minutes each:** (1) why you patch at the import site rather than the definition site, using the stale-price story as the example; (2) when async helps and when it does nothing, with the café model and the CPU-bound counter-example; (3) your retry policy — what it retries, how long it waits, why jitter exists, and why 404 is excluded.

**Then re-read your own Monday tests** for five minutes. Ask one question of each: if this test failed six months from now, would its name tell me what broke? Rename anything that fails that test.

**Finally, the concurrency sketch.** On paper, draw the fetcher: 20 tickers, semaphore of 5, retries, gather, quarantine, report. Then mark the two places where a failure could be silently swallowed. Note the two topics that felt shakiest as need-revision — they will surface again in Week 3 (idempotency and timeouts) and Week 4 (client resilience), so name them now rather than hoping.
items.why: Speaking a concept without notes is the only reliable test of whether you own it, and these three explanations are near-guaranteed interview questions in exactly this form.
reflection: Explain to a PM, in two sentences with no jargon, why the fetcher went from 20 seconds to 2 without any new hardware.
Which of this week's bugs (fixture scope, wrong patch path, timeout=None, blocking sleep, retry predicate) would you be slowest to spot in someone else's code, and why?
done: Three explanations delivered aloud from memory without notes
Test names reviewed and at least one renamed for clarity
Concurrency sketch drawn from memory with the two silent-failure points marked
Two need-revision topics written down by name

items.title: Week 2 quiz
items.concept: Seven questions on the week: fixture scope, patch paths, retry policy, the async mental model, gather versus sequential, timeout configuration and PR hygiene. Attempt every question before checking any answer, and treat a wrong answer as a pointer to the exact lesson to re-skim rather than as a score.
items.why: Retrieval under mild pressure is what moves this week from 'read it' to 'have it', and these are the questions interviewers ask almost verbatim.
reflection: Which wrong answer surprised you most, and what will you re-read because of it?
done: Quiz completed with a score of 70% or better
Every wrong answer traced back to the lesson that covers it

questions.q: A test passes when run alone but fails when the whole suite runs. What is the first hypothesis?
options: pytest is running tests in a random order and the suite needs -p no:randomly
A fixture with module or session scope is being mutated by one of the tests
The test needs a longer timeout because the suite loads more modules
Assert introspection behaves differently when more tests are collected
questions.explain: Order-dependent failures almost always mean shared mutable state — typically a widened fixture scope handing the same object to every test. Function scope, or copying inside the test, restores isolation.

questions.q: report.py contains 'from aie_lab.core.market import fetch_price'. Your test patches 'aie_lab.core.market.fetch_price' and still passes, but production shows stale data. Why did the mock not apply?
options: monkeypatch cannot patch functions, only attributes and environment variables
The from-import bound a separate reference in report.py's namespace at import time, so report still calls the real function
The patch was undone before the call because monkeypatch reverts at the end of each statement
Patching only works if the target module has been imported inside the test function
questions.explain: A from-import copies the object reference into the importing module's namespace. Patch where the name is looked up — aie_lab.core.report.fetch_price — or import the module and call market.fetch_price() so the lookup happens at call time.

questions.q: Which set of failures should your retry policy cover?
options: Any exception, with four attempts — a retry never makes things worse
Timeouts, connection errors, 429 and 5xx only; 4xx and validation errors fail fast
Only timeouts, since HTTP status errors mean the server processed the request
5xx and 404, because a resource may appear on a later attempt
questions.explain: Retry only what a second identical attempt could plausibly succeed at. Retrying 400/401/403/404 or a validation failure just triples the latency and burns rate-limit budget — which is why the Week-1 hierarchy separates RetryableFetchError from DataFetchError.

questions.q: An async endpoint calls time.sleep(0.2) once per request. What happens under 50 concurrent requests?
options: Nothing measurable; 0.2s is short and asyncio schedules around it
Every request is delayed by 0.2s independently, so throughput is unaffected
The event loop thread is blocked for each sleep, so the sleeps serialise and add roughly 10 seconds across the batch
asyncio automatically moves blocking calls to a thread pool
questions.explain: One thread runs the loop, and time.sleep does not yield. Each sleep freezes every other task, so the total grows to the sum of sleeps. Use await asyncio.sleep(), or asyncio.to_thread() for blocking libraries you cannot replace.
