questions.q: You write httpx.Client(base_url=BASE, timeout=None) after a colleague complains about flaky timeout errors. What have you actually changed?
options: You restored httpx's default behaviour, which has no timeout
You disabled all four timeouts, so a stalled read can hang the process indefinitely
You set an infinite connect timeout but kept the 5-second read timeout
Nothing — httpx ignores None and falls back to 5 seconds
questions.explain: httpx defaults to 5 seconds; timeout=None removes every timeout, so a connection that is accepted and then goes quiet blocks forever. The fix for genuine slowness is a larger per-kind timeout plus retries, never disabling.

questions.q: Ten HTTP calls take 0.9s each. Give the approximate wall time for (a) a sequential loop of awaits and (b) asyncio.gather, and explain the difference in one sentence.
questions.answer: Sequential is roughly 9 seconds (the sum of the latencies, since each await completes before the next starts); gather is roughly 1 second (about the slowest single call plus overhead), because all ten requests are in flight at once and the event loop resumes whichever coroutine's response arrives. The saving is waiting overlapped, not work parallelised — ten CPU-bound tasks would show no improvement.

questions.q: You are about to merge your own PR with nobody else to review it. Name three things self-reviewing the diff is likely to catch, and one thing the PR description should contain that the diff cannot.
questions.answer: Self-review typically catches leftover debug artefacts (breakpoint(), print statements), hard-coded paths or credentials, tests that assert nothing or were left skipped, unused code the linter did not flag, and unclear naming that only reads badly in diff form. The description must carry the why — the reason the change exists and the trade-off chosen — plus a how-to-verify command, because a diff shows what changed but never why it was worth changing.

title: APIs That Don't Fall Over
objective: Build, secure, harden, test and DEPLOY a real FastAPI service.
narrative: Every AI system you'll ever ship is wrapped in an API. This week you go from 'I've used FastAPI in a tutorial' to 'I deployed a service with auth, rate limits and tests, and I can explain every line.' Ship day is Day 6 — a real URL on the internet, cold starts and all.
whatYouCanBuild: A deployed, authenticated, rate-limited JSON API with tests — plus the vocabulary to discuss idempotency and error design in interviews.
whyProfessionally: AI Solutions and Applied AI roles are 60% backend engineering. FastAPI specifically is the lingua franca of AI services in 2026.

items.title: HTTP — methods, status codes, headers
items.concept:
A request is a method, a path, headers and (sometimes) a body. A response is a status line, headers and a body. That is the whole protocol, and every framework you will use is a way of producing the second from the first. Being able to read a raw exchange is what lets you debug across language and framework boundaries.

**The status codes that actually matter**, with the situation each one names: **200** OK (here is your result), **201** Created (a resource now exists — include a Location header), **204** No Content (done, deliberately nothing to say — typical for DELETE), **301** Moved Permanently (the path changed; note that clients historically rewrite POST to GET on 301/302, which is why **308** exists), **400** Bad Request (malformed at the protocol or syntax level), **401** Unauthorized (you have not authenticated — always send WWW-Authenticate or an equivalent hint), **403** Forbidden (authenticated, but not allowed), **404** Not Found (no such resource), **409** Conflict (state collision — duplicate key, version mismatch, edit conflict), **422** Unprocessable Content (syntactically fine, semantically invalid — FastAPI's validation default), **429** Too Many Requests (rate limited — send Retry-After), **500** Internal Server Error (we broke; never leak a traceback), **502/503** (upstream failed or we are temporarily unavailable — 503 pairs with Retry-After).

**Headers that earn their keep:** Content-Type (what the body is; get this wrong and parsers guess), Authorization (credentials), Retry-After (when to come back, in seconds or as a date), Location (where the created thing lives), Idempotency-Key (tomorrow), and X-Request-ID (Day 4, for tracing).

**Safe versus idempotent — memorise the table.** Safe means no observable state change: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS. Idempotent means N identical requests leave the same state as one: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE. POST is neither, and PATCH is idempotent only if you write it that way (setting a field is; incrementing one is not). Everything about retries, caching and proxy behaviour follows from this table.

The recurring sin in the exchanges below is returning a status code that describes a different situation from the one that occurred. Every wrong code is a lie your clients will encode into their retry logic.
items.why: Choosing the wrong status code is the API design mistake reviewers spot in ten seconds, and it breaks clients quietly — a 200 with an error body means every consumer must special-case your service instead of using standard error handling.

learn.focus: Read: 'Components of HTTP-based systems', 'Basic aspects of HTTP', 'HTTP flow' and 'HTTP Messages'. Skip: the protocol-version history and the 'APIs based on HTTP' section at the end.

Read the summary table, then the entries for GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE and HEAD. Read the safe / idempotent / cacheable properties in each entry carefully — that is the examinable part. Skip: CONNECT and TRACE.
Do not read all of them. Read the four class descriptions, then only these entries: 200, 201, 204, 301, 308, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 429, 500, 502, 503.

build.task: Annotate the three raw HTTP exchanges below: for each, name the situation, the status code that was returned, the correct code, and what the client will do wrong because of the mistake.
steps: For each exchange write four lines: situation, code returned, code that should have been returned, and the concrete client consequence
Exchange 1: ask what a generic client does with a 200 — does its error handling run at all?
Exchange 2: name TWO problems, the code and the body (what does the response leak, and to whom?)
Exchange 3: consider what a retrying client concludes from this code, and which header is missing that would have told it when to return
For each exchange, write the corrected response — status line, the one or two headers that should be present, and a one-line JSON error body
Sanity check your corrections against the safe/idempotent table: for the two POSTs, is retrying safe as designed?
build.hint: The tell in all three is the same question: if the only thing your client could see was the status line, would it behave correctly? Bodies are for humans; status codes are for machines.
build.code:
=== Exchange 1 === POST /v1/notes HTTP/1.1 Host: api.notes.dev Content-Type: application/json {"body": "Ring the auditor back before Friday"} HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: application/json {"ok": false, "error": "title is required"} === Exchange 2 === GET /v1/notes/9f3ac1 HTTP/1.1 Host: api.notes.dev Authorization: Bearer nk_live_8f2c1d HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error Content-Type: text/html 
KeyError: '9f3ac1'
  File 'store.py', line 41, in get_note
    return self._notes[note_id]
=== Exchange 3 === POST /v1/notes HTTP/1.1 Host: api.notes.dev Content-Type: application/json Idempotency-Key: 7c1e4b90-2f55-4a11-9a0e-2b6d5f0c1a33 {"title": "Audit", "body": "Ring back"} HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable Content-Type: application/json {"error": "rate limit exceeded: 5 requests per minute per key"}

items.challenge: Write the safe/idempotent table from memory (six methods, two columns), then decide for each one whether an automatic client retry after a timeout is acceptable. That table is the whole basis of tomorrow's idempotency lesson.

debugMission.scenario: An integration 'succeeds' every night and creates nothing. The client logs a successful POST, the server logs no created note, and nobody has looked at the status line for a fortnight.
debugMission.artifact:
# client, using httpx with follow_redirects=True
response = client.post('/v1/notes', json=note)
if response.status_code < 400:
    logger.info('note created id=%s',
                response.json().get('id'))

# wire trace
POST /v1/notes HTTP/1.1
Host: api.notes.dev
Content-Type: application/json

{"title": "Audit", "body": "Ring back"}

HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: /api/v1/notes

GET /api/v1/notes HTTP/1.1
Host: api.notes.dev

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
[]

# client log
INFO note created id=None
hints: Follow the trace: how many requests were sent, and what method was the second one?
The API moved its path prefix last month and left a 301 behind. What do clients historically do to a POST body when they follow a 301?
The client checks status_code < 400. Which perfectly ordinary success codes does that treat as 'it worked'?
debugMission.solution: The server answered the POST with a 301, and the client followed it — rewriting the method to GET and dropping the body, per the long-standing behaviour that 301 and 302 encode. It then received a 200 with an empty list, and the client's status_code < 400 check accepted it as success, logging an id of None every night. Three fixes, all worth making: point the client at the current path (redirects are not an integration strategy), have the server use 308 Permanent Redirect if it must redirect a POST, since 308 preserves method and body, and tighten the client to assert the specific expected code (201) plus the Location header rather than 'not an error'. General lesson: 'anything under 400' is not a success check — it silently accepts redirects, 204s and 202s that mean something entirely different from what you asked for.

reflection: For each of 401, 403, 404, 409 and 422, write the one-sentence situation that makes it the only right answer.
Which status code do you suspect you would have got wrong before today, and in which direction?
done: All three exchanges annotated with situation, wrong code, right code and client consequence
Corrected responses written out, including the missing header in each case
The safe/idempotent table reproduced from memory
You can explain why a 200 with an error body is worse than a 500

keyConcepts.def: N identical requests leave the resource in the same state as one — GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE; POST is not.
400 means the request was malformed; 422 means it parsed fine but the content is semantically invalid — FastAPI's validation default.
401 means not authenticated (credentials missing or bad); 403 means authenticated but not permitted.
Header telling a client when to come back, in seconds or as a date; belongs on every 429 and most 503s.

items.title: REST design and idempotency
items.concept:
REST resource naming is a small set of rules that make an API predictable: **plural nouns for collections** (/notes), **the identifier as a path segment** (/notes/{id}), **sub-resources for relationships** (/notes/{id}/tags), and **query parameters for filtering, sorting and pagination** (?tag=audit&limit=20&cursor=...). Verbs in paths are the smell — /createNote, /notes/{id}/delete, /getNotesByTag — because the method already is the verb.

**POST versus PUT versus PATCH.** POST creates a resource whose identity the server assigns (not idempotent). PUT replaces a resource wholesale at an identifier the client knows (idempotent: the same PUT twice leaves the same state). PATCH applies a partial change, idempotent only if the change is absolute rather than relative. If you can let the client choose the id, PUT gives you idempotency for free — that is a design lever, not a technicality.

**Why idempotency keys exist.** A client sends POST /payments, the response is lost to a timeout, and the client has no way to know whether the charge happened. Retrying might double-charge; not retrying might lose the payment. Stripe's answer is the canonical one: the client generates a unique key per logical operation and sends it as **Idempotency-Key**; the server stores the key with the response it produced, and if the same key arrives again it replays the stored response without re-executing. Same key plus a different body is a client bug and should be rejected (409). Keys have a retention window — Stripe's is 24 hours — because storing them forever is not free.

The rule that follows: **the key must be generated once per logical operation, not per attempt.** A key generated inside your retry loop is a new key every time, which is elaborate ceremony that changes nothing.

Design output today, code on Day 6: a notes service with list, create (idempotent), read, replace, patch and delete, an error envelope, pagination, and explicit status codes per operation. Deciding this on paper first is how professionals avoid discovering their API shape by accident.
items.why: 'How would you make this endpoint safe to retry?' is a standard interview question for backend and AI-platform roles, and every LLM endpoint you build is expensive enough that duplicate execution costs real money.

learn.focus: Read the whole page — it is short: the Idempotency-Key header, how a repeated key replays the original response, the retention window, and what happens when the same key arrives with different parameters.

Skim only, as a reference: the URL structure and naming section, the standard request/response headers section, and the HTTP status code guidance. Do not read it end to end — use it to settle arguments later.

build.task: Write the design document (markdown) for the notes API you will implement on Day 6, including an idempotent create.
steps: Resource table: for each of GET /notes, POST /notes, GET /notes/{id}, PUT /notes/{id}, PATCH /notes/{id}, DELETE /notes/{id} give the purpose, success status, and every error status it can return
Schemas: NoteIn (title, body, tags) and NoteOut (id, title, body, tags, created_at, updated_at) — note explicitly which fields are server-owned and must never be accepted from a client
Pagination: choose limit + cursor (or limit + offset) and write one sentence justifying the choice for a notes list
Idempotent create: specify the Idempotency-Key header, the storage shape (key -> status, body, created_at), the TTL, and the response when the same key returns with a different body
Error envelope: fix the shape now — {'error': {'code': 'not_found', 'message': '...', 'request_id': '...'}} — and list the codes you will use
Write the three curl-shaped example exchanges you would put in a README: create, replay of the same key, and a validation failure
Review your own document against the verbs-in-paths smell and the safe/idempotent table; fix anything that fails either check
build.hint: Decide now whether DELETE on a missing note returns 404 or 204. Both are defensible; 204 makes DELETE genuinely idempotent, which is usually what a retrying client wants. Write down which you chose and why — that sentence is the interview answer.
build.code:
# design.md — extract

## POST /notes  (create, idempotent via header)
Request headers:
  Content-Type: application/json
  X-API-Key: <key>
  Idempotency-Key: <uuid4, one per logical create>

201 Created
  Location: /notes/{id}
  body: NoteOut
200 OK        replay of a stored response for a seen key
409 Conflict  same key, different request body
422           validation failed (envelope)
429           rate limited (Retry-After header)

## Idempotency store
key -> {
  'request_hash': sha256 of the canonical body,
  'status': 201,
  'response': <serialised NoteOut>,
  'created_at': epoch seconds,
}
TTL: 24 hours; sweep on read.

## Error envelope (every 4xx and 5xx)
{
  "error": {
    "code": "validation_error",
    "message": "title must not be empty",
    "request_id": "3f8c1d2a"
  }
}

items.challenge: Add an optimistic-concurrency section: PUT /notes/{id} with If-Match and an ETag so two editors cannot silently overwrite each other, returning 412 Precondition Failed. You will not build it this week, but knowing the shape is what separates 'CRUD' from 'API design'.

debugMission.scenario: A payments integration duplicated 14 charges during an upstream wobble. The team had implemented idempotency keys weeks earlier, and the server-side logic is provably correct — every duplicate had a different key.
hints: The server replays a response only when it sees the SAME key twice. Look at the three keys in the log.
Where in the code is uuid4() called, and how many times does that line run during four retry attempts?
What is the logical operation here — the HTTP attempt, or the charge?
debugMission.solution: The key is generated inside the retried function, so every attempt sends a fresh uuid4 and the server correctly treats each one as a new operation — the idempotency mechanism was working perfectly on data that made it meaningless. The key must identify the logical operation, so generate it once by the caller and pass it in: create_charge(client, payload, idempotency_key) with the retry decorator on that function, so all four attempts carry the same key. The 504 also matters: a timeout means unknown, not failed, and unknown is exactly the state idempotency keys exist to resolve. General lesson: an idempotency key belongs to the business operation, and any code path that can regenerate it per attempt (a default argument evaluated per call, a key derived from time, a key created inside the retry) silently disables the entire protection.

reflection: Which of your notes endpoints are naturally idempotent, and which needed a design decision to become so?
Explain to a PM in two sentences why a duplicate charge is an engineering design problem rather than a bug someone introduced.
done: design.md exists with a resource table covering six operations and every status code each can return
NoteIn and NoteOut are specified with server-owned fields marked
The idempotent-create design names the header, the store shape, the TTL and the same-key-different-body behaviour
The error envelope shape and its code vocabulary are fixed in writing
No verbs appear in any path

keyConcepts.def: A client-generated identifier for one logical operation; the server stores its response and replays it if the key repeats.
Plural nouns for collections, identifiers as path segments, filters as query parameters — the method supplies the verb.
PUT replaces a resource at a client-known id and is idempotent; POST creates under a server-assigned id and is not.
One fixed error body shape (code, message, request_id) used by every failure so clients parse errors one way.

items.title: FastAPI — first endpoints
items.concept:
FastAPI is your Week-1 typing discipline turned into a web framework. You annotate a function's parameters; the framework parses the request, validates it against those types, returns 422 with a precise error when it fails, and generates OpenAPI documentation from the same annotations. Nothing is declared twice.

**The three parameter sources.** A parameter whose name matches a segment in the path template is a **path parameter**; a parameter typed as a Pydantic model is a **body** (tomorrow); everything else is a **query parameter**. Constraints ride along with Annotated: **Annotated[int, Query(ge=1, le=100)] = 20** gives a default of 20, rejects 0 and 500 with a 422, and documents the range in /docs automatically.

**Enums for closed sets.** A path or query parameter typed as a str Enum accepts only the listed values and rejects everything else with 422 before your function runs — so your handler never contains 'if exchange not in (...)'. Validation at the boundary, exactly as in Week 1, now enforced by the framework.

**Route order matters** because matching is top-down: define /instruments/summary before /instruments/{isin}, or the literal path will be swallowed as an isin. This bites everyone once.

**The dev loop:** uv run uvicorn aie_lab.api.main:app --reload starts a server that restarts on save. Open /docs once, marvel at the interactive documentation you did not write, submit one request through it — then close the tab. It is a debugging convenience, not a test suite, and treating it as one is how people ship endpoints they have never called from code.

Return types are annotations too: '-> Instrument' makes FastAPI serialise and filter the response through that model, which is tomorrow's response_model lesson arriving early.
items.why: FastAPI is the default framework for AI services in 2026 — every model-serving example, every vendor SDK sample, every job description. The type-driven validation you get here is also the reason LLM services written in it are less fragile than the Flask equivalents.

learn.focus: Read: the minimal app, running with uvicorn, 'Check it' and the interactive docs, and 'Recap, step by step'. Skip: the OpenAPI schema internals and the alternative API docs section.

Read: Path parameters, 'Path parameters with types', 'Data validation', 'Order matters', and 'Predefined values' (the Enum section — that is the part you will use today). Skip: 'Path parameters containing paths'.

Read: Query parameters, defaults, optional parameters, type conversion and required query parameters. Then follow the single link to 'Query Parameters and String Validations' and read the Annotated + Query(...) form with ge/le/max_length.

build.task: Create the aie-lab API package with /health and two instrument endpoints using enum path validation and constrained query parameters.
steps: uv add fastapi 'uvicorn[standard]'; create src/aie_lab/api/__init__.py and src/aie_lab/api/main.py with app = FastAPI(title='aie-lab', version='0.3.0')
GET /health returning {'status': 'ok', 'version': ...} — no auth, no dependencies, because Render will call it every 30 seconds
GET /instruments/{isin}: isin as Annotated[str, Path(min_length=12, max_length=12)]; look up in the Week-1 fixture data; raise HTTPException(404) when absent
GET /instruments: query parameters exchange (an Exchange str Enum, optional), limit (Annotated[int, Query(ge=1, le=100)] = 20) and offset (ge=0, default 0)
Add GET /instruments/summary and place it ABOVE the {isin} route; prove the ordering trap by moving it below and watching it 404 as an invalid isin
Run uv run uvicorn aie_lab.api.main:app --reload; exercise each endpoint with curl, including limit=0 and limit=500 to see the 422 body shape
Read one 422 response carefully: loc, msg, type — that structure is what you will wrap in your own envelope on Day 3
build.hint: Import Annotated from typing and Query/Path from fastapi. If a query parameter shows up as required when you meant it optional, you gave it a constraint but no default — the default lives outside the Annotated brackets.

items.challenge: Add ?sort=price|-price using a str Enum, and return 422 for anything else. Then open /docs and check that a stranger could use your API from the generated documentation alone — if they could not, your annotations are underspecified.

debugMission.scenario: A pagination endpoint works from /docs but crashes when called by the fetcher. The traceback blames a slice, which the author insists is fine because 'limit is obviously an integer'.
debugMission.artifact:
@app.get('/instruments')
def list_instruments(limit=20, offset=0):
    rows = list(STORE.values())
    return rows[offset:offset + limit]

$ curl 'api.notes.dev/instruments?limit=5'
HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error

# server traceback
  File 'main.py', line 4, in list_instruments
    return rows[offset:offset + limit]
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not 'int') to str

# but this works
$ curl 'api.notes.dev/instruments'
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
hints: The call with no query parameters works; the call with limit=5 does not. What is different about the value the function receives?
How does FastAPI know a parameter should be an int? What did the signature tell it?
Query strings are text. Something has to convert them, and something has to be told what to convert them to.
debugMission.solution: The parameters carry no type annotations, so FastAPI has nothing to validate or convert against and passes the raw query string through: limit arrives as the string '5', and '0' + '5' fails at the slice. With the default values it never touches a query value, which is why the bare call succeeds. Fix: annotate them — limit: Annotated[int, Query(ge=1, le=100)] = 20 and offset: Annotated[int, Query(ge=0)] = 0 — and FastAPI both converts and rejects out-of-range values with a 422 before your code runs. General lesson: in FastAPI the annotation IS the validation, so an unannotated parameter silently opts out of the entire safety mechanism. This is the Week-1 typing lesson with a 500 attached: types you skip become runtime errors somebody else finds.

reflection: Which validations did you get for free that you would otherwise have hand-written in the handler?
Why is /health deliberately the dullest endpoint in the service?
done: uvicorn serves /health, /instruments/summary, /instruments/{isin} and /instruments
limit=0 and limit=500 both return 422, and an invalid exchange value does too
You demonstrated the route-ordering trap and fixed it
You can name the three sources FastAPI reads parameters from

keyConcepts.def: FastAPI parses, converts and validates request data from the annotations alone, returning 422 before your handler runs.
Attaches constraints (ge, le, max_length) and documentation to a parameter while keeping the plain default outside the brackets.
Routes match top-down, so literal paths must be declared before parameterised ones that would otherwise swallow them.

items.title: Bodies and response models
items.concept:
A parameter annotated with a Pydantic model is the request body. FastAPI reads the JSON, validates it against the model, and hands your function a typed object — or returns 422 with the exact field paths that failed, before a line of your code runs. This is Week 1's validate-at-the-boundary rule, now enforced by the framework.

**Input and output models are different models.** SummarizeIn(text, max_words) is what you accept; SummarizeOut(summary, word_count) is what you return. Declaring the return type (or response_model=) filters the response through that model, so anything not on it — internal ids, the raw prompt, a user's email, the API key that reached the handler — cannot leak even if your handler returns an object that carries it. The FastAPI docs' password example is the whole lesson: a model with a password field, filtered by an output model without one.

**Status codes belong on the decorator:** @app.post('/notes', status_code=201). Creation returns 201, not 200.

**Constraints live in the model, not in your handler.** Field(min_length=1, max_length=5000) for text, Field(ge=10, le=500) for max_words. When the constraint is in the model, the 422 explains itself and the /docs schema shows the limit; when it is an if-statement in your handler, only you know.

Today's endpoint is deliberately a fake summariser — first sentence plus a word count. In Week 4 the body of this exact function becomes an LLM call, and nothing else about the endpoint changes: same request model, same response model, same validation, same tests. That is the point of building it now.
items.why: Response models are the cheapest data-leak prevention in existence, and the request/response contract you fix today is what your Week-4 LLM endpoints inherit. Leaking internal fields in a JSON response is a genuine security incident, not a style issue.

learn.focus: Read: importing BaseModel, creating and declaring the model, 'Results', 'Request body + path parameters' and 'Request body + path + query parameters'. Skip: the 'Without Pydantic' note at the end.

Read: 'Return type' and response_model, then 'Add an output model' carefully — the password-leak example is the entire lesson. Also read response_model_exclude_unset. Skip: the list/union response-model variants for now.

build.task: Build POST /summarize with validated request and filtered response models, returning 201 and rejecting oversized text with a useful 422.
steps: Create src/aie_lab/api/schemas.py: SummarizeIn(text: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=5000), max_words: int = Field(default=50, ge=10, le=500))
SummarizeOut(summary: str, word_count: int) — and deliberately have your internal function return a richer object (with prompt_used and elapsed_ms) so the filtering has something to filter
Implement the fake summariser: first sentence, truncated to max_words, with the true word count of the summary
Wire @app.post('/summarize', status_code=201, response_model=SummarizeOut) (or the return-type annotation) and confirm prompt_used never appears in the response
Test the edges with curl: empty text, 5001 characters, max_words=5, max_words=501 — read each 422 body and note that the limit value appears in the error
Add a nested model: SummarizeIn.options: Options(style: Literal['plain','bullets'] = 'plain') and confirm nested validation errors report the full path, options.style
Write the three-line docstring on the endpoint and check it renders in /docs — free documentation for whoever integrates
build.hint: Do not hand-write the 'text too long' check. Field(max_length=5000) produces a 422 whose message already contains the limit, and one source of truth for the number.
build.code:
from typing import Literal
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class Options(BaseModel):
    style: Literal['plain', 'bullets'] = 'plain'

class SummarizeIn(BaseModel):
    text: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=5000)
    max_words: int = Field(default=50, ge=10, le=500)
    options: Options = Options()

class SummarizeOut(BaseModel):
    summary: str
    word_count: int

class SummaryInternal(BaseModel):
    summary: str
    word_count: int
    prompt_used: str
    elapsed_ms: float

@app.post('/summarize', status_code=201,
          response_model=SummarizeOut)
def summarize(payload: SummarizeIn) -> SummaryInternal:
    'Summarise text. In Week 4 the body of this function becomes an LLM call.'
    first = payload.text.split('.')[0].strip()
    words = first.split()[:payload.max_words]
    return SummaryInternal(
        summary=' '.join(words),
        word_count=len(words),
        prompt_used='fake-summariser-v1',
        elapsed_ms=0.4,
    )

items.challenge: Add a model_validator on SummarizeIn rejecting text whose word count is already below max_words (there is nothing to summarise) with a message naming both numbers. Cross-field validation belongs in the model, not in the handler.

debugMission.scenario: A code review flags that POST /summarize 'accepts anything'. The reviewer's evidence: a request with no text field at all returned 500 rather than 422, and a request with max_words set to the string 'lots' was accepted.
hints: What did the annotation tell FastAPI to validate the body against?
A dict is a perfectly valid type. Which fields does it require, and which value types does it constrain?
Also look at what came back in the response body — is anything there that a client should not see?
debugMission.solution: The body is annotated as dict, so FastAPI validates only that the payload is a JSON object — no required fields, no types, no constraints — and every guarantee you thought you had was actually a .get() with a default. Missing text produced a silent empty summary with a 201, and a string max_words reached a slice and became a 500. There is a second bug in the same six lines: with no response model, prompt_used leaks to the client. Fix: annotate the body as SummarizeIn and the response as SummarizeOut. General lesson: dict and Any as body annotations switch off the entire validation layer while looking like ordinary typing, and an endpoint with no response model returns whatever the handler happens to build — including fields nobody meant to publish.

reflection: Which internal field in your own service would be most damaging to leak through a response, and what stops it today?
Why is a constraint in the model better than the identical check in the handler?
done: POST /summarize returns 201 with only summary and word_count in the body
Empty text, oversized text and out-of-range max_words all return 422 with the limit visible in the message
prompt_used exists internally and provably never reaches a client
Nested validation errors report the full field path
You reproduced the dict-typed-body bug and can explain both defects it caused

keyConcepts.def: A Pydantic-typed parameter that FastAPI validates before the handler runs, returning 422 with exact field paths on failure.
The output schema a response is filtered through, so internal fields cannot leak regardless of what the handler returns.
Typing a body as dict or Any accepts any JSON object, silently disabling all field and type checking.

items.title: Dependency injection
items.concept:
A dependency is a function whose return value FastAPI passes into your handler: **settings: Annotated[Settings, Depends(get_settings)]**. FastAPI calls get_settings for each request that needs it, resolves anything IT depends on first, and caches the result within a single request so a dependency shared by three others runs once.

**Why this beats module-level globals**: overrides. In tests, app.dependency_overrides[get_settings] = lambda: Settings(api_key='test-key') replaces the real provider for that test and nothing else changes — no environment juggling, no monkeypatching of import paths, no risk of a test hitting a live service. Compare with a module-level 'settings = Settings()' evaluated at import: to change it you must patch every module that imported it, which is exactly the Week-2 patch-path bug waiting to happen.

**The three shapes you need this week.** A **cached provider**: get_settings decorated with functools.lru_cache so the config is parsed once per process rather than per request. A **resource provider with lifecycle**: get_client yielding a shared httpx.AsyncClient, created at startup via lifespan and closed at shutdown — never one client per request. A **parameter bundle**: a pagination dependency returning a small object from limit and offset query parameters, reused across every list endpoint so the constraints are defined once.

**Dependencies compose.** A dependency can itself declare dependencies, so require_api_key can depend on get_settings, and an endpoint just asks for require_api_key. You can also attach dependencies that return nothing to a route or a whole router (dependencies=[Depends(require_api_key)]) purely for their side effect of enforcing something — that is how Day 4 protects a set of routes in one line.

Async and sync both work: a 'def' dependency runs in a threadpool, an 'async def' one runs on the loop. Follow Week 2's rule — if it does I/O, it should be async, and it must not block.
items.why: Dependency overrides are what make a FastAPI service testable at all; without them your test suite needs real config, real credentials and a real network. Every AI service you build will inject a settings object, an HTTP client and an auth check exactly this way.

learn.focus: Read: 'First steps', 'What is Dependency Injection', 'To async or not to async', and 'Share Annotated dependencies' (the type-alias trick you will use everywhere). Then follow the link to 'Dependencies with yield' and read the setup/teardown pattern. Skip: classes as dependencies on first pass.

build.task: Wire Settings and a shared httpx client into your endpoints as dependencies, then override both in a test.
steps: src/aie_lab/api/deps.py: get_settings() decorated with @lru_cache returning Settings(); alias SettingsDep = Annotated[Settings, Depends(get_settings)]
Add a lifespan context manager on the app that creates one httpx.AsyncClient at startup (with the Week-2 Timeout) and closes it at shutdown; store it on app.state
get_client(request: Request) -> httpx.AsyncClient returning request.app.state.client; alias ClientDep
Pagination dependency: def pagination(limit: Annotated[int, Query(ge=1, le=100)] = 20, offset: Annotated[int, Query(ge=0)] = 0) -> Page; use it on /instruments and remove the duplicated parameters
Refactor at least two endpoints to take SettingsDep instead of importing a module-level settings object

Write a test using TestClient with app.dependency_overrides[get_settings] = lambda: Settings(api_key='test-key', api_base_url='...'), assert the endpoint behaves, then clear the overrides in a fixture teardown

Prove the caching: add a print or counter inside get_settings, call an endpoint that depends on it twice in one request path, and confirm it runs once per request (and once per process with lru_cache)
build.hint: Define the Annotated aliases once in deps.py and import those. Repeating Annotated[Settings, Depends(get_settings)] in twelve signatures is how the override you forgot to update becomes a mystery.
build.code:
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from functools import lru_cache
from typing import Annotated

import httpx
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, Query, Request

from aie_lab.core.config import Settings

@lru_cache
def get_settings() -> Settings:
    return Settings()

SettingsDep = Annotated[Settings, Depends(get_settings)]

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    app.state.client = httpx.AsyncClient(
        timeout=httpx.Timeout(connect=3.0, read=10.0,
                              write=10.0, pool=5.0))
    yield
    await app.state.client.aclose()

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)

def get_client(request: Request) -> httpx.AsyncClient:
    return request.app.state.client

ClientDep = Annotated[httpx.AsyncClient, Depends(get_client)]

# tests/api/conftest.py
@pytest.fixture
def client() -> Iterator[TestClient]:
    app.dependency_overrides[get_settings] = (
        lambda: Settings(api_key='test-key'))
    with TestClient(app) as test_client:
        yield test_client
    app.dependency_overrides.clear()

items.challenge: Add a dependency that returns a request-scoped 'context' object (request id, start time, resolved API key name) and inject it into two endpoints. That object becomes the thing you log and the thing you attach to error envelopes tomorrow.

debugMission.scenario: An endpoint that depends on Settings returns a 500 at startup of the first request, with a validation error mentioning a field the developer is certain they never asked for. The same code works when the function is called directly.
hints: Read the traceback location: this fired at import time, not during a request. What ran when the module was defined?
Compare Depends(get_settings) with Depends(get_settings()) character by character.
If FastAPI never holds a reference to your provider function, what is there for dependency_overrides to replace?
debugMission.solution: Depends(get_settings()) calls the function immediately at import time and hands FastAPI the resulting object as a fixed default, so config is read while the module loads (crashing before the app can even start when an env var is absent) and the override registry has no provider to replace — dependency_overrides matches on the function object, which FastAPI never received. Fix: pass the function, not its result — Depends(get_settings), ideally through the SettingsDep alias so the mistake cannot be made twice. General lesson: Depends takes a callable, and the parentheses are the difference between 'resolve this per request, overridable in tests' and 'evaluate this once at import, forever'.

reflection: Which globals in your service are secretly hard to test, and which of them should become dependencies?
Why does one shared httpx client at app lifespan beat creating one per request?
done: get_settings is cached and injected via an Annotated alias in at least two endpoints
One httpx.AsyncClient is created in lifespan and closed at shutdown, injected as a dependency
A pagination dependency replaces duplicated limit/offset parameters
A test overrides both providers via dependency_overrides and clears them afterwards
You reproduced the Depends(get_settings()) bug and can explain both symptoms it caused

keyConcepts.def: Declares a request-scoped provider whose return value is injected into the handler; results are cached within one request.
Test-time registry mapping a provider function to a replacement, giving fake settings, clients or auth without patching imports.
Async context manager running startup and shutdown code — where shared resources like an HTTP client are created and closed.

items.title: Errors as API design
items.concept:
Your error responses are part of your API contract, and clients depend on them more heavily than on your success payloads — success is handled once, failure is handled in five places.

**One envelope, everywhere:** {'error': {'code': 'not_found', 'message': 'note 9f3ac1 does not exist', 'request_id': '3f8c1d2a'}}. **code** is a stable machine-readable string clients can branch on (never the human message, which you will reword next month). **message** is for a developer reading logs. **request_id** is what a customer quotes in a support email and what you grep for.

**HTTPException** covers the local case: raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail='note not found') inside a handler. But your Week-1 exception taxonomy is raised deep in the core, far from any handler, and that is where **exception handlers** earn their place: @app.exception_handler(DataFetchError) registers a function that turns any escape of that type into a proper response, anywhere in the call stack. The mapping for this service: DataFetchError to 502 (an upstream we depend on failed), DataParseError to 502 as well (they sent us nonsense), your own validation errors to 422, and everything unhandled to 500 with a generic message.

**FastAPI's own errors need wrapping too.** A request that fails Pydantic validation raises RequestValidationError, which FastAPI answers with its default {'detail': [...]} shape — which is NOT your envelope. Register a handler for it (and for Starlette's HTTPException) so every failure your API can produce has one shape. A client that must parse two different error formats will parse one of them wrongly.

**Never leak internals.** A 500 body says 'internal error' and carries the request_id; the traceback goes to your logs, at ERROR, with logger.exception. Stack traces in responses hand an attacker your file layout, library versions and sometimes your queries.
items.why: Consistent error envelopes are what let a client write one error handler instead of five, and 'never leak stack traces' is a security requirement, not a preference. Interviewers ask what your 500 body contains — the answer reveals whether you have run anything in production.

learn.focus: Read: 'Use HTTPException', 'Add custom headers', 'Install custom exception handlers', 'Override the default exception handlers' (both the RequestValidationError and HTTPException overrides), and 'Reuse FastAPI's exception handlers'. It is all directly applicable today.

build.task: Give the service one error envelope, produced by handlers for your domain errors, validation errors and unhandled exceptions.
steps: src/aie_lab/api/errors.py: an ErrorBody Pydantic model and a helper error_response(status, code, message, request_id) returning JSONResponse in the envelope shape
Register @app.exception_handler(DataFetchError) -> 502 with code 'upstream_unavailable', and DataParseError -> 502 with code 'upstream_bad_payload'; log both with logger.exception
Register a handler for RequestValidationError converting FastAPI's detail list into your envelope with code 'validation_error' and a message naming the first failing field
Register a handler for Starlette's HTTPException so 404s raised with HTTPException also come out in the envelope, preserving the status code
Register a catch-all Exception handler returning 500 with code 'internal_error' and a generic message — plus the full traceback in the logs, never in the body
Pull request_id from request.state (Day 4's middleware sets it; until then default to a uuid4 hex) so every error body carries one
Tests: assert the envelope shape for 404, 422, 502 and 500, and assert no response body anywhere contains the word Traceback or a file path
build.hint: Handlers are matched by exception class including subclasses, so registering AppError alone would catch everything in your Week-1 hierarchy. Register the specific ones first if you want different status codes — and keep the mapping in one dict so the policy is readable in one place.

items.challenge: Add a docs section listing every error code your API can return, with the status and the client's recommended action (retry, fix request, contact support). That table is what a client integration engineer actually needs, and almost nobody writes it.

debugMission.scenario: A client integration crashes on invalid input. The team's error envelope is implemented and tested, and every handler test is green — but the client's parser throws a KeyError on 'error' for exactly one class of failure.
debugMission.artifact:
@app.exception_handler(AppError)
async def handle_app_error(request, exc):
    return envelope(502, 'upstream_unavailable',
                    str(exc), rid(request))

# tests/api/test_errors.py  (all passing)
def test_fetch_error_envelope(client):
    body = client.get('/instruments/BADISIN000X').json()
    assert body['error']['code'] == 'upstream_unavailable'

# client-side crash, from production logs
POST /summarize  422
response body:
{"detail": [{"type": "string_too_short",
  "loc": ["body", "text"], "msg": "String should have at
  least 1 character", "input": ""}]}
KeyError: 'error'
hints: Which exception type produced this response, and is it one of yours?
The handler is registered for AppError. Where does a Pydantic body-validation failure sit in that hierarchy?
List every way your API can produce a 4xx or 5xx, then check which of them pass through a handler you wrote.
debugMission.solution: Body validation failures raise FastAPI's RequestValidationError, which is not part of the Week-1 AppError hierarchy, so it never reaches the custom handler and FastAPI answers with its built-in {'detail': [...]} shape. The envelope was real but partial, and the tests only exercised the domain errors, so nothing caught it. Fix: register handlers for RequestValidationError and for Starlette's HTTPException as well, mapping both into the envelope, and add tests that assert the envelope shape for a 422 and a 404, not only for the domain errors. General lesson: an error contract must cover every error the framework can emit, not only the ones you raise deliberately — enumerate the failure sources (validation, routing 404, method not allowed, auth, rate limit, domain, unhandled) and check each one against the contract.

reflection: What does your 500 body contain, exactly, and what would an attacker learn from it?
Why should clients branch on a code string rather than on the message text?
done: Every 4xx and 5xx your API can produce comes back in the same envelope, proven by tests for 404, 422, 502 and 500
Domain errors map to deliberate status codes via exception handlers, not try/except in handlers
No response body contains a traceback, file path or library name; the logs contain all three
Every error body carries a request_id

keyConcepts.def: A single response shape for all failures (code, message, request_id) so clients parse errors one way.
An app-level function that converts an exception type raised anywhere in the stack into a response, keeping handlers free of error plumbing.
FastAPI's own validation failure; it bypasses your domain-error handlers unless you register one for it explicitly.

items.title: Auth — API keys now, OAuth2/JWT understood
items.concept:
Two ideas people constantly merge: **authentication** is who you are, **authorisation** is what you may do. 401 answers the first (no or bad credentials), 403 answers the second (known caller, not permitted). Getting these backwards is the most common auth bug in code review.

**Tier 1, which you build today: API keys.** A key is a long random string sent in a header (X-API-Key). It is appropriate for server-to-server calls, internal tools and early-stage products — which is nearly everything you will build this quarter. Three rules that separate a real implementation from a toy: keys come from Settings or a store, never from source; comparison uses **secrets.compare_digest** rather than == so response timing cannot leak the key one character at a time; and the key is never logged, only a stable prefix or hash for identification.

FastAPI supplies **APIKeyHeader** and **Security()**, which wire the key into the OpenAPI schema so /docs grows an authorise button. Attach the dependency to a router (dependencies=[Depends(require_api_key)]) so protection is a property of the route group and cannot be forgotten on a new endpoint.

**Tier 2, which you must understand rather than build: OAuth2 with JWT.** Walk the flow with the docs open: the client posts credentials to a token endpoint; the server verifies them (against a password hash — argon2 or bcrypt, never your own scheme) and returns a signed **JWT**. A JWT is three base64url segments — header, claims payload, signature — where the claims carry sub (the subject), exp (expiry) and often scopes. The client sends 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' and the server verifies the signature with its secret or public key and checks exp. Critically, **the payload is signed, not encrypted**: anyone can read it, so it holds identity and permissions, never secrets.

Two things you should be able to say in an interview: you never roll your own crypto or token format, and stateless JWTs are hard to revoke before expiry — which is why refresh tokens and short expiries exist.

**Scopes** are the bridge to authorisation: a key or token carries a set of permissions (notes:read, notes:write), and a dependency compares required against granted. Missing scope is 403, not 401 — the caller is perfectly well authenticated.
items.why: Every AI service you deploy is a key away from someone else's bill: an unauthenticated LLM endpoint on a public URL is a cost incident waiting to happen. API-key auth done properly is the minimum bar for anything you show a client.

learn.focus: Read the whole page for the mental model: what a security dependency is, how OAuth2PasswordBearer becomes an /docs authorise button, and the explicit note that it verifies nothing by itself. You are reading for shape, not to implement it.

Read for understanding only, do not implement: 'About JWT', the password-hashing section (note that a library does it), token creation with an expiry claim, and 'Update the dependencies' where the token is decoded and verified. Skip: the scopes chapter that follows.

build.task: Protect the write endpoints with API-key auth: correct 401 versus 403, constant-time comparison, keys from Settings.
steps: Extend Settings with api_keys: dict[str, KeyRecord] mapping a client name to {key, scopes}, loaded from an env var as JSON; never a literal key in code
src/aie_lab/api/security.py: api_key_header = APIKeyHeader(name='X-API-Key', auto_error=False) so YOU control the failure status

require_api_key dependency: no header -> 401 with code 'unauthenticated' and a WWW-Authenticate-style hint; header present but unknown -> 401 'invalid_key'; use secrets.compare_digest against each configured key
Return a small Principal object (key_name, scopes) from the dependency so handlers know who is calling without re-parsing the header
Add require_scope('notes:write') as a dependency factory: authenticated but missing scope -> 403 with code 'forbidden'
Attach the dependency to the protected routes (or the router) and leave /health open; confirm /docs shows the authorise control
Tests: no header -> 401, wrong key -> 401, valid key without scope -> 403, valid key with scope -> 200; and assert no log line contains the key value
build.hint: Set auto_error=False on APIKeyHeader. With the default, FastAPI raises its own 403 when the header is missing — which is the wrong code for 'you did not authenticate' and is exactly the bug in today's mission.

items.challenge: Add key rotation: Settings holds a current and a previous key per client, both accepted, with a log line at WARNING when the previous one is used. Rotation without downtime is a five-line feature that clients ask about constantly.

debugMission.scenario: The auth test suite has one stubborn failure: a request with no API key at all returns 403 instead of the 401 the spec demands. The dependency clearly raises 401, and the developer has added print statements that never fire.
debugMission.artifact:
api_key_header = APIKeyHeader(name='X-API-Key')

def require_api_key(
    settings: SettingsDep,
    presented: Annotated[str, Security(api_key_header)],
) -> Principal:
    print('dependency running')  # never printed
    if presented is None:
        raise HTTPException(401, detail='unauthenticated')
    ...

# tests
def test_missing_key_is_401(client):
    response = client.post('/summarize', json=PAYLOAD)
    assert response.status_code == 401

# E  assert 403 == 401
# E  response.json() == {'detail': 'Not authenticated'}

def test_bad_key_is_401(client):        # PASSES
    response = client.post('/summarize', json=PAYLOAD,
                           headers={'X-API-Key': 'nope'})
    assert response.status_code == 401
hints: Your print never runs, so the 403 is produced before your dependency does. Who else is in the chain?
The wrong-key test passes and the missing-key test fails. What is different about the two paths through APIKeyHeader?
Look up the auto_error parameter and what APIKeyHeader raises when the header is absent.
debugMission.solution: APIKeyHeader defaults to auto_error=True, so when the header is missing the security scheme itself raises before your dependency body runs — and it raises 403 'Not authenticated', which is both the wrong code and the wrong layer for your error envelope. With a header present but wrong, the scheme passes the value through and your own 401 fires, which is why only one test failed. Fix: APIKeyHeader(name='X-API-Key', auto_error=False) and annotate the parameter as str | None, then raise your own 401 for the missing case. General lesson: framework-supplied auth helpers have opinions about status codes; when your API has a documented error contract, take control of the failure path (auto_error=False) rather than inheriting a default that contradicts your own spec — and remember 401 means unauthenticated, 403 means authenticated-but-not-allowed.

reflection: Explain to a PM in two sentences why the API key must never appear in a log line, even at DEBUG.
A client asks 'why not just use JWTs?'. Give a two-sentence answer that covers when each is appropriate.
done: Protected routes return 401 with no key, 401 with a bad key, 403 with a valid key lacking the scope, and 200 otherwise

No log line or error body contains a key value, verified by a test
/health remains open and /docs shows the authorise control
You can narrate the OAuth2 password + JWT flow end to end without notes

keyConcepts.def: Who you are (401 when it fails) versus what you may do (403 when it fails).
secrets.compare_digest compares secrets without an early exit, so response timing cannot reveal a key character by character.
A signed (not encrypted) token carrying claims such as subject, expiry and scopes; readable by anyone, verifiable only with the key.
A named permission attached to a key or token; a missing scope is a 403 because the caller is authenticated but not permitted.

items.title: Middleware — request IDs and timing
items.concept:
**Middleware wraps every request**; a dependency runs only for the routes that ask for it. Choose by scope: cross-cutting concerns that must apply to unknown future endpoints — request ids, timing, CORS, compression — are middleware. Anything that produces a value your handler uses, or that only some routes need, is a dependency. Auth is the interesting boundary case: as a dependency it appears in /docs and can be overridden in tests, which is why it belongs there.

**Request IDs make logs answerable.** Generate a uuid4 hex per request unless the caller supplied X-Request-ID (honour it — that is how a trace survives across services), store it on request.state, log it with every line the request produces, and return it in the response header. When a customer says 'it failed at 14:02', one grep for their id yields the entire story instead of a thousand interleaved lines from concurrent requests.

To get the id into log lines that are emitted deep in your core code, a **contextvars.ContextVar** set by the middleware and read by a logging filter is the pattern that survives async: unlike thread locals, a ContextVar is correct when hundreds of coroutines interleave on one thread.

**Timing** costs one line: perf_counter before call_next, subtract after, add X-Response-Time-Ms to the response and duration_ms to the log. Do it now and you will have latency data on day one of the deployment rather than adding it during your first incident.

Order matters: middleware added later wraps earlier ones (the last-added runs first on the way in), so the request-id middleware must be outermost if the timing middleware's logs are to carry the id. And CORS, which you need the moment a browser calls your API from another origin, is a middleware you configure rather than write: allowed origins, methods and headers — with a real list of origins, never a wildcard alongside credentials.
items.why: Request IDs are the difference between debugging a production incident in ten minutes and doing archaeology for two hours. Every service you deploy from here on gets this middleware on day one, and interviewers treat 'how do you trace a request' as a proxy for operational experience.

learn.focus: Read the whole page — it is short: the @app.middleware('http') decorator, the call_next contract, adding a response header, the timing example (which is nearly today's build), and the note about where middleware sits relative to dependencies and exception handlers.

build.task: Add middleware that assigns a request id and duration, exposes both as response headers, and puts the id into every log line for that request.
steps: src/aie_lab/api/middleware.py: an @app.middleware('http') function reading X-Request-ID from the incoming headers or generating uuid4().hex[:12]
Set request.state.request_id and a contextvars.ContextVar so code far from the handler can read it

Time the request with time.perf_counter() around call_next; add X-Request-ID and X-Response-Time-Ms headers to the response
Log one structured line per request at INFO: method, path, status, duration_ms, request_id, and the principal name when authenticated
Wire the id into the Day-3 error envelope so a failed request's body and headers carry the same id

Test it: assert response.headers['x-request-id'] is present, that supplying your own id echoes it back rather than replacing it, and (with caplog) that a log record from inside the handler carries the SAME id as the header
build.hint: Do not read the request body in middleware. Starlette streams it, and consuming the stream leaves your handler with an empty body or a hang — which is precisely today's debug mission.
build.code:
import time
import uuid
from contextvars import ContextVar

from fastapi import Request

request_id_var: ContextVar[str] = ContextVar(
    'request_id', default='-')

@app.middleware('http')
async def request_context(request: Request, call_next):
    incoming = request.headers.get('x-request-id')
    request_id = incoming or uuid.uuid4().hex[:12]
    request.state.request_id = request_id
    token = request_id_var.set(request_id)
    start = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        response = await call_next(request)
    finally:
        request_id_var.reset(token)
    duration_ms = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000
    response.headers['X-Request-ID'] = request_id
    response.headers['X-Response-Time-Ms'] = (
        str(round(duration_ms, 1)))
    logger.info('request method=%s path=%s status=%s '
                'duration_ms=%.1f',
                request.method, request.url.path,
                response.status_code, duration_ms)
    return response

class RequestIdFilter(logging.Filter):
    def filter(self, record: logging.LogRecord) -> bool:
        record.request_id = request_id_var.get()
        return True

items.challenge: Propagate the id outward: when your service calls another API through the shared httpx client, send the same X-Request-ID header. One id then follows a user's action across every service that respects the convention — the cheapest distributed tracing there is.

debugMission.scenario: After adding audit middleware that logs request bodies, every POST hangs until the client times out. GET requests are unaffected. Removing the middleware fixes it, and the author cannot see why logging would break anything.
debugMission.artifact:
@app.middleware('http')
async def audit(request: Request, call_next):
    body = await request.body()
    logger.info('audit path=%s body=%s',
                request.url.path, body[:500])
    response = await call_next(request)
    return response

# client
$ curl -X POST api.notes.dev/notes -d '{"title":"x"}'
(no response; client timeout after 30s)

# server log
INFO audit path=/notes body=b'{"title":"x"}'
# ... nothing further; the handler never logs

# GET /health is fine
INFO request method=GET path=/health status=200
hints: The audit line logs successfully, so the middleware ran. What never ran afterwards?
How does a request body reach your application — as a value already in memory, or as a stream that is consumed once?
GET requests have no body. Why does that make them immune?
debugMission.solution: await request.body() consumes the ASGI receive stream, and by default nothing puts it back; the endpoint then awaits a body that will never arrive, so the request hangs until the client gives up. GETs have no body to consume, which is why only POSTs stall. The fix depends on what you actually need: for auditing, log metadata (method, path, content-length, principal, request id) in middleware and log the body inside the endpoint where the parsed model is already available; if you truly must read the body early, re-inject it by replacing request._receive with a replayed message, which is fiddly enough to be a strong hint you are at the wrong layer. General lesson: middleware sits below your framework's parsing, so it deals in streams — anything that consumes the request or the response body there breaks the layer beneath, and 'it hangs only on POST' is the fingerprint.

reflection: Which of your service's cross-cutting concerns belong in middleware and which are genuinely per-route dependencies?
What could you diagnose with a request id that you currently cannot?
done: Every response carries X-Request-ID and X-Response-Time-Ms
An incoming X-Request-ID is honoured rather than overwritten
A log record emitted inside a handler carries the same id as the response header, proven by a test
One structured request line per request records method, path, status and duration_ms
Error envelopes contain the same request id as the headers

keyConcepts.def: Middleware wraps every request for cross-cutting concerns; dependencies run per-route, appear in the schema and can be overridden in tests.
A per-request identifier, generated or propagated from X-Request-ID, logged with every line and returned in the response header.
Async-safe per-task storage; the correct way to carry a request id to code deep in the call stack when many coroutines share a thread.

items.title: Timeouts, rate limits, idempotency
items.concept:
Three defences, and they are the same defence seen from both sides of the wire. Week 2 taught you to be a well-behaved client: timeouts, retries, backoff with jitter. Today you build the server that deserves that behaviour.

**Rate limiting** protects you from one caller consuming everything — accidentally, usually via a retry loop. slowapi gives FastAPI a decorator: a Limiter with a key_func that identifies the caller (use the API-key name from yesterday's Principal, never the IP, which is shared and spoofable), then @limiter.limit('5/minute') on the expensive routes. When the limit is exceeded, answer **429 with Retry-After** telling the client exactly when to return; a 429 without that header forces every client to guess, and their guess will be 'immediately'. Note the in-memory storage default is per-process, so it is honest only for a single worker — Redis is the real answer, and Week 9 builds it.

**Timeouts, server side.** Your handler calls upstreams that can hang; if you await without a timeout, the request occupies a worker until the client gives up, and 20 such requests can occupy the whole service. Every outbound call gets a timeout (Week 2's client already does), and a slow endpoint should fail with 504 rather than hang forever.

**Idempotency, implemented.** POST /notes with an Idempotency-Key: look the key up in a store; a miss means execute normally and record key -> (status, response body, request hash, timestamp); a hit means replay the stored response without re-executing. Same key with a different body is a client bug — 409. Entries expire on a TTL (24 hours is Stripe's choice) and today's store is a dict with timestamps swept on read, which is honest for a single process and clearly labelled as such.

The three fit together: a client that retries (Week 2) plus a server that rate-limits and dedupes (today) is a system where a network blip costs a few hundred milliseconds instead of a duplicated charge and an outage.
items.why: An unauthenticated or unlimited endpoint on a public URL is a bill waiting to happen, and duplicated LLM calls cost real money per retry. Being able to demonstrate the duplicate-then-fixed sequence is one of the strongest signals of production experience you can show.

learn.focus: Read: Quick start (Limiter, key_func, registering the RateLimitExceeded handler, the middleware note), 'Decorating your routes' — including the requirement that the endpoint accept a request parameter — and the storage backends section. Skip: the async-specific caveats at the end.
Read: 'Timeouts', 'Retries and backoff' and 'Jitter' — the jitter graphs are the entire argument. Skip: the AWS SDK configuration specifics at the end.

debugMission.artifact:
# client
@retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3),
       retry=retry_if_exception_type(httpx.TimeoutException),
       reraise=True)
def create_note(client, payload):
    return client.post('/notes', json=payload,
                       timeout=httpx.Timeout(read=2.0))

# server log for one customer
14:02:11.418 POST /notes key=acme 201 created id=n_881
  duration_ms=2140
14:02:13.602 POST /notes key=acme 201 created id=n_882
  duration_ms=2110
14:02:15.744 POST /notes key=acme 201 created id=n_883
  duration_ms=1980

# client log
14:02:15.9 ERROR create_note failed: ReadTimeout
hints: The server says 201 three times; the client says it failed. Who is right?
Compare the read timeout with the handler's duration_ms. What happens to work the server has already completed when the client stops waiting?
POST is not idempotent. What would have to be true for the second and third attempts to be harmless?
debugMission.solution: Each attempt reached the server and succeeded — the handler took about 2.1 seconds while the client's read timeout was 2.0, so the client abandoned each response just before it arrived and retried, creating three notes and then reporting failure. A timeout means unknown, not failed: the request may have been fully processed. Two fixes, and you need both: raise the read timeout above the realistic p99 of the endpoint (and speed the endpoint up), and make create idempotent so a retried attempt with the same Idempotency-Key replays the original response instead of creating a second note. Note the key must be generated once per logical note, outside the retry. General lesson: retries and non-idempotent writes are a duplicate-generating machine, and the only real defence is server-side deduplication — which is exactly why every payment API in the world ships an idempotency key.

reflection: Which of your endpoints would cost the most money if a client's retry loop hit it 500 times in a minute?
Why is a 429 without Retry-After close to useless for a well-behaved client?
done: The sixth request in a minute returns 429 with Retry-After, wrapped in your error envelope
You reproduced duplicate creates with a too-short timeout, then eliminated them with an idempotency key — both runs recorded
A replayed key returns the identical stored response; a reused key with a different body returns 409
The idempotency store expires entries on a TTL and sits behind an interface a Redis version could replace
The rate limiter keys on the API-key identity, not the IP address

keyConcepts.def: Capping requests per caller per window, answering 429 with Retry-After so clients back off correctly instead of guessing.
A key-to-response record with a TTL that lets a repeated Idempotency-Key replay the original result instead of re-executing.
A client timeout says nothing about whether the server completed the work, which is why retried writes need server-side deduplication.

items.title: Background tasks — the small escape hatch
items.concept:
**BackgroundTasks** lets a handler return a response and then do work: declare a 'tasks: BackgroundTasks' parameter, call tasks.add_task(fn, *args), and FastAPI runs fn after the response has been sent. Perfect for the small after-the-fact jobs — writing an audit record, sending a notification email, invalidating a cache entry — where the caller should not wait and a failure is survivable.

**Know exactly what it is not.** The task runs in your own process: it is lost if the process is redeployed, killed or crashes; it does not retry; it does not survive a scale-down; and it competes for the same event loop, so a slow or blocking task degrades the requests being served alongside it (Week 2's blocking-sleep lesson applies here in full). There is no queue, no visibility, no dead-letter.

**Failures are invisible by default.** The response has already gone; nothing propagates back to the client, and an unhandled exception in the task may never appear in your logs unless you put it there. Wrap every task body in try/except and log with logger.exception — a background task without error logging is a silent data-loss mechanism.

The honest decision rule: use BackgroundTasks when losing the work occasionally is acceptable and the work is short. When the work must happen — payment capture, email that a customer is waiting for, an expensive LLM job — you need a real queue with persistence and retries. Week 9 builds exactly that; today you build the small version and label its limits in the README, which is what a senior engineer does rather than pretending the escape hatch is a solution.
items.why: Every AI API eventually wants to return fast and do slow work afterwards, and knowing precisely where the in-process version stops being acceptable is the difference between a pragmatic engineer and one who loses a client's data.

learn.focus: Read the whole page: the BackgroundTasks parameter, add_task with arguments, using background tasks with dependency injection, and the 'Caveat' section explaining when you need a real queue instead. Ten minutes.

build.task: Write an audit log entry after the response via a background task, with error handling and a test that proves it ran.
steps: Write append_audit(entry: AuditEntry) -> None appending one JSON line to an audit file path from Settings; wrap the whole body in try/except Exception with logger.exception so a failure is loud in logs
Add tasks: BackgroundTasks to POST /notes and POST /summarize; add_task(append_audit, entry) with request_id, principal name, path, status and a timestamp
Confirm the ordering: log a line inside the handler and one inside the task, and observe in the server log that the task line appears after the response was sent
Measure: assert (informally, with curl) that the endpoint's response time did not grow by the file-write time
Test with TestClient that the audit file contains exactly one line with the matching request_id after a request (TestClient runs background tasks before the context manager exits)
Test the failure path: point the audit path at an unwritable directory, assert the endpoint still returns 201, and assert the failure was logged with caplog
Write two sentences in the README naming what is lost if the process restarts mid-task, and what you would replace it with
build.hint: Keep the task function pure and cheap: pass it plain data, not a request or a database session. Request-scoped objects may already be closed by the time the task runs, and that failure is invisible for exactly the reasons this lesson is about.
build.code:
import json
import logging
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass
from fastapi import BackgroundTasks

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AuditEntry:
    request_id: str
    principal: str
    path: str
    status: int
    at: float

def append_audit(entry: AuditEntry, path: str) -> None:
    try:
        with open(path, 'a', encoding='utf-8') as handle:
            handle.write(json.dumps(asdict(entry)) + '\n')
    except Exception:
        logger.exception('audit write failed request_id=%s',
                         entry.request_id)

@app.post('/notes', status_code=201)
def create_note(payload: NoteIn, request: Request,
                tasks: BackgroundTasks,
                settings: SettingsDep,
                principal: PrincipalDep) -> NoteOut:
    note = STORE.create(payload)
    tasks.add_task(
        append_audit,
        AuditEntry(request.state.request_id, principal.name,
                   request.url.path, 201, time.time()),
        settings.audit_path,
    )
    return note

items.challenge: Add a shutdown-safety note in code: register a lifespan shutdown hook that logs a warning if audit entries were queued in the last second before shutdown. You cannot fix in-process loss, but you can make it visible — visibility is the first half of every reliability improvement.

debugMission.scenario: The audit file has gaps. Roughly one in fifty requests has no audit line, always during busy periods, and there are no errors anywhere in the logs. The endpoint returns 201 every time.
debugMission.artifact:
def append_audit(entry: AuditEntry, path: str) -> None:
    with open(path, 'a', encoding='utf-8') as handle:
        handle.write(json.dumps(asdict(entry)) + '\n')

@app.post('/notes', status_code=201)
def create_note(payload: NoteIn, tasks: BackgroundTasks,
                settings: SettingsDep) -> NoteOut:
    note = STORE.create(payload)
    tasks.add_task(append_audit, note.to_audit_entry(),
                   settings.audit_path)
