items.title: Chunking strategies
items.concept:
You chunk documents for three reasons. **Embedding dilution**: one vector summarising a 30-page report averages every topic into mush and matches nothing well. **Context budget**: you can only pack a few thousand tokens of retrieved text into the prompt. **Citation granularity**: 'section 4, paragraph 2' earns trust; 'somewhere in the annual report' does not.

Three strategies, in rising order of care: **fixed-size with overlap** (character or token windows; simple, structure-blind), **recursive by separators** (try paragraph breaks first, then sentences, then raw size — keeps natural units intact), and **structure-aware** (split on headings, carry the heading text into every chunk from that section).

Chunk size is a real tradeoff, not a magic number. Small chunks embed crisply and match precisely, but split facts across boundaries and lose surrounding context. Large chunks keep facts whole but dilute the vector and burn prompt budget. A sane starting point is 200-500 tokens with 10-20% overlap — then you MEASURE (that is Week 7's whole point).

Anthropic's contextual retrieval takes structure-awareness further: prepend a short model-written line of document context to each chunk before embedding ('This chunk is from the financial review section of Arden Foods' 2025 annual report...'). Their published numbers: roughly a third fewer retrieval failures from that alone, up to two-thirds fewer combined with BM25 and reranking. Read it as a reference today; you will earn those techniques with measurements in Week 7.
items.why: Most 'the model hallucinated' complaints in production RAG trace back to ingestion — facts sliced in half or drowned in oversized chunks. Chunking is where retrieval quality is won or lost, and it is entirely under your control.

Implement chunk_recursive(text) splitting on '

' first, then '
', then '. ', only falling back to size when a piece is still too big

build.hint: For chunk_fixed the window start advances by (size - overlap) each step. Assert overlap < size before you loop, or enjoy an infinite generator.
build.code:
DOC = '''
# Arden Foods plc - Annual Report 2025 (extract)

## Overview
Arden Foods makes chilled and frozen ready meals for UK retailers.
The group operates four production sites and employs 2,300 people.

## Financial review
Group revenue grew by 23% in Q3, reaching 412 million pounds for the full year.
Operating margin widened from 6.1% to 8.4% as input costs eased.
Net debt fell to 48 million pounds, or 0.9 times EBITDA.

## Principal risks
Raw material inflation remains the largest single risk to margins.
A prolonged cold-chain failure at the Leeds site could halt 40% of output.
Customer concentration is high: the top three retailers are 61% of sales.

## Outlook
The board expects mid single digit revenue growth in 2026.
Capacity at the new Peterborough line comes online in the second quarter.
'''

def chunk_fixed(text, size=280, overlap=40):
  step = size - overlap
  return [text[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(text), step)]

def stats(name, chunks):
  sizes = sorted(len(c) for c in chunks)
  broken = sum(1 for c in chunks if not c.rstrip().endswith(('.', '!', '?')))
  print(name, '| n =', len(chunks), '| min/med/max =', sizes[0],
        sizes[len(sizes) // 2], sizes[-1],
        '| broken-end rate =', round(broken / len(chunks), 2))

stats('fixed', chunk_fixed(DOC))
# now write chunk_recursive(text) and chunk_structure(md) yourself

items.title: Debug mission — the mid-sentence chunk
items.concept:
A retrieval bug walks like a model bug: the answer is wrong or missing, so people tune prompts. This mission trains the correct reflex — **look at the chunks first**. A number split from its label ('Group revenue grew by' in one chunk, '23% in Q3' in another) is unfindable: the fragment holding the number shares no vocabulary with the question, so it ranks nowhere, and the fragment that ranks well is missing the fact.

You will reproduce the failure with a bad ingest config, read the actual chunk boundaries, fix them with overlap plus structure-aware splitting, and prove the fix by re-running the query. The full diagnostic chain — question, retrieved chunks, chunk contents, boundary positions — is the same one you will run on production systems.
items.why: In consulting engagements the client says 'the AI is hallucinating'; half the time the ingest pipeline shredded their documents. Being the person who checks the chunks first saves weeks.

The label fragment matches the query ('revenue grew') but lacks the fact; the number fragment contains the fact but shares no query vocabulary, so it ranks invisibly low. Fix: overlap (so boundary sentences appear whole in at least one chunk) plus splitting on structure before size. After re-ingest, the top-1 chunk contains both 'grew by' and '23%' and the answer carries the figure. General lesson: when RAG misses a fact you can see in the source, diff the chunk boundaries against the sentence boundaries before touching a single prompt.

items.title: Qdrant — a real vector store
items.concept:
Your numpy matrix was perfect for 40 sentences. At 100k chunks you need three things it lacks: **persistence** (vectors survive restarts), **metadata filtering** (only search doc X, or section Y, or dates after Z), and **approximate nearest-neighbour search** — HNSW graphs that find near-matches in milliseconds by giving up the guarantee of exact top-k. That trade is what 'vector database' means.

Qdrant's embedded/local mode needs no server: QdrantClient(path='./qdrant_data') stores everything in that folder, and QdrantClient(':memory:') gives you a throwaway instance for tests — same API as the real cluster, so nothing you write today is toy code. One caveat: embedded mode is single-process; a second process opening the same path gets a storage-lock error.

The objects: a **collection** is created with the vector size and distance metric (VectorParams(size=384, distance=Distance.COSINE) for MiniLM). You **upsert** PointStruct(id, vector, payload) where payload is arbitrary JSON metadata — text, doc_id, section, page. You query with query_points(), optionally passing query_filter=Filter(must=[FieldCondition(...)]) so the vector search only considers matching payloads.

Chroma is the simpler alternative (collection.add / collection.query, minimal setup) — fine for prototypes; you outgrow it when you want richer filtering and server parity. Know it exists; build on Qdrant.
items.why: Filtered vector search is the shape of every enterprise RAG deployment — 'answer from THIS client's documents only' is a security boundary, not a feature. You will wire exactly that filter as tenant isolation in Week 10.

learn.focus: Follow the local quickstart end to end: install qdrant-client, create a collection with VectorParams and Distance.COSINE, upsert points with payloads, and run query_points with and without a Filter. Use the embedded client; skip anything about running the Docker server.
Five-minute skim: what collection.add and collection.query look like. You are not using Chroma this quarter — just note what the simpler tool trades away in filtering and deployment parity.

build.code:
from qdrant_client import QdrantClient
from qdrant_client.models import (Distance, VectorParams, PointStruct,
                                  Filter, FieldCondition, MatchValue)
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer('all-MiniLM-L6-v2')
client = QdrantClient(path='./qdrant_data')   # embedded mode: no server
# QdrantClient(':memory:') = same API, vanishes with the process

if not client.collection_exists('arden'):
  client.create_collection('arden',
    vectors_config=VectorParams(size=384, distance=Distance.COSINE))

vecs = model.encode([c['text'] for c in chunks])   # Day-2 chunks
points = [PointStruct(id=i, vector=vecs[i].tolist(),
            payload={'text': c['text'], 'doc_id': 'arden-2025',
                     'section': c['section']})
          for i, c in enumerate(chunks)]
client.upsert('arden', points=points)

q = model.encode(['What are the biggest risks?'])[0].tolist()
plain = client.query_points('arden', query=q, limit=3).points
flt = Filter(must=[FieldCondition(key='section',
                                  match=MatchValue(value='Principal risks'))])
scoped = client.query_points('arden', query=q, limit=3, query_filter=flt).points
for h in scoped:
  print(round(h.score, 3), h.payload['section'], '|', h.payload['text'][:50])

items.title: PDFs -> clean text
items.concept:
A PDF is a set of drawing instructions, not a text document. Extraction gives you what was PAINTED, in painting order: running headers and footers repeated on every page, page numbers mid-stream, hyphen-\nated words at line breaks, multi-column text interleaved, tables flattened into number soup. Clean text is something you make, not something you get.

PyMuPDF is the workhorse: import pymupdf (older code says import fitz — same library), doc = pymupdf.open(path), iterate pages, page.get_text() for plain text, doc.metadata for title/author. It is fast and accurate enough for born-digital PDFs.

Cheap cleaning heuristics carry you far: collect line frequencies across pages and drop any line appearing on most pages (that is your header/footer), drop bare page numbers, re-join hyphenated line-breaks, collapse whitespace. Perfect is not the bar — 'good enough that chunks read like prose' is.

Pick a real corpus now and make it one you will enjoy interrogating for two weeks: any FTSE company's annual report from their investor-relations page is ideal (long, structured, full of numbers and named risks).
items.why: Something like 80% of enterprise knowledge lives in PDFs. Every RAG engagement starts with an ingestion fight, and the consultant who budgets for extraction cleanup looks senior on day one.

What should an ingest pipeline DO when a page yields near-zero characters — carry on, or refuse loudly?
debugMission.solution: The brochure is a scanned/image-only PDF: there is no text layer, so get_text() returns empty strings, and the pipeline happily embedded 96 empty chunks. Image PDFs need OCR, which is out of scope this week — the correct behaviour is to detect and refuse: if mean chars per page is under a threshold (say 200), raise IngestError('no text layer - needs OCR') instead of indexing vapour. Week-1 lesson, new costume: validate at the boundary and fail fast; a pipeline that silently indexes nothing is worse than one that crashes.

reflection: Which cleaning step would you refuse to run without eyeballing its output first, and what could it silently destroy?
done: A real annual report extracted, cleaned, chunked, embedded and indexed with page payloads
Boilerplate filter output reviewed by eye before applying
Three sanity queries return text you can locate in the actual PDF
Empty-extraction guard added: near-zero text per page fails ingest loudly

keyConcepts.def: The selectable text stream inside a born-digital PDF; scanned PDFs lack one and need OCR before any RAG ingestion.
Removing lines that repeat across most pages (headers, footers, page numbers) before chunking, usually via cross-page frequency.

items.title: Retrieve, pack, answer, cite
items.concept:
RAG in one breath: embed the question, pull top-k chunks from the index, pack them into the prompt with provenance labels, instruct the model to answer ONLY from that context citing the labels, then map the citations in the answer back to chunk ids and quotes. Every stage is code you already own — Week 5's context_packer, Week 4's llm_client.

**Packing with provenance**: number each chunk [1], [2], ... and prefix its source (doc id, page). The numbers give the model something concrete to cite and give you a mechanical way to map citations back. Order matters: your Week-5 lost-in-the-middle work applies — put the strongest chunks first, never buried mid-pack.

**The contract prompt**: 'Answer using ONLY the numbered context blocks. Cite evidence for every claim as [n]. If the context does not contain the answer, say so.' Temperature 0. This is a boundary, and like every boundary since Week 1, you validate what crosses it: parse the [n] markers out of the answer and resolve each to {chunk_id, quote}.

**Show sources with answers, always.** An uncited RAG answer is a rumour with good grammar. The citations are also your debugging trace — when an answer is wrong, the cited chunks tell you which stage to blame.
items.why: This loop is the beating heart of the most-deployed LLM pattern in industry. Building it from parts — no framework — means that in interviews and incidents alike you can point at any stage and say exactly what it does.

build.task: Write ask(question) over your indexed PDF corpus returning {answer, citations: [{chunk_id, quote}]}, then run 5 real questions and grade the results by eye.
steps: Write pack(hits): numbered blocks, each prefixed [n] (doc_id p.page), best score first
Write the system contract prompt: answer only from context, cite [n], refuse if absent
Call your Week-4 llm_client at temperature 0 with packed context + question
Parse cited [n] markers from the answer; map each to {chunk_id, quote} from the hits list
Ask 5 questions you can verify against the PDF; record answer quality and citation correctness in your log
Add a guard: any cited n outside 1..len(hits) is logged as a hallucinated citation
build.hint: Keep ask() pure enough to test: retrieval client, packer and llm call injected as parameters or module-level seams you can monkeypatch (Week 2 muscle).
build.code:
import re

SYSTEM = ('Answer using ONLY the numbered context blocks. '
          'Cite evidence for every claim as [n]. '
          'If the context does not contain the answer, say: '
          'I do not know based on these documents.')

def pack(hits):
  blocks = []
  for n, h in enumerate(hits, start=1):
    tag = '[' + str(n) + '] (' + h.payload['doc_id'] + ' p.' + str(h.payload['page']) + ') '
    blocks.append(tag + h.payload['text'])
  return '\n\n'.join(blocks)

def ask(question, k=5):
  qv = model.encode([question])[0].tolist()
  hits = client.query_points('corpus', query=qv, limit=k).points
  answer = llm(system=SYSTEM, temperature=0,
               prompt='Context:\n' + pack(hits) + '\n\nQuestion: ' + question)
  cited = sorted({int(n) for n in re.findall('\\[(\\d+)\\]', answer)})
  citations = [{'chunk_id': hits[n - 1].id,
                'quote': hits[n - 1].payload['text'][:120]}
               for n in cited if 1 <= n <= len(hits)]
  return {'answer': answer, 'citations': citations}

items.challenge: Add a verify pass: for each citation, check that some 10+ character span of the answer sentence containing [n] also occurs in the cited chunk; flag mismatches. You have just hand-rolled your first groundedness check — Week 7 formalises it.

debugMission.scenario: Users report that the displayed sources 'never say what the answer says'. The answers themselves look right. Trust in the tool is evaporating fast — nobody believes a citation that does not contain its claim.
debugMission.artifact:
# citation mapping (the suspect lines)
cited = sorted({int(n) for n in re.findall('\\[(\\d+)\\]', answer)})
citations = [{'chunk_id': hits[n].id, 'quote': hits[n].payload['text'][:80]}
             for n in cited if n < len(hits)]

# python ask.py 'What was net debt at year end?'
answer: Net debt fell to 48 million pounds at year end [2].
citations:
  [2] chunk 11: 'Raw material inflation remains the largest single
      risk to margins. A prolonged cold-chain failure...'
# the shown source does not contain the number it supposedly supports
hints: The packer numbered blocks starting at [1]. What index does hits[n] fetch for citation [2]?
Which chunk IS hits[1] here, and which chunk did the model actually mean by [2]?
There is a second, quieter bug in the guard condition on the same line.
debugMission.solution: Off-by-one: labels start at [1] but hits is 0-indexed, so citation [n] must resolve to hits[n - 1]; as written, every displayed source is the chunk AFTER the one the model cited. The guard has the twin bug: it should be 1 <= n <= len(hits), otherwise [len(hits)] is dropped and [0] would sneak through. Fix both, then add the containment assertion from the challenge so a wrong mapping can never render again. Lesson: the model did nothing wrong — your glue code lied about what it said. Verify the whole chain mechanically.

reflection: Which failure would you catch first with citations displayed: retrieval pulling the wrong chunk, or the model inventing a number? How does each look to the user?
Why is temperature 0 the right default here but not for the Week-5 drafting endpoint?
done: ask() returns {answer, citations} with every citation resolving to a real indexed chunk
5 questions run; answer quality and citation correctness logged
Out-of-range citation guard in place and tested with a forced bad marker
Strongest chunk packed first, per your Week-5 packing rules

keyConcepts.def: The [n] tag plus source metadata attached to each packed chunk, giving the model a citable handle you can resolve mechanically.
The system-prompt rule restricting the model to supplied context, with an explicit refusal phrasing for absent answers.
Parsing [n] markers from the answer and resolving them to chunk ids and quotes — with bounds checks, because models cite freely.

items.title: Grounding and refusal
items.concept:
The grounding contract has two halves. The famous half: answer only from context. The neglected half: **when the context does not contain the answer, say so** — in a fixed, detectable phrasing. A fixed refusal string ('I do not know based on these documents') is not stylistic laziness; it is machine-checkable behaviour you can test and monitor.

Why refusal beats eloquence: a wrong-but-confident answer gets acted on, then discovered, then destroys trust in every future answer — in enterprise settings it can mean a mis-stated liability or a compliance breach. A refusal is recoverable: the user rephrases, adds documents, or escalates to a human. Errors of omission are cheaper than errors of confident commission.

Tuning is two-sided. Too soft and the model 'helpfully' fills gaps from pre-training (ask it about a competitor's margins and watch). Too aggressive and it refuses questions the context clearly answers — over-refusal is a real regression, so you test BOTH directions: unanswerable questions must refuse, answerable ones must answer.
items.why: Honest refusal is the single behaviour enterprise buyers probe first — nobody deploys a document assistant that improvises. Being able to demonstrate tested refusal behaviour is a differentiator in demos and interviews alike.

build.task: Tune your ask() contract until 3 unanswerable questions refuse and 3 answerable ones still answer, using a tiny pass/fail harness.
steps: Write 3 answerable and 3 unanswerable questions for your corpus (unanswerable: facts genuinely absent — salaries, competitors, the future)
Encode expectations in a CASES list and script the pass/fail loop below
Run it; record which cases fail on the first attempt
Tighten the contract wording until all 6 pass (fixed refusal phrase, 'only from the numbered blocks', no outside knowledge)
Re-run twice to check stability at temperature 0
build.hint: If an unanswerable case keeps answering, check what got retrieved — plausible-looking chunks tempt the model into stitching an answer. Naming the trap in the prompt ('context may be irrelevant to the question') helps.
build.code:
CASES = [
  ('What was group revenue for the year?',            'answer'),
  ('How much net debt does the group carry?',         'answer'),
  ('What did the board say about growth next year?',  'answer'),
  ('What is the chief executive paid?',               'refuse'),
  ('How did the share price react to results day?',   'refuse'),
  ('What are the main competitor margins?',           'refuse'),
]

REFUSAL = 'I do not know based on these documents'

for q, want in CASES:
  out = ask(q)
  got = 'refuse' if REFUSAL.lower() in out['answer'].lower() else 'answer'
  print('PASS' if got == want else 'FAIL', '|', 'want', want,
        '| got', got, '|', q)

items.challenge: Add a nastier case: a question whose answer is only PARTLY in context ('How did revenue and headcount change?' when only revenue is covered). Tune until you get a partial answer plus an explicit gap statement rather than an invented headcount.

debugMission.scenario: After you tightened the contract, 'What was operating margin last year?' started refusing — but the margin sentence is plainly in the PDF. The team wants to weaken the refusal wording again. Something else is wrong.
debugMission.artifact:
# python ask.py 'What was operating margin last year?'
answer: I do not know based on these documents.

# debug print of the packed context for that call (k=3):
[1] (arden-2025 p.7) Customer concentration is high: the top three...
[2] (arden-2025 p.2) The group operates four production sites and...
[3] (arden-2025 p.9) The board expects mid single digit revenue...

# python ask.py 'What was operating margin last year?' --k 8
answer: Operating margin widened from 6.1% to 8.4% [2].
hints: Before blaming the prompt: was the margin sentence anywhere in the packed context at k=3?
Which stage failed — generation, or retrieval? What single log line settles it instantly?
debugMission.solution: The refusal was CORRECT: at k=3 the margin chunk was never retrieved, so the model honestly reported an absent answer; at k=8 it appears and gets answered. The bug is a retrieval miss, not an over-strict prompt — weakening the contract would have converted an honest refusal into a hallucination. Standing rule from today: log the packed context with every answer, and when you see a refusal, check 'was the fact in the context?' FIRST. That one question splits every RAG failure into retrieval problems vs generation problems — it is the debugging fork you will use for the rest of your career.

reflection: Why is a confident wrong answer worse than a refusal in enterprise settings? Answer in two sentences as if to a sceptical client.
Where would over-refusal hurt commercially — what does a user do after the third needless 'I don't know'?
done: All 6 harness cases pass at temperature 0, twice in a row
Refusal uses the fixed detectable phrase, verified by the harness string check
Packed context logged with every answer for the retrieval-vs-generation split
The 3 unanswerable questions saved — they seed your gold set on Day 6

keyConcepts.def: Restricting answers to claims supported by supplied context rather than the model's parametric memory.
A fixed, machine-detectable phrasing the model must use when context lacks the answer — testable behaviour, not vibes.
The opposite failure: refusing questions the context does answer, usually after an over-aggressive contract tightening.

items.title: Failure-modes tour (break it yourself)
items.concept:
You will now deliberately break your working RAG five ways and watch each failure's distinctive symptom. Breaking systems on purpose is how you build the symptom-to-cause lookup table that makes you fast in production.

The tour: **k=1** — the single retrieved chunk often lacks the answer; symptom: frequent honest refusals, occasional lucky hits. **k=20** — the right chunk is in there somewhere, drowned; symptoms: vaguer answers, drifting citations, doubled latency and token cost. **Tiny chunks (80 chars, no overlap)** — Day 2's fact-splitting at scale; symptom: answers that trail off ('revenue grew, rate not stated'). **No overlap at sane size** — subtler: only boundary-straddling facts break, so it looks 'mostly fine'. **Vocabulary mismatch** — ask 'How profitable is the group?' when the document says 'operating margin'; embeddings bridge jargon-to-plain-English only weakly, so retrieval lands on nearby-but-wrong chunks.

For each run you record symptom, cause, fix in a failure log. That table is your personal RAG pathology reference — and Week 7 turns its rows into measured, automated evals. The discipline matters more than the specific bugs: change one variable, observe, write it down.
items.why: Diagnosing RAG from symptoms alone is THE applied-AI consulting skill — clients show you a weird answer, not a stack trace. A rehearsed symptom-to-cause table is what lets you say 'that smells like drowned context' in the first meeting.

build.task: Run the 5-config breakage grid over 5 fixed questions and produce a failure log table: config, symptom observed, cause, fix.
steps: Fix 5 questions covering: a number lookup, a section summary, a vocabulary-mismatch phrasing, a multi-part question, one unanswerable
Run the baseline config first and save its answers — your control
Run each broken config from the grid below (re-ingest when chunk params change)
For every config x question cell, note the symptom in one phrase
Write the failure log table in failure_log.md with a fix column
Restore the baseline config AND re-ingest — leave the system healthy
build.hint: Keep the model, prompt and temperature identical across all runs — you are isolating retrieval variables. One change at a time or you learn nothing.
build.code:
QUESTIONS = [
  'How fast did revenue grow in Q3?',        # number lookup
  'What are the principal risks?',           # section summary
  'How profitable is the group?',            # vocabulary mismatch
  'How did revenue and net debt change?',    # multi-part
  'What is the chief executive paid?',       # unanswerable
]

CONFIGS = [
  {'name': 'baseline',   'k': 5,  'size': 350, 'overlap': 60},
  {'name': 'k1',         'k': 1,  'size': 350, 'overlap': 60},
  {'name': 'k20',        'k': 20, 'size': 350, 'overlap': 60},
  {'name': 'tiny',       'k': 5,  'size': 80,  'overlap': 0},
  {'name': 'no_overlap', 'k': 5,  'size': 350, 'overlap': 0},
]

for cfg in CONFIGS:
  reingest(size=cfg['size'], overlap=cfg['overlap'])  # re-chunk + re-index
  print('=== ' + cfg['name'] + ' ===')
  for q in QUESTIONS:
    out = ask(q, k=cfg['k'])
    print(q[:40].ljust(42), '->', out['answer'][:80])
# failure_log.md columns: | config | question | symptom | cause | fix |

items.challenge: Add a sixth experiment: keep k=5 but pack the chunks in REVERSED score order so the best chunk sits last. Compare answers with baseline — you are watching lost-in-the-middle (Week 5's paper) happen to your own system.

debugMission.scenario: Next morning, with the config file showing baseline values, every answer is worse than yesterday's control run. Nobody changed the code. The grid experiment is the prime suspect.
debugMission.artifact:
# config.py says: size=350, overlap=60, k=5   (baseline)
# python run_tour.py
=== baseline ===
How fast did revenue grow in Q3?    -> The context mentions revenue grew, but the ra
What are the principal risks?       -> Raw material inflation is noted. Other risks

# python -c 'print(client.count("arden"))'
count=87
# yesterday's baseline ingest logged: 'indexed 14 chunks'
hints: The config FILE is baseline. Is the INDEX baseline? What does 87 vs 14 tell you?
Which grid config produces roughly 87 chunks from this document?
What makes a config change 'take effect' in this system — editing the file, or re-ingesting?
debugMission.solution: The last grid run was tiny (size=80): its 87 midget chunks are still in the collection, because editing config.py does not touch the index — the index is state, built by ingest. Fix now: re-ingest with baseline params. Fix forever: encode chunking params into the collection name (arden_s350_o60) or a collection metadata check at startup, so a config/index mismatch fails loudly instead of degrading silently. This is your first taste of a rule that returns in Week 9: derived state must carry the version of everything it was derived from.

reflection: Which failure mode produced the most DANGEROUS output — not the worst, the most plausible-looking? Why is that the one to fear?
Your failure log has a fix column — which fixes can you verify today by eye, and which need Week 7's metrics to trust?
done: All 5 configs run over all 5 questions with the baseline control saved first
failure_log.md committed with symptom, cause and fix per broken config
Index restored to baseline and verified via chunk count
One symptom-to-cause pair recited from memory to your rubber duck

keyConcepts.def: Retrieving so many chunks that the relevant one is buried — answers go vague while retrieval metrics look 'fine'.
Query phrased in words the document never uses ('profitable' vs 'operating margin'); embeddings only partly bridge the gap.
A running symptom-cause-fix table built from deliberate breakage — your diagnostic lookup for production incidents.

items.title: Query rewriting
items.concept:
Users write questions for humans; retrieval wants questions phrased like the document. Query rewriting inserts an LLM step that converts one into the other. Three techniques, cheapest first:

**Expansion**: add likely document vocabulary ('How profitable?' gains 'operating margin, profit, EBITDA'). Directly attacks yesterday's vocabulary-mismatch failure. **Decomposition**: split multi-part questions into sub-queries ('revenue AND net debt' becomes two retrievals whose results you union). **HyDE-lite**: have the model draft a one-sentence hypothetical answer and embed THAT as the query — a guessed answer shares vocabulary and shape with the real passage even when the guess is wrong.

The price: an extra LLM call per question (latency + cost) and a new failure surface — a rewrite can DROP the exact term that mattered. Two engineering rules make it safe: never replace the original query (search with both, merge results), and keep the step only where your worst-query measurements say it helps. This is engineering, not ritual — plenty of corpora need no rewriting at all.
items.why: Query rewriting is the cheapest retrieval win available without touching the index, and knowing when NOT to add a pipeline stage is precisely the judgement consultants are paid for.

build.task: Add a rewrite step to retrieval and A/B it on the 5 worst queries from your Day-5 failure log; keep it only where it wins.
steps: Write the rewrite prompt: add document vocabulary, preserve every exact name, code and number, return only the rewritten query
Retrieve with BOTH original and rewritten queries; merge and dedupe hit lists
For each of your 5 worst queries, table: baseline top-3 vs rewritten top-3, and whether the needed chunk surfaced
Try decomposition on your multi-part question: two sub-queries, union of hits
Decide per technique: keep, drop, or 'only when baseline score is weak' — write the decision and evidence in your log
build.hint: Judge the A/B on retrieval (did the right chunk appear, at what rank), not on final answers — smaller variance, faster loop, and it isolates the stage you changed.
build.code:
REWRITE_PROMPT = (
  'Rewrite the user question as a search query for an annual report.\n'
  'Add likely report vocabulary (finance terms the document would use).\n'
  'Keep every exact name, code and number from the original.\n'
  'Return only the rewritten query.\n\nQuestion: {q}')

def rewritten_search(q, k=5):
  rq = llm(prompt=REWRITE_PROMPT.format(q=q), temperature=0)
  hits_a = retrieve(q, k)           # ALWAYS search the original too
  hits_b = retrieve(rq, k)
  merged = dedupe_by_id(hits_a + hits_b)
  return rq, merged[:k]

for q in WORST_FIVE:                # from your Day-5 failure log
  rq, hits = rewritten_search(q)
  print(q, '\n  rewritten ->', rq)
  print('  top-1 now:', hits[0].payload['text'][:70])

items.challenge: Implement the conditional version: rewrite only when the baseline top-1 score falls below a threshold you pick from your logged score distributions. What fraction of queries now pay the extra LLM call?

debugMission.scenario: An enthusiastic v1 wired the rewriter in front of ALL retrieval. Vague queries improved — but 'What is net debt as a multiple of EBITDA?', which used to hit its chunk at rank 1, now misses entirely. Rewriting made a good query worse.
debugMission.artifact:
# v1: the rewriter REPLACES the query
def rewritten_search(q, k=5):
  rq = llm(prompt=REWRITE_PROMPT.format(q=q), temperature=0)
  return retrieve(rq, k)

# python ask.py 'What is net debt as a multiple of EBITDA?'
rewritten: 'leverage ratio borrowings indebtedness balance sheet strength'
top-1 [0.44] 'Operating margin widened from 6.1% to 8.4% as input costs eased...'

# baseline (no rewrite) for the same question:
top-1 [0.71] 'Net debt fell to 48 million pounds, or 0.9 times EBITDA.'
hints: Compare the rewritten query with the original word by word. Which term vanished?
The rewrite prompt SAYS keep exact names and codes — did the model comply? What is your enforcement mechanism when it does not?
Where did the original query go in v1's retrieval?
debugMission.solution: The rewrite dropped 'EBITDA' and 'net debt' — the exact terms the document uses — replacing them with synonyms the document never says; and because v1 REPLACED the query, the original's perfect match was thrown away. Fix: always retrieve with the original query too and merge (prompt instructions are requests, not guarantees — enforce in code). Better still, gate rewriting on weak baseline scores. Lesson: every pipeline stage you add is a new way to lose; additive designs (union, merge) fail softer than replacement designs.

reflection: HyDE embeds a guessed answer that may be factually wrong. Why can that still improve retrieval — and what does that tell you about what embeddings measure?
done: A/B table for 5 worst queries: baseline vs rewritten top-3 with needed-chunk rank
Original query always searched alongside the rewrite, verified in code
Keep/drop/conditional decision recorded per technique with evidence
Multi-part question answered correctly via decomposition

keyConcepts.def: Adding likely document vocabulary to the query so it shares terms with the passages that answer it.
Hypothetical Document Embeddings — embed a model-drafted hypothetical answer as the search query; the guess shares shape and vocabulary with the real passage.
Splitting a multi-part question into sub-queries, retrieving per sub-query, and merging results before answering.

items.title: Mini-project — Ask-My-Docs v1 + gold set
items.concept:
Assemble the week into one tool: a CLI and a small API answering questions over a 2-3 document PDF corpus, with citations, metadata filtering and tested refusal. Ingest and ask are separate commands because they are separate lifecycles — ingest is slow, occasional and stateful; ask is fast, frequent and stateless.

The deliverable that outlives the code is **gold.jsonl**: 25 question/expected-answer/expected-source triples spread across easy, medium, hard and unanswerable. Week 7 turns this file into your evaluation harness, baselines and money tables — every metric you will ever quote about this system traces back to the quality of these 25 rows.

Quality bar per case: the expected answer is one a domain expert would accept as correct and complete; expected_sources name the real chunk ids that support it (go find them in the index — this forces honesty); unanswerable cases are genuinely absent from the corpus, not merely obscure. Easy = single chunk, direct phrasing. Medium = paraphrased or two-chunk. Hard = vocabulary mismatch or multi-part. Unanswerable = 5 cases that must refuse.
items.why: A working RAG demo is a commodity; a RAG system WITH a gold dataset is an engineering asset. Bringing your own eval set to an interview conversation instantly separates you from tutorial-followers.

build.task: Ship the ask-my-docs CLI + API over your PDF corpus, and commit a 25-case gold.jsonl that Week 7 will run evals against.
steps: Milestone 1 — corpus: ingest 2-3 PDFs (your annual report plus 1-2 contrasting docs) via 'ingest <path> --doc-id <id>'; payloads carry doc_id, page, section
Milestone 2 — ask CLI: 'ask <question> [--doc <id>] [--k N]' printing the answer, then numbered citations with doc and page
Milestone 3 — --doc flag wired as a Qdrant payload filter; verify scoped vs unscoped answers differ sensibly
Milestone 4 — API: POST /ask {question, doc_id?} on FastAPI reusing the same core function (Week 3 skeleton); include citations in the response model
Milestone 5 — gold set: write 25 cases in gold.jsonl (10 easy / 5 medium / 5 hard / 5 unanswerable) following the format below, spread across all docs
Milestone 6 — verify: script checks every expected_source id exists in the index; run the 5 unanswerable cases — all must refuse
Commit code + gold.jsonl; README section: corpus, commands, known limitations
build.hint: Write gold questions while reading the PDFs, not from memory of your own answers — you want cases the SYSTEM has never seen, including at least 3 phrased nothing like the document.
build.code:
# gold.jsonl - one JSON object per line (shown wrapped here for reading;
# keep each object on ONE line in the file). 25 cases total:
# 10 easy, 5 medium, 5 hard, 5 unanswerable.
{"id": "g01", "difficulty": "easy", "answerable": true,
 "q": "What was group revenue for the full year?",
 "expected_answer": "412 million pounds",
 "expected_sources": ["arden-2025:c06"]}
{"id": "g14", "difficulty": "hard", "answerable": true,
 "q": "How leveraged is the business?",
 "expected_answer": "Net debt is 48 million pounds, 0.9 times EBITDA",
 "expected_sources": ["arden-2025:c07"]}
{"id": "g21", "difficulty": "unanswerable", "answerable": false,
 "q": "What is the chief executive paid?",
 "expected_answer": "Refusal - the documents do not state this",
 "expected_sources": []}
# difficulty guide: easy = one chunk, direct wording. medium = paraphrase
# or two chunks. hard = vocabulary mismatch or multi-part. unanswerable
# = genuinely absent from the corpus (verify by searching yourself).

items.challenge: Add 'ask --json' machine-readable output and pipe 5 gold questions through it with jq — a preview of how Week 7's harness will drive this exact interface.
reflection: Which of your 25 gold cases do you predict your current system fails? Mark them now — Week 7 checks your calibration.
What made a question 'hard' to write? What does that suggest about your corpus coverage?
done: ingest and ask commands work end to end over 2-3 real PDFs
--doc filter changes retrieval scope via payload filtering, demonstrated with one query
POST /ask returns {answer, citations} through the same core function as the CLI
gold.jsonl committed with 25 cases in the 10/5/5/5 split and every expected_source verified against the index
All 5 unanswerable cases refuse with the fixed phrase

keyConcepts.def: A hand-curated file of question / expected-answer / expected-source cases that defines what 'working' means for your system.
The chunk id(s) a correct answer must draw from — what makes retrieval itself measurable, not just final answers.

items.title: Week 6 review — explain it aloud
items.concept:
Thirty minutes, spoken aloud, no rereading of resources — retrieval practice beats rereading and it suits how your brain works. The protocol:

- Re-read Monday's numpy similarity code top to bottom; say what each line does without comments.
- Explain to an imaginary PM why chunking exists, using the mid-sentence bug as the story: the label in one chunk, the 23% in another, and why no prompt could fix it.
- Write the cosine similarity formula from memory on paper, plus one sentence on why normalised vectors let you use a plain dot product. Check it against your notes only AFTER writing.
- Walk the RAG loop stages aloud: embed, retrieve, pack, answer, cite, verify.
- Pick the 2 concepts that felt wobbliest and add them to your revision queue. Two, not five.
items.why: If you can narrate the pipeline and its failure modes without notes, interview questions on RAG become recall, not improvisation.
reflection: Explain to a PM in three sentences why the system says 'I don't know' on purpose — and why that behaviour was worth a day of tuning.
Which day's material would collapse first under a sharp follow-up question? That is your first revision item.
done: Cosine formula and normalised-dot equivalence written from memory, then checked
Chunking story told aloud PM-style in under two minutes
Two need-revision concepts queued

items.title: Week 6 quiz
items.concept: Take the Week 6 quiz below. It probes the failure modes, not the trivia: similarity maths, chunk-size symptoms, what embeddings miss, filtering, and the grounding contract. Attempt every question before revealing anything; wrong answers go straight to the revision queue — they are the most valuable output of the quiz.
items.why: Retrieval practice with feedback is the fastest consolidation tool in the box.
reflection: Which wrong answer surprised you most, and what exactly was the gap — a fact, or a mental model?
done: Quiz completed with a score of 70% or higher
Every miss converted into a revision-queue entry

questions.q: Two sentence embeddings have been L2-normalised to unit length. Their dot product is 0.92. What is their cosine similarity?
options: Cannot be determined without the original vector norms
0.92 — for unit vectors, cosine similarity equals the dot product
0.46 — the dot product must be halved for two vectors
0.08 — cosine similarity is one minus the dot product
questions.explain: Cosine is dot(a,b)/(norm(a)*norm(b)); with both norms equal to 1, the denominators vanish and cosine equals the dot product. That equivalence is why pipelines normalise once and use fast matrix multiplies.

questions.q: Which query is MOST likely to embarrass pure vector search over a maintenance manual?
options: Summarise the safety guidance
What does error code E4409 mean?
How do I keep the pump running well?
What are the most common failure causes?
questions.explain: Exact identifiers like E4409 get diluted across the embedding, and a near-identical code (E4402) looks almost the same — this is a lexical lookup, where keyword search (BM25, arriving Week 7) wins.

questions.q: You index 2,000-token chunks. Which symptom pattern points at chunks being too LARGE?
options: Facts split across chunk boundaries so answers trail off mid-fact
Vague matches — chunk vectors average many topics — plus retrieved text wasting most of the context budget
Citations that point to precise sentences
The index takes up too little disk space
questions.explain: Oversized chunks dilute the embedding (matching vaguely) and each retrieved hit drags in mostly-irrelevant text. Split facts are the signature of chunks that are too SMALL or lack overlap.

questions.q: Your RAG refuses often, but when it does answer it is almost always right. Most likely cause?
options: k is too large, drowning the model in context
Temperature is too high
k is too small — the needed chunk frequently is not retrieved, so the model honestly reports absence
The refusal phrase is too polite
questions.explain: Frequent honest refusal with high precision when answering is the k-too-small signature: generation is behaving; retrieval is starving it. k-too-large shows the opposite — fluent, vague, drifting answers.

questions.q: 'Profits rose sharply' vs 'Profits fell sharply' score cosine 0.91. Why?
options: The embedding model is broken and should be replaced
They share topic, register and almost all vocabulary — embeddings encode that heavily, and negation barely moves the vector
The vectors were not normalised before comparison
0.91 means the sentences are paraphrases
questions.explain: Semantic similarity is topical closeness, not logical equivalence. Negation, number changes and entity swaps all hide inside high cosine scores — the reason hybrid retrieval and cross-encoders exist.

questions.q: 40 documents are indexed in one collection. A user must get answers ONLY from the 2025 Arden report. The right mechanism is:
options: Raise k so the right document appears somewhere in the results
Add 'only use the Arden 2025 report' to the prompt
A payload filter on doc_id at query time, constraining the vector search itself
Lower the temperature to zero
questions.explain: Metadata filtering constrains WHICH points are searched — a hard scope boundary. Prompt-level scoping is a polite request the model can fail; in Week 10 this same filter becomes tenant isolation, where it is a security control.

questions.q: State the grounding contract you gave your RAG system, and explain in two sentences why a confident wrong answer is worse than a refusal in an enterprise setting.
questions.answer: The contract: answer using only the provided context, cite every claim, and if the context does not contain the answer, say so in a fixed phrase ('I do not know based on these documents'). A confident wrong answer gets acted on and silently poisons trust in every future answer — and it can create real liability; a refusal is recoverable because the user can rephrase, add documents or escalate.

questions.q: A query returns the chunk 'Group revenue grew by' as top-1 and the answer lacks the growth figure. Name the ingestion mistake and two fixes.
questions.answer: Fixed-size chunking with no overlap cut the sentence mid-fact, separating the label from '23% in Q3'; the number-bearing fragment shares no query vocabulary so it never ranks. Fixes: add chunk overlap so boundary sentences appear whole in at least one chunk, and split on document structure (paragraphs/headings) before falling back to size.

title: Measure It or It Doesn't Work — RAG II + Evaluation
objective: Build a real evaluation harness (retrieval metrics + LLM-judged answer quality), then use it to measurably improve retrieval with hybrid search and reranking.
narrative: This is the week that separates professionals from demo-builders. You'll turn last week's 25 gold questions into an eval harness, get baseline numbers, and only then add hybrid search and reranking — proving each change with your own metrics. Evals come before agents in this curriculum on purpose: you'll never again ship an AI change without knowing if it helped.
whatYouCanBuild: An evaluated RAG service with before/after metrics — and the permanent habit of measuring every AI change.
whyProfessionally: "How do you evaluate it?" is the question that ends most AI-engineer interviews. You'll have a real answer with real numbers from a real project.

items.title: Golden datasets — your unfair advantage
items.concept:
Hamel Husain's essay is the closest thing applied AI has to a canon, and its argument is blunt: teams fail at AI products because they never build evaluation systems tied to THEIR data. Generic benchmarks measure someone else's problem. His prescription runs in a loop: **look at your actual data**, do error analysis on real failures, and grow evals from what you find — Level 1 assertions and unit tests, Level 2 human and model grading, Level 3 A/B tests. The gold dataset that powers all of it encodes domain judgement your competitors do not have. That is why he calls evals the moat.

Today you upgrade last week's 25 cases to 40. New cases come from four directions: **paraphrase variants** (same fact, completely different words — retrieval robustness), more **hard** cases from your Day-5 failure log (the queries that actually hurt), coverage of every document in the corpus, and a couple more **unanswerable** traps near real content.

Every case must pass the expert-acceptance bar: would a domain expert accept the expected answer as correct AND complete? And every answerable case carries the id of the chunk(s) that support it — you verify each against the live index, because a gold set that drifts from the corpus measures nothing.

Then you protect the asset: a validator script that checks schema, id uniqueness and source existence on every edit. Gold sets are code. They get review, version control and CI like code.
items.why: Consultancies win engagements by showing the client a 40-case gold set in week one — it reframes the project from vibes to engineering. And 'how would you build the eval set?' is the follow-up to every RAG interview answer.

learn.focus: Read the full essay in one sitting (~35 min): the Three Levels of evaluation, unit tests/assertions, the LLM-as-judge critique with the critique-shadowing workflow, and the case-study numbers. This is the highest-value single read of the programme — no skipping.

build.task: Grow gold.jsonl from 25 to 40 cases with difficulty tags, expected sources and paraphrase variants, then write validate_gold.py to keep it honest.
steps: Re-read your Week-6 failure log; write 5 hard cases from the query patterns that actually failed
Write 5 paraphrase variants of existing easy cases — same fact, zero shared phrasing (thesaurus, different angle)
Add 3-5 cases covering the corpus documents your first 25 barely touched, and 2 unanswerable traps adjacent to real content
Tag every case: difficulty (easy/medium/hard/unanswerable), answerable flag, expected_sources chunk ids verified against the index
Apply the expert bar: reject any expected_answer you could not defend to a domain expert line by line
Write validate_gold.py (skeleton below) and wire it to exit 1 on any problem; run it clean
build.hint: Paraphrase variants are cheap to write and brutal on retrieval — write the fact on a card, put the source away, then ask for it the way a rushed executive would.

items.challenge: Add a 'supporting_quote' field to every answerable case — the exact sentence from the source chunk that proves the expected answer. Tedious for 20 minutes, priceless on Day 3 when the judge needs evidence anchors.

debugMission.scenario: Dry-running tomorrow's eval, case g07 fails: the system says 412 million, the gold file expects 23 million. You check the PDF — the system is right. Your gold set has a bug, and it nearly went down as a system failure.
debugMission.artifact:
# eval dry-run output for case g07
q:        'What was group revenue for the full year?'
expected: '23 million pounds'
system:   'Group revenue reached 412 million pounds for the full year [1].'
verdict:  FAIL - answer contradicts expected

# gold.jsonl line for g07 points at chunk arden-2025:c02; its text:

The gold author worked from the same chunk. What did they transcribe wrong?
Which extra per-case field would have made this transcription error impossible to miss in review?

Fix the case, then fix the process: every answerable case carries a supporting_quote copied verbatim from the source chunk, so a reviewer can see expected answer and evidence side by side. Lesson: gold sets are code with bugs of their own; 'gold-wrong' becomes an official failure category in Thursday's taxonomy, and the first suspect whenever a 'failure' looks too strange.

reflection: Which 3 of your 40 cases would you show a sceptical client first, and what does each one prove about the system?
Hamel calls evals a moat. What exactly is hard to copy — the harness code, or the 40 judgements inside gold.jsonl?
done: gold.jsonl has 40 cases tagged by difficulty with verified expected_sources
At least 5 paraphrase variants and 5 failure-log-derived hard cases included
validate_gold.py exits 0 on the committed file and 1 when you break a line on purpose
Every expected_answer passes the domain-expert acceptance bar

keyConcepts.def: A versioned, validated set of question/expected-answer/expected-source cases encoding what 'correct' means for YOUR system.
A gold case asking for a known fact in entirely different words — measures retrieval robustness to phrasing.
Hamel's ladder: Level 1 assertions and unit tests, Level 2 human and model grading, Level 3 A/B tests.

items.title: recall@k and MRR — retrieval scored
items.concept:
Retrieval evaluation is cheap, deterministic and fast — no LLM calls, no judge, just set membership and ranks. That is why it runs FIRST: if retrieval misses the needed chunk, nothing downstream can save the answer, so fix retrieval before spending a penny judging generations.

**recall@k**: the fraction of gold cases where at least one expected source appears in the top k retrieved chunks. **MRR (mean reciprocal rank)**: for each case take 1/rank of the FIRST relevant chunk (rank 1 gives 1.0, rank 4 gives 0.25, a miss gives 0), then average. Recall@k asks 'did it show up?'; MRR asks 'how high?' — you need both, because a system that always buries the right chunk at rank 5 has perfect recall@5 and lousy MRR.

Tiny worked example — four cases whose first relevant chunk lands at ranks 2, 7, 1, and not-found: recall@1 = 1/4 = 0.25 (only the rank-1 case), recall@3 = 2/4 = 0.50 (ranks 2 and 1), recall@10 = 3/4 = 0.75 (the miss never counts). MRR = (1/2 + 1/7 + 1/1 + 0) / 4 = 0.411.

Unanswerable cases have no expected source — exclude them from retrieval metrics (they return on Day 3 as refusal-accuracy cases). Run the eval, write the baseline numbers down somewhere permanent. Everything this week gets measured against them.
items.why: Retrieval metrics are the difference between 'we added hybrid search' and 'hybrid search moved recall@5 from 0.68 to 0.84' — only one of those sentences survives an interview or a client review.

build.task: Write metrics.py with tested recall@k and MRR, then eval_retrieval.py producing your baseline table over the gold set.
steps: Implement rank_of_first_hit, recall_at_k and mrr exactly as specified below, with the worked-example asserts
Write eval_retrieval.py: for each answerable gold case retrieve k=10, compute the rank against expected_sources
Print the table: recall@1, recall@3, recall@5, MRR, n; verify one case's rank by hand against raw search output
Save the baseline row (date, config name, metrics) to results/history.jsonl
Write the three worst-ranked cases' ids in your log — Day 2 targets them
build.hint: Compute at k=10 once and derive recall@1/3/5 from the stored ranks — one retrieval pass, three metrics.

items.challenge: Break recall@k down by difficulty tag. Easy cases near 1.0 and hard cases near 0.4 is the expected shape — if easy cases are failing, you have an ingestion or id-mapping bug, not a retrieval-quality problem.

debugMission.scenario: Your first baseline run prints recall@5 = 1.00 and MRR = 0.98. Perfection on attempt one. You are (rightly) suspicious — Week 6's failure tour proved several of these queries miss.

# gold case g03:  expected_sources: ['arden-2025']    <- doc id

At what granularity did the gold file specify relevance, and at what granularity did retrieval return ids?
How would you have caught this instantly with one hand-checked case?
debugMission.solution: Two stacked bugs: the gold case stored a DOC id instead of a chunk id, and the helper used substring matching, so ANY chunk from the right document counted as a hit — near-guaranteed at k=5. Fix: exact equality on chunk-level ids, and validate_gold.py already rejects ids not present in the index — run it. Then re-verify one known-bad case by hand. Lesson: a metric that flatters you is a bug until proven otherwise; always hand-verify one case you KNOW fails before trusting any score.

reflection: Your recall@5 is 1.0 but MRR is 0.45 — describe what users experience and which pipeline stage (Day 2's reranker) that combination is begging for.
Why exclude unanswerable cases from retrieval metrics rather than scoring them as automatic hits or misses?

One case's rank verified by hand against raw search output

keyConcepts.def: Fraction of gold cases where at least one expected source chunk appears in the top k results.
Mean reciprocal rank: average of 1/rank of the first relevant result per case, 0 for misses — rewards ranking the right chunk high.
Score retrieval before generation: it is deterministic, free, and upstream — a retrieval miss caps everything downstream.

items.title: BM25 + vectors — hybrid search
items.concept:
Week 6's probe pairs showed what vectors fumble: exact terms, codes, names, numbers. Keyword search nails precisely those — which is why 2026 production retrieval is almost always hybrid, not either/or.

**BM25** is the keyword workhorse: tf-idf with two refinements. Term-frequency **saturation** — the k1 parameter makes the 10th occurrence of a word worth far less than the 2nd, so keyword-stuffed text cannot dominate. **Length normalisation** — the b parameter stops long documents winning just by containing more words. Rare terms (high idf) like 'EBITDA' or 'E4409' carry the score; common words carry almost nothing.

Merging is the interesting problem: BM25 scores are unbounded, cosine lives in a narrow band — rescaling one onto the other is fragile. **Reciprocal Rank Fusion** ignores scores entirely and fuses RANKS: RRF(d) = sum over systems of 1/(k + rank_s(d)), with rank starting at 1 and k around 60. Worked example: a chunk ranked 1st by BM25 only scores 1/61 = 0.0164; a chunk ranked 3rd by BOTH systems scores 2/63 = 0.0317 and wins. Consensus beats single-system enthusiasm — and the k constant keeps one system's #1 from steamrolling everything (with k=0, rank 1 would score 1.0 and nothing else could catch it).

Then the discipline that makes this week different: re-run yesterday's eval on the SAME gold set and record the delta. Hybrid usually buys its biggest wins on exact-term and name queries — check whether YOUR corpus agrees.
items.why: 'Why hybrid search?' is a standard interview question, and the strong answer names the query types vectors lose (codes, names, exact phrases) plus a fusion method — with your own before/after numbers, you are quoting evidence, not blog posts.

learn.focus: Read the README end to end (one page): install, building BM25Okapi from tokenised docs, get_scores and get_top_n. Ignore the BM25L/BM25Plus variants beyond noting they exist.

build.task: Build a BM25 index beside Qdrant, fuse both rankings with RRF, and re-run the retrieval eval to measure the delta.
steps: uv add rank-bm25; write tokenize(text) — lowercase, split, strip punctuation — and use it for BOTH indexing and queries
Build BM25Okapi over the same chunks Qdrant holds, keyed by the same chunk ids
Implement rrf_merge(rankings, k=60) per the formula; unit-test it with the worked example from the concept
hybrid_search(query): BM25 top-20 + vector top-20, RRF-fused, return top-5
Re-run eval_retrieval.py with hybrid; append the new row to results/history.jsonl and compute the delta vs baseline
Inspect 3 cases hybrid fixed and 1 it did not — which query types moved?
build.hint: Keep bm25_top() returning ids in rank order only — RRF never looks at raw scores, which is the whole point.

items.challenge: Sweep k over 10, 60 and 300 and re-run the eval each time. Explain the trend in one sentence: what does small k reward, and what does large k converge towards?

debugMission.scenario: Hybrid shipped, but recall on several exact-term gold cases went DOWN vs pure vectors. Worse, 'What is EBITDA leverage?' — the case hybrid was built for — gained nothing. BM25 seems to be contributing noise or silence.

# index side (ingest.py)
tokenized = [c['text'].lower().split() for c in chunks]
bm25 = BM25Okapi(tokenized)

# query side (search.py)
scores = bm25.get_scores(query.split())     # no lower()

# repl check

0.0                    # ??? the report says EBITDA on page 4
