hints: The index was built from LOWERCASED tokens. What exact string does the query side look up?
Lexical search is exact by definition — what is the contract between index-time and query-time tokenisation?
Where else could the two sides drift apart? Think punctuation: 'EBITDA.' at a sentence end.
debugMission.solution: The index lowercases; the query side does not, so 'EBITDA' looks up a token that does not exist and silently scores zero — BM25 degrades to a no-op for every capitalised query, and punctuation causes the same class of miss ('ebitda.' vs 'ebitda'). Fix: ONE tokenize() function imported by both ingest and search — asymmetric tokenisation is impossible when there is only one tokenizer. Add the canary test: a query for a term you know is in the corpus must produce a nonzero BM25 score. Lesson: lexical search has no fuzzy forgiveness; the tokenizer IS the contract.

reflection: Which of your gold cases did hybrid rescue, and could you have predicted them from Week 6's probe-pair takeaways?
Why is fusing ranks more robust than normalising and adding scores from two different scoring systems?
done: rrf_merge unit test passes the consensus-beats-enthusiasm example
Shared tokenize() used by both index and query sides, with a nonzero-score canary test
Hybrid eval row in results/history.jsonl with delta vs baseline recorded
Three fixed cases and one unfixed case analysed in your log

keyConcepts.def: Keyword ranking: tf-idf with term-frequency saturation (k1) and document-length normalisation (b); rare exact terms dominate the score.
Merge rankings by summing 1/(k + rank) per system (k around 60, ranks from 1) — no score normalisation needed, consensus wins.
Running lexical and vector search in parallel and fusing results, covering each method's blind spots.

items.title: Reranking — precision on top
items.concept:
Your embedding model is a **bi-encoder**: it encodes query and document separately, so all document vectors are precomputed and search is one dot product each — fast, but the two texts never see each other, which caps precision. A **cross-encoder** feeds query and document through the model TOGETHER, attending token-to-token ('does THIS 23% refer to revenue growth?'). Far more accurate — and unusable for search, because it must run a full forward pass per candidate pair at query time.

So production systems stack them: retrieve WIDE with the cheap stage (hybrid top-20), then rerank that shortlist with the cross-encoder down to a sharp top-5. Twenty forward passes on a small model is tens of milliseconds on CPU — affordable precision exactly where it counts, on the finalists.

Local and free: sentence-transformers CrossEncoder with the ms-marco MiniLM checkpoint, .predict() on (query, passage) pairs. Managed alternative: Cohere Rerank — same concept as an API call; know it for client conversations. One semantics warning: cross-encoder outputs are raw relevance logits — they can be negative, they are not probabilities, and they only mean anything relative to the other candidates in the same batch.

Then produce the week's money table: baseline, hybrid, hybrid+rerank — recall@1/3/5, MRR, and added latency per stage. Three rows that justify (or veto) every stage in your pipeline.
items.why: The retrieve-wide-then-rerank pattern is in virtually every serious RAG deployment, and the cost/benefit story — 'rerank bought 9 points of MRR for 40ms' — is exactly the kind of quantified engineering judgement senior interviews look for.

learn.focus: Read the Cross Encoder usage page: loading a pretrained CrossEncoder, predict() on (query, passage) pairs, and the rank() convenience method. Skip training and distillation sections entirely.

Five-minute skim of the overview: request shape (query + documents in, relevance scores out) and the pricing model. You integrate the local model today; know the managed option exists and what it costs.

build.task: Add a cross-encoder rerank stage after hybrid retrieval, re-run the eval, and produce the three-row money table with per-stage latency.
steps: uv add sentence-transformers if not present; load the ms-marco MiniLM cross-encoder once at startup, not per query
Implement rerank(query, candidate_ids, top=5) per the skeleton, timing the predict() call
Wire the pipeline: hybrid top-20 into rerank into top-5; keep a flag to disable each stage for A/B runs
Re-run eval_retrieval.py; append the hybrid+rerank row to results/history.jsonl
Build the money table: three configs, recall@1/3/5, MRR, added p50 latency per stage — paste it into your README draft
Read the 2 cases where reranking changed the top-1 — did token-level attention catch what cosine missed?
build.hint: Rerank quality depends on candidate quality: if recall@20 from the hybrid stage is low, the reranker has nothing to promote. Check recall@20 before blaming the cross-encoder.
build.code:
import time
from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder

ce = CrossEncoder('cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2')  # local, free

def rerank(query, candidate_ids, top=5):
  texts = [chunk_by_id[cid]['text'] for cid in candidate_ids]
  t0 = time.perf_counter()
  scores = ce.predict([(query, t) for t in texts])   # raw logits
  ms = round((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000)
  ranked = sorted(zip(candidate_ids, scores), key=lambda p: -p[1])
  return [cid for cid, s in ranked[:top]], ms

# pipeline: wide and cheap, then narrow and sharp
ids, ms = rerank(q, hybrid_search(q, k=20))
print('rerank took', ms, 'ms for 20 candidates')

# money table (fill every cell from eval runs on the SAME gold set):
# | stage           | recall@1 | recall@5 | MRR | added latency |
# | vector baseline |          |          |     | -             |
# | + hybrid RRF    |          |          |     | +? ms         |
# | + rerank        |          |          |     | +? ms         |

items.challenge: Rerank top-50 instead of top-20 and measure both metric delta and latency delta. Where does YOUR corpus stop paying for extra candidates? That number is a config constant worth a comment.

debugMission.scenario: After 'a small quality tweak' to the rerank stage, refusals on answerable questions tripled. Retrieval metrics look fine at the hybrid stage. Something between hybrid and the prompt is quietly eating the context.
debugMission.artifact:
def rerank(query, candidate_ids, top=5):
  pairs = [(query, chunk_by_id[c]['text']) for c in candidate_ids]
  scored = list(zip(candidate_ids, ce.predict(pairs)))
  keep = [(c, s) for c, s in scored if s > 0]   # drop 'irrelevant' ones
  return [c for c, s in sorted(keep, key=lambda p: -p[1])[:top]]

# python run_evals.py
refusal rate on ANSWERABLE cases: 0.31      (last week: 0.06)

# spot-check case g09 candidates and scores:
#   [-2.1, -3.4, -4.0, -5.5, -6.2, ...]  all negative
#   keep == []  ->  packed context is EMPTY  ->  honest refusal
hints: What does a cross-encoder score of -2.1 mean in absolute terms? Compare with the other candidates for the same query.
For some queries every candidate scores negative. What does the filter do then, and what does the model see?
What is the correct use of these scores: thresholding, or ordering?
debugMission.solution: Cross-encoder outputs are unbounded relative logits, not probabilities — for many legitimate queries EVERY candidate scores below zero, so the s > 0 filter empties the shortlist, the packer sends no context, and the model correctly refuses. Fix: use the scores to ORDER, never to threshold raw; take top-n regardless of sign. If you genuinely need an 'is anything relevant?' gate, apply sigmoid and calibrate the cutoff against your gold set (Day 3's calibration discipline, same idea). Lesson: know the semantics of every score you consume — 'bigger is better' does not imply 'positive means good'.

reflection: The bi-encoder compresses each text to one vector before comparison; the cross-encoder compares tokens directly. Connect that difference to the Week-6 negation probe pair.
For which product would you SKIP reranking entirely and why — think latency budgets.
done: Rerank stage wired behind a toggle, model loaded once at startup
Money table complete: three configs, four metrics, per-stage latency
hybrid+rerank row appended to results/history.jsonl with deltas
Score-semantics note written: order by logits, never threshold them raw

keyConcepts.def: Encodes query and document separately into vectors compared by dot product — precomputable and fast, but the texts never interact.
Scores a (query, document) pair in one forward pass with full token-level attention — precise, so costly it only fits a shortlist.
Cheap stage pulls top-20+; expensive stage re-orders the finalists to a sharp top-5 — precision where it pays.

items.title: Groundedness and LLM-as-judge
items.concept:
Retrieval metrics stop at 'the right chunk was present'. Two answer-level metrics cover the rest. **Groundedness**: is every factual claim in the answer supported by the retrieved context? This catches hallucination even when the answer sounds plausible. **Correctness vs gold**: does the answer match the expected answer? An answer can be grounded but wrong-for-the-question, or correct by luck while citing nothing — you want both measured, separately.

Checking 40 answers by hand every run does not scale, so you build an **LLM judge**: a rubric prompt plus your Week-4 structured-output muscle returning {score, unsupported_claims[]} at temperature 0. Use a cheap model while iterating; escalate to a strong one for release runs.

Judges inherit model biases, and you must know the catalogue: **position bias** (in pairwise comparisons, favouring the first — or last — option shown; mitigate by swapping order and averaging), **verbosity bias** (longer answers score higher regardless of content), **self-preference** (models rate their own family's phrasing higher), and **sycophancy toward confident tone** (assertive-and-wrong outscores hedged-and-right).

So: never trust an uncalibrated judge. **Calibration discipline**: hand-label 10+ answers yourself FIRST — including deliberately corrupted ones — run the judge on the same set, compute agreement, and read every disagreement. Below roughly 8/10 agreement, fix the rubric and re-calibrate; only then does the judge earn a place in your harness. A judge is a measurement instrument, and instruments get calibrated before use.
items.why: LLM-judged evals are how every serious team scores subjective quality at scale in 2026 — and 'how do you know your judge is right?' is the interview follow-up that filters out everyone who never calibrated one.

learn.focus: Read: the eval-design guidance — defining success criteria, graded vs exact-match scoring, and the LLM-based grading section with rubric examples. Skip any console/UI walkthrough parts.
Skim: how OpenAI structures graders and eval datasets — map their terminology onto the harness you are hand-rolling. Skip platform setup and dashboard sections.

build.task: Build judge.py (groundedness + correctness, structured verdicts), then calibrate it against 10 hand-labelled answers including manufactured failures.
steps: Define GroundednessVerdict (Pydantic): claims, unsupported_claims, score 1-5; wire it through your structured-output path at temperature 0
Write the groundedness rubric: list claims, demand a supporting quote per claim, ignore style and confidence, score by the anchored scale
Write judge_correctness(answer, expected): verdict correct/partial/wrong with a one-line reason
Generate answers for 10 gold cases; label them yourself BEFORE running the judge
Corrupt 3 copies deliberately (change a number, add an invented fact, swap an entity) and label those too
Run the judge on all 13; build the calibration table (your label vs judge, agreement %); read every disagreement and adjust the rubric once
build.hint: Anchor the score scale in the rubric with concrete descriptions (5 = every claim quoted, 3 = minor unsupported detail, 1 = core claim unsupported) — unanchored 1-10 scales drift with the judge's mood.
build.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel

class GroundednessVerdict(BaseModel):
  claims: list[str]               # factual claims found in the answer
  unsupported_claims: list[str]   # claims with no supporting quote
  score: int                      # 1-5 on the anchored scale

JUDGE_SYSTEM = (
  'You grade whether an ANSWER is supported by CONTEXT.\n'
  'List every factual claim in the answer. For each, find a verbatim\n'
  'supporting quote in the context; claims without one go in\n'
  'unsupported_claims. Ignore style, length and confidence entirely.\n'
  'score: 5 = every claim supported, 3 = minor unsupported detail,\n'
  '1 = a core claim is unsupported.')

def judge_groundedness(answer, context):
  return llm_structured(          # your Week-4 structured-output call
    system=JUDGE_SYSTEM, schema=GroundednessVerdict, temperature=0,
    prompt='CONTEXT:\n' + context + '\n\nANSWER:\n' + answer)

# calibration table to fill BEFORE trusting the judge:
# | case | your label (ok/bad) | judge score | agree? |
# agreement below ~8/10 -> fix the rubric, not your labels.

items.challenge: Run the same 13 answers through the judge twice at temperature 0 and once at 0.7. Any verdict that flips between runs is measurement noise — how much noise can your thresholds tolerate?

debugMission.scenario: Your calibration table shows 10/10 agreement and you are feeling smug. A colleague plants an answer with a fabricated dividend figure; the judge scores it 5/5. How did a perfectly-calibrated judge miss an obvious hallucination?
debugMission.artifact:
calibration run, 10 hand-labelled answers:
  your labels:   ok ok ok ok ok ok ok ok ok ok
  judge scores:   5  5  4  5  5  5  4  5  5  5    agreement: 10/10

# the plant: corrupted answers the judge was never calibrated on
  corrupted #1 (412 -> 390):            judge score 5
  corrupted #2 (+ invented dividend):   judge score 5
  corrupted #3 (Leeds -> Luton):        judge score 4
hints: Look at the labels column of the calibration set. How many BAD answers did the judge ever see during calibration?
What is 10/10 agreement worth if both graders would say 'ok' to anything?
How do you get known-bad answers when your system mostly produces good ones?
debugMission.solution: The calibration set contained only passing answers, so 10/10 agreement proved nothing — a judge that returns 5 unconditionally would have scored the same. Calibration sets need both classes, and when your system rarely fails you MANUFACTURE failures: corrupt good answers (change a number, invent a fact, swap an entity) and verify the judge catches each. Those corrupted cases then live on as permanent judge regression tests. Lesson: you validated the judge on the easy half of its job; a measurement instrument is calibrated across its whole range or not at all.

reflection: Which judge bias worries you most for YOUR system's typical answers, and what specifically in your rubric counters it?
When is a cheap-model judge good enough, and what triggers escalating to the strong model?
done: judge.py returns structured verdicts for groundedness and correctness at temperature 0
Calibration table filled: 13 cases including 3 manufactured failures, agreement computed
All 3 corrupted answers caught by the judge after rubric fixes
Judge biases listed from memory in your notes with one mitigation each

keyConcepts.def: The share of an answer's factual claims supported by the retrieved context — the anti-hallucination metric.
A model scoring outputs against a rubric with structured verdicts — cheap, scalable, and biased until calibrated.
Position bias, verbosity bias, self-preference, and sycophancy toward confident tone — systematic errors every judge inherits.
Hand-label first (including manufactured failures), measure agreement with the judge, fix the rubric until it tracks you.

items.title: Debug mission — the judge that grades itself generous
items.concept:
A generous judge is worse than no judge: it stamps green on regressions and you ship them with confidence. Generosity has a mechanism — vague rubrics ('rate the quality') let the model fall back on what it finds easy to reward: fluency, structure, confidence. Those correlate with good answers just often enough to look right.

The repair pattern is always the same: make the judge SHOW ITS WORK. Require a quote-level evidence trail per claim before any score, make unquoted claims cost points mechanically, and separate the axes — groundedness and style scored independently so eloquence cannot subsidise fabrication. Then re-run your calibration set to prove the fix. Judges need evals too; this mission is you giving your judge its first one.
items.why: In production, the judge IS your quality gate — CI thresholds, regression alerts, model-swap decisions all hang off it. A generous judge quietly converts all of those into theatre.

debugMission.scenario: Your v1 judge gives 9/10 to a fluent answer containing a number that appears nowhere in the context. Reproduce the failure with the artifact below, rebuild the rubric so evidence is mandatory, and prove the same answer now fails.
debugMission.artifact:
# judge prompt v1 (the bug is in here)
'Rate the quality of this answer from 1-10 given the context.'

context (excerpt):
  'Group revenue grew by 23% in Q3, reaching 412 million pounds
   for the full year. Operating margin widened from 6.1% to 8.4%.'

answer being graded:
  'Revenue grew an impressive 23% in Q3 to reach 415 million pounds,
   the strongest performance in a decade, while margins also widened.'

judge verdict:
  {'score': 9, 'comment': 'Clear, well-structured, accurate summary.'}
hints: List the factual claims in the graded answer. Which are supported verbatim by the context? Check the numbers digit by digit.
Read rubric v1 again: what does 'quality' instruct the judge to reward? Where does it demand evidence?
Restructure the output: claims with quotes FIRST, score derived from them after. What schema forces that order?
debugMission.solution: Two fabrications sailed through: 415 (context says 412) and 'strongest performance in a decade' (appears nowhere) — because 'rate the quality' measures fluency, and this answer is fluent. Fix: rubric requires a claim-by-claim table with a verbatim supporting quote or the tag UNSUPPORTED; score is computed FROM that table (any unsupported core claim caps the score at 2); style, if you want it at all, is a separate field. Re-run: the same answer now returns unsupported_claims=['415 million pounds', 'strongest performance in a decade'] and score 1-2. Keep this answer as a permanent judge regression case. Lesson: a score without an evidence trail is an opinion — make the judge show its work, then test the judge like any other component.

reflection: Fluency correlating with correctness is exactly what makes verbosity bias dangerous. Where else in your pipeline could a 'looks good' proxy be standing in for a real check?
done: Failure reproduced: v1 rubric scores the fabricated answer 8+
v2 rubric requires quote-level evidence and caps scores on unsupported core claims
Same answer now fails with both fabrications listed in unsupported_claims
The case saved into your permanent judge regression set

keyConcepts.def: Rubrics that demand a supporting quote per claim before any score — scores computed from evidence, not impressions.

days.title: Harness engineering — then ship and fix DocQA

items.title: The eval harness — pytest for your AI
items.concept:
You have metrics and a judge; now make them a HARNESS — evals as code, run like tests. run_evals.py executes every gold case through the live pipeline, writes one row per case to results.jsonl (query, retrieved ids, ranks, answer, judge verdicts, cost, latency), aggregates a summary, and — the part that changes your behaviour — asserts **thresholds**: recall@5 >= 0.80, groundedness >= 0.90, refusal accuracy on unanswerable cases = 100%. Any breach prints the failures and exits 1, exactly like pytest. That exit code is what makes an eval a REGRESSION GATE instead of a dashboard.

Repeatability rules: temperature 0 everywhere, pinned model versions, a FIXED sample for iteration (the first 10 cases, never a random draw) so run-to-run deltas measure your change and nothing else. Cost control: sample runs while iterating, the full 40 before anything you would call done.

And memory: every run appends config name + metrics to results/history.jsonl. Six weeks from now, 'when did groundedness dip and what changed?' is a one-liner over that file. Thresholds catch regressions at the door; history explains them afterwards.
items.why: This file is the answer to the interview-ending question. 'Every merge runs 40 gold cases; recall@5 under 0.80 fails the build' is a sentence that gets people hired — and it is Week 10's CI eval-smoke, already built.

build.task: Wire run_evals.py end to end with thresholds, then break one on purpose and watch it fail loudly.
steps: Write evaluate_case(case): retrieve, rank, answer, judge — returns the full row dict including cost and latency
Aggregate summarise(rows): recall@1/3/5, MRR, mean groundedness, refusal accuracy, total cost, p50 latency
Add THRESHOLDS and the exit-1 path; print failures with metric, value and threshold
Append every run to results/history.jsonl with config name and case count
Support a sample argument taking the FIRST n cases for cheap iteration
Sabotage test: set k=1, run, watch recall@5 breach and the process exit 1; restore and go green
build.hint: evaluate_case should call the same public ask() the CLI uses — evaluating a private code path tells you nothing about what users hit.

items.challenge: Add a cost guard: if projected spend for the run exceeds a configured cap, refuse to start and print the estimate. Runaway eval bills are a real (and embarrassing) production incident.

debugMission.scenario: You are A/B testing a chunking tweak with cheap 10-case runs. The numbers swing wildly: 0.90, then 0.70, then 0.80 — including across runs where you changed NOTHING. The eval itself is untrustworthy.
debugMission.artifact:
# the 'cheap iteration' line someone added
cases = random.sample(cases, 10)

# python run_evals.py 10   (before the chunking change)
recall_at_5: 0.90   groundedness: 0.95
# python run_evals.py 10   (after the chunking change)
recall_at_5: 0.70   groundedness: 0.88
# python run_evals.py 10   (change reverted)
recall_at_5: 0.80   groundedness: 1.00
hints: Three runs, three subsets. What population is each 0.x0 actually describing?
With 10 cases, one hit or miss moves recall by 0.10. How much of the swing is sampling, how much is your change?
What must stay constant for a before/after comparison to mean anything?
debugMission.solution: random.sample draws a different 10 cases each run, so the 'deltas' measured which questions were drawn, not whether the change helped — and at n=10 each case is worth 10 points of recall, so subset luck dominates. Fix: a fixed, stable slice for iteration (cases[:10]), the full set before any release claim, and if you ever randomise, seed it and log the seed. Lesson: an A/B comparison is valid only when everything except the change is held constant — including which cases you ask.

reflection: Where should thresholds come from — your baseline, user impact, or contract commitments? Defend your recall@5 number in one sentence.
What is the equivalent of results/history.jsonl in classical software engineering, and why do AI systems need it more?
done: run_evals.py produces results.jsonl + summary and appends to history.jsonl
Sabotage test performed: k=1 breaches recall@5 and exits 1; restored to green
Iteration uses a fixed 10-case slice; full 40 for release runs
Thresholds documented with a one-line rationale each

keyConcepts.def: A metric floor that fails the eval run (exit 1) when breached — the mechanism that turns evals into regression gates.
Append-only log of every eval run's config and metrics — the memory that lets you date and explain regressions.
Iterating on a stable subset of gold cases so run-to-run deltas measure your change, not sampling luck.

items.title: Error analysis — read your transcripts
items.concept:
Metrics tell you THAT something is wrong; transcripts tell you WHAT. Hamel's discipline, now yours: after every eval run, read the 5 worst cases end to end — query, retrieved chunks, packed context, answer, judge verdict — and tag each with a failure category:

- **retrieval-miss**: the needed chunk never surfaced
- **packing**: retrieved fine, then truncated or buried in the prompt
- **hallucination**: context was sufficient; the model invented anyway
- **refusal-miss**: refused an answerable question, or answered an unanswerable one
- **gold-wrong**: the dataset is the bug (you met one on Day 1)

Then the rule that keeps you honest: **fix the category, not the case**. A hack that rescues case g17 overfits your gold set; a fix for 'vocabulary-mismatch retrieval misses' improves queries you have not seen yet. Category counts choose your next engineering move — highest count wins, and your Week-6 failure log already predicted several of them.
items.why: Error analysis is the highest-leverage habit in applied AI — teams that read transcripts outrun teams that stare at dashboards. It is also how you generate the 'we found X, fixed Y, moved Z' stories interviews feed on.

learn.focus: Re-read only the error-analysis and 'look at your data' sections, this time as a working checklist against your own transcripts. Skip everything you absorbed on Day 1.

build.task: Start failure_log.md from your real worst cases, tag categories, ship one category-level fix, and record its measured delta.
steps: Run the full eval; sort rows by judge score ascending; take the 5 worst
Read each transcript end to end and tag its category — add the tag into results rows so tallying is scriptable
Tally categories with the snippet below; pick the biggest bucket
Design ONE fix at category level (retrieval-miss dominated by vocabulary gaps points at your Day-2 hybrid weights or W6 rewriting, packing points at your packer budget)
Re-run the FULL eval; record the delta in history.jsonl and the fix in failure_log.md
Note any case your fix regressed — zero-regression is part of the definition of done
build.hint: Tag fast and rough — 30 seconds per transcript. The value is in the counts, not in agonising over edge-case taxonomy.
build.code:
# failure_log.md - grows with every eval run. fix categories, not cases.
#
# | run        | case | category       | evidence                       |
# |------------|------|----------------|--------------------------------|
# | 2026-09-10 | g14  | retrieval-miss | gold chunk at rank 9, k=5      |
# | 2026-09-10 | g17  | retrieval-miss | vocab gap: leverage vs EBITDA  |
# | 2026-09-10 | g22  | refusal-miss   | answered from prior knowledge  |
# | 2026-09-10 | g07  | gold-wrong     | expected had growth % as total |

import json
tally = {}
for row in map(json.loads, open('results/results.jsonl')):
  if not row['passed']:
    cat = row.get('category', 'untagged')
    tally[cat] = tally.get(cat, 0) + 1
print(sorted(tally.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1]))
# biggest bucket = this week's engineering priority

items.challenge: Write the one-paragraph 'state of the system' summary a tech lead would want: top failure category, the fix shipped, the delta, and the next category in line. You will reuse this format in every job you ever have.

debugMission.scenario: Motivated by failing case g17, someone shipped a 'retrieval booster'. g17 now passes — and the full run dropped from 0.82 to 0.74 recall@5. The fix made the system worse while making its target case better.
hints: What happens to a question about production risks when four finance terms are bolted onto it?
Was this a category fix or a case fix wearing a category costume? Which category was g17 actually in?
What rule about eval runs would have caught this before it merged?
debugMission.solution: The hack appends finance vocabulary to EVERY query, so unrelated questions now retrieve financial-review chunks and their gold sources fall out of the top-5 — one case rescued, five poisoned. The honest category fix for a vocabulary gap is conditional rewriting (Week 6: gate on weak baseline scores, never replace the original) or hybrid weighting — mechanisms that help the query type without taxing everyone else. Process fix: any change must re-run the FULL eval and show aggregate improvement with no new failures before merging. The threshold gate from this morning exists precisely to catch generous-looking hacks like this one.

reflection: Which failure category is cheapest to fix per point of recall, on your evidence so far?
Why does 'fix the category' generalise while 'fix the case' overfits — and where have you met that exact distinction before in classical ML or testing?
done: 5 worst transcripts read end to end and tagged in results rows
failure_log.md committed with category tally
One category-level fix shipped; full-run delta recorded with zero new failures
Next-priority category named in the log

keyConcepts.def: Tagging each failed case as retrieval-miss, packing, hallucination, refusal-miss or gold-wrong — so counts, not anecdotes, choose your next fix.
Repairing the mechanism behind a class of failures rather than patching one case — the difference between generalising and overfitting your gold set.

items.title: Medium Project B — DocQA productionized
items.concept:
Merge seven weeks into one service. DocQA is your Week-3 API discipline wrapped around your Week-6 RAG pipeline, upgraded with this week's hybrid+rerank stack and — the differentiator — an eval suite that travels WITH the service and runs in one command. This repo becomes the platform Weeks 9, 10 and 11 build on: queues, Docker and multi-tenancy all land here. Invest accordingly.

Two design rules carry the day. **One core, two shells**: the CLI and the API call the same ask/ingest functions — logic lives in neither shell. **Evaluate the service, not the internals**: run_evals drives the HTTP endpoint (auth key and all), so the number you quote is the number users get, including serialization, middleware and rate-limit interactions.

The confidence field deserves thought, not theatre: derive it from the top rerank score bucketed against cutoffs you choose by eyeballing your gold-set score distributions (what score range did correct top-1s occupy?). Calibrated-ish beats decorative. Document what it means and what it does not.
items.why: This is portfolio centrepiece material: a deployed-quality RAG service WITH its own eval suite and metrics table is the artifact that turns 'I built a RAG demo' into 'I ship measured AI systems' — the exact line consultancies and AI teams hire across.

build.task: Ship DocQA: FastAPI service with PDF ingest, hybrid+rerank /ask with citations and confidence, auth, rate limits, and the eval suite runnable in one command.
steps: Milestone 1 — scaffold from your Week-3 skeleton: routers, Settings, error envelope, X-API-Key auth, request IDs; rate-limit /ask at 5/min/key

Milestone 2 — POST /documents: PDF upload via UploadFile, PyMuPDF extract + clean, structure-aware chunking with overlap, embed, Qdrant upsert with {doc_id, page, section}; returns doc_id + chunk count; reject non-PDFs and empty text layers with your Week-6 guard (sync is fine — Week 9 makes it a job)
Milestone 3 — POST /ask {question, doc_id?, k?}: hybrid top-20, rerank to 5, pack, answer at temperature 0; response {answer, citations[{chunk_id, doc_id, page, quote}], confidence, latency_ms}
Milestone 4 — confidence: bucket the top rerank score into high/medium/low with cutoffs chosen from your gold-run score distributions; document the method in the README
Milestone 5 — evals against the service: run_evals.py hits the HTTP endpoint with an eval API key; 'uv run python run_evals.py' green on the full gold set
Milestone 6 — tests: 401 without key, 429 after burst, 422 envelope on bad payload, ingest rejects a scanned PDF, ask happy-path with a tiny fixture corpus and mocked LLM
Milestone 7 — README: architecture sketch, the money table (baseline / hybrid / +rerank), threshold list, limitations section written honestly
build.hint: Do milestones in order and commit per milestone — a half-wired rerank stage plus a half-wired eval is undebuggable; two finished milestones are a system.
build.code:
# DocQA - target surface
# POST /documents   multipart PDF -> {doc_id, pages, chunks}
# GET  /documents   -> [{doc_id, title, pages, chunks}]
# POST /ask         {question, doc_id?, k?} ->
#   {answer, citations: [{chunk_id, doc_id, page, quote}],
#    confidence: 'high'|'medium'|'low', latency_ms}
# GET  /healthz     -> {status: 'ok'}   (no auth)
# auth: X-API-Key everywhere else; 429 + Retry-After past 5/min
#
# /ask pipeline:
#   embed(q) -> qdrant top-20 ---+
#   bm25(q)  -> top-20 ----------+-> RRF -> cross-encoder -> top-5
#   -> pack with [n] provenance -> llm at temp 0 -> parse citations
#   -> confidence from top rerank score (cutoffs from gold runs)
#
# eval:  uv run python run_evals.py        # full gold set, thresholds
#        uv run python run_evals.py 10     # fixed iteration slice

items.challenge: Add POST /feedback {request_id, verdict: up|down, note?} storing to a JSONL file. Every thumbs-down is a future gold case — you have just built the data flywheel that keeps eval sets alive in production.
reflection: Which single component would you swap first under client pressure — embedder, reranker, or answer model — and what does your history.jsonl say the risk is?
What breaks first at 100x load, and which Week-9 topic fixes it?
done: curl demo works: upload PDF, ask question, receive cited answer with confidence
run_evals.py exits 0 against the running service on the full gold set
Tests green: 401, 429, 422 envelope, scanned-PDF rejection, mocked happy path
README carries the money table, thresholds and an honest limitations section
Repo tagged v0.7.0 — the Week 9/10/11 platform baseline

keyConcepts.def: A service whose repo ships its own gold set, harness and thresholds — quality is reproducible by anyone with one command.
Mapping top rerank scores to high/medium/low via cutoffs read from gold-run distributions — honest, documented, and better than decoration.

items.title: Fix-the-bad-RAG mission
items.concept:
Consulting simulation: you inherit a RAG system some predecessor configured catastrophically, and you may NOT peek at your good config. Your instruments are the ones professionals actually have on day one at a client: the eval harness and the transcripts.

The method is the deliverable. Swap in config_bad.py below, re-ingest, run the full eval, and record the wreckage as your bad baseline. Then loop: read the worst transcripts, tag categories (Thursday's taxonomy), change ONE config key, re-ingest if chunking changed, re-run, record the delta. Repeat until you clear the targets: **recall@5 up at least 25 points and groundedness up at least 15 vs the bad baseline**.

One change at a time is non-negotiable — it is what makes your writeup table causal evidence rather than an anecdote. Expect surprises worth writing down: temperature 1.0 wrecks groundedness while leaving retrieval metrics untouched, and k=1 can look 'precise' on MRR while recall starves. The writeup table (change, metrics, delta, one-line why) is the artifact; a stranger should be able to reproduce your path from it alone.
items.why: Diagnosing an unfamiliar broken system with measurements — not folklore — is the daily reality of applied-AI consulting, and 'walk me through a debugging war story with numbers' is a standard senior interview. After today you have one.

build.task: Start from the provided deliberately-bad config, and fix the system stepwise to +25 recall@5 and +15 groundedness, documenting each change's measured delta.
steps: Copy config_bad.py over your active config; re-ingest; run the FULL eval; commit the bad-baseline row to history.jsonl
Read the 5 worst transcripts; tag failure categories; write your predicted first fix BEFORE making it
Fix one key, re-ingest when chunking changed, full eval, append the writeup row: change, recall@5, MRR, groundedness, delta, one-line why
Repeat single-change loops until both targets clear (expect roughly 4-6 loops)
Diff your final config against last week's good one; note anything the evidence made you set DIFFERENTLY from before
Commit writeup.md with the full table and three lessons
build.hint: Sequence matters: broken chunking hides retrieval gains and starving retrieval hides generation problems — fix ingest-side damage before query-side, and leave temperature for when retrieval is stable enough to show its effect cleanly.
build.code:
# config_bad.py - drop in as your active config, re-ingest, measure.
# Rules: no peeking at your good config until writeup.md is done.
CONFIG = {
  'chunk_strategy': 'fixed',     # structure ignored entirely
  'chunk_size': 120,             # characters
  'chunk_overlap': 0,
  'retrieve_k': 1,
  'hybrid': False,               # vector-only
  'rerank': False,
  'pack_order': 'as_returned',
  'answer_temperature': 1.0,
  'refusal_contract': False,     # system prompt: 'Answer the question.'
}
# mission rules:
#   1. one key changed per loop
#   2. full eval after every change, appended to results/history.jsonl
#   3. every loop adds a row to writeup.md: change -> metric deltas
# targets vs bad baseline: recall@5 +25 points, groundedness +15

items.challenge: After clearing the targets, find the CHEAPEST passing config: walk back the most expensive stages (rerank off? smaller k?) and see what still clears thresholds. Cost-floor hunting is a real client conversation.
reflection: Which single change bought the most recall — and would that ordering hold for a corpus of code documentation instead of an annual report?
What did temperature 1.0 damage, and why did retrieval metrics not notice?
done: Bad baseline recorded from config_bad.py after re-ingest, full eval
Every change is a single key with a full-eval row in writeup.md
recall@5 improved by >= 25 points and groundedness by >= 15 vs bad baseline
writeup.md committed with the change table and three lessons
Prediction-vs-reality noted: which fix surprised you

keyConcepts.def: Changing one variable per eval run so each metric delta has exactly one cause — the difference between evidence and anecdote.

items.title: Eval report writeup
items.concept:
Condense the week into one page a decision-maker reads in 90 seconds. Structure: three sentences of context (system, corpus, gold-set size), the money table (one row per pipeline change with recall@5, MRR, groundedness and latency), three lessons each anchored to a number from the table, and an honest 'what we did not fix' section.

Write for a sceptical PM, not a peer: no jargon without a gloss, numbers over adjectives, and the limitations section prominent — in consulting, disclosed limitations read as seniority, while discovered-by-the-client limitations read as failure. This document format (before/after table + lessons + residual risk) is the one consultants get hired off; every future engagement report you write is this page with more zeros.
items.why: Engineers who can compress a week of measurement into one credible page are rare and conspicuously promotable — this artifact goes straight into the portfolio and the interview folder.

build.task: Write the one-page before/after eval report from your writeup table and commit it to the repo.
steps: Draft reports/rag_eval_report.md following the skeleton below, pulling real numbers from results/history.jsonl
Anchor each of the three lessons to one specific number from the table
Write the residual-limitations paragraph: what is still weak, and what it would take to fix
Read it aloud once, cut 20% of the words, link it from the README
build.hint: Lead with the table, not the narrative — busy readers scan tables and only read prose that explains a surprising cell.
build.code:
# reports/rag_eval_report.md - one page, 90-second read
#
# 1. Context (3 sentences): what DocQA is, corpus, 40-case gold set
# 2. The money table (real rows from YOUR history.jsonl):
#    | pipeline change   | recall@5 | MRR  | grounded | p50 lat |
#    | bad baseline      | 0.31     | 0.22 | 0.66     | 0.9 s   |
#    | sane chunking     | ...      | ...  | ...      | ...     |
#    | k=5               | ...      | ...  | ...      | ...     |
#    | + hybrid (RRF)    | ...      | ...  | ...      | ...     |
#    | + rerank          | 0.86     | 0.73 | 0.94     | 1.3 s   |
#    (first and last rows shown as format examples - use YOUR numbers)
# 3. Three lessons, each citing one cell of the table
# 4. Not fixed yet: known weak spots + cost of fixing (honesty section)

items.challenge: Write the alternative 3-sentence executive summary for someone who will not even read the page. If you can only keep one number, which is it and why?
reflection: Which cell of your money table would a sceptical client poke first, and can you defend it aloud right now?
done: reports/rag_eval_report.md committed with real numbers from history.jsonl
Each lesson cites a specific table cell
Limitations paragraph present and honest
Linked from the README

keyConcepts.def: The before/after metrics table — one row per change, one column per metric — that lets a reader audit your engineering in ten seconds.

items.title: Week 7 review
items.concept:
Thirty minutes, out loud, notes closed. The protocol:

- Recite your pipeline stages in order — vector, BM25, RRF, rerank, pack, answer, judge — and attach YOUR metric delta to each stage from memory. Then check against results/history.jsonl; note any number you misremembered.
- Explain LLM-judge failure modes to an imaginary sceptic who says 'you are using AI to grade AI, that is circular': name position bias, verbosity bias, self-preference, sycophancy — then describe the calibration discipline that answers the objection.
- Define recall@k and MRR precisely, with the ranks 2, 7, 1, miss example, on paper from memory.
- Re-tell the fix-the-bad-RAG story in 90 seconds: baseline numbers, first fix, biggest win, final numbers.
- Queue exactly two wobbly concepts for revision.
items.why: These are the four stories every applied-AI interview asks for: pipeline, metrics, judge scepticism, and a debugging war story with numbers. Rehearsed aloud now, retrievable under pressure later.
reflection: Explain to a sceptic in three sentences why an LLM judge can be trusted at all. If your answer does not contain the word 'calibrate', try again.
Which metric delta from this week would you put on your CV, and can you defend how it was measured?
done: Pipeline stages plus deltas recited from memory, then verified against history.jsonl
Judge biases and calibration explained aloud without notes
Two concepts queued for revision

items.title: Week 7 quiz
items.concept: Take the Week 7 quiz below. It tests the reasoning — metric definitions with numbers, which query types hybrid rescues, rerank economics, judge biases, and threshold discipline. Attempt every question before revealing answers; each miss goes to the revision queue with a note on WHY you missed it.
items.why: A week about measurement ends by measuring you — only fair.
reflection: Did you miss on definitions or on judgement calls? The two gaps need different revision strategies.
done: Quiz completed at 70% or above
Every miss logged to the revision queue with a one-line cause

questions.q: Across 10 gold cases, the first relevant chunk always lands at exactly rank 4. What are recall@5 and recall@3?
options: recall@5 = 1.0, recall@3 = 0.0
recall@5 = 0.4, recall@3 = 0.3
recall@5 = 1.0, recall@3 = 1.0
recall@5 = 0.8, recall@3 = 0.4
questions.explain: Rank 4 is within the top 5 for every case (recall@5 = 10/10) and outside the top 3 for every case (recall@3 = 0/10). The pair of numbers together tells you the ranking is consistent but never high — reranker territory.

questions.q: Three gold cases have first-relevant ranks 1, 2, and not-found. What is the MRR?
questions.explain: MRR averages the reciprocal ranks with 0 for misses: (1.0 + 0.5 + 0) / 3 = 0.5. The miss is counted in the denominator — dropping misses would inflate the metric.

questions.q: Which query type gains MOST from adding BM25 to vector search?
options: Broad summarisation: 'summarise the outlook section'
Exact-term lookup: 'What is the penalty clause for part number X-77J?'
Conceptual: 'how did profitability trend over the year'
Comparative: 'compare this year with last year'
questions.explain: Rare exact tokens like X-77J carry huge idf weight in BM25 but get diluted in embeddings (Week 6's probe pairs). Conceptual and summary queries are where vectors already do well.

questions.q: With RRF at k=60, chunk A is ranked 1st by BM25 only; chunk B is ranked 3rd by BOTH systems. Who wins?
options: A — a first place always beats third places
B — 1/63 + 1/63 = 0.0317 beats A's 1/61 = 0.0164; consensus across systems outweighs one system's enthusiasm
They tie, and the tie is broken by raw scores
A, but only because k is large
questions.explain: RRF sums 1/(k + rank) per system, so appearing in both lists roughly doubles the contribution. The k constant (~60) deliberately dampens the advantage of a single #1 — that is the design intent, not an accident.

questions.q: Your judge consistently scores the LONGER of two equally-grounded answers higher. Which bias is this, and what is the standard mitigation?
options: Position bias — swap the order of candidates and average the verdicts
Self-preference — use a judge from a different model family
Verbosity bias — instruct the rubric to ignore length and check calibration on length-varied pairs
Sycophancy — lower the judge temperature
questions.explain: Rewarding length regardless of content is verbosity bias. The fix is rubric-level (grade evidence, ignore style/length) plus calibration cases that vary length while holding groundedness fixed. Order-swapping addresses position bias, a different family addresses self-preference.

questions.q: After a chunking change, run_evals prints 'recall_at_5 0.78 < 0.80' and exits 1. The professional next move is:
options: Lower the threshold to 0.78 — the change is probably fine
Re-run a few times in case it passes
Treat it as a regression: read the newly-failing transcripts, then fix the cause or revert before merging
Switch to a stronger judge model so the numbers look better
questions.explain: The threshold is a regression gate — the whole point is that breaches block the change until explained. Loosening thresholds or rerolling the dice converts your eval harness into decoration.

questions.q: Why does production RAG retrieve ~20 candidates cheaply and cross-encode only those, rather than (a) cross-encoding the whole corpus or (b) just taking the vector top-5?
questions.answer: A cross-encoder needs one full forward pass per (query, document) pair at query time, so scoring the whole corpus is computationally impossible at any scale — while bi-encoder vectors are precomputed and cost one dot product each. But the bi-encoder's top-5 is imprecise because query and document never interact token-to-token. Retrieve-wide-rerank-narrow buys cross-encoder precision exactly where it matters (the finalists) at a bounded, affordable latency cost.

questions.q: Describe the calibration step you must run before trusting an LLM judge, including what belongs in the calibration set and the metric you compute.
questions.answer: Hand-label 10+ real answers yourself before the judge sees them, and include manufactured failures (corrupt a number, invent a fact, swap an entity) so both classes are represented. Run the judge on the same set and compute agreement with your labels, reading every disagreement; below roughly 8/10 you fix the rubric and re-calibrate. This protects against the judge's systematic biases — verbosity, position, self-preference, sycophancy — being mistaken for measurement.

title: Agents and Workflows — and When Not To
objective: Build deterministic workflows and a from-scratch agent loop, compare them honestly on the same task, and evaluate agent runs.
narrative: Anthropic's own guidance says most "agent" products are better as workflows — you'll learn both and, more importantly, the judgment to choose. No frameworks: your agent loop is ~50 lines of Python you fully understand, which means you can debug it — a claim most framework users can't make.
whatYouCanBuild: A working agent with tools, state, approval gates and an eval harness — plus a workflow version of the same task and an evidence-based comparison.
whyProfessionally: "When would you NOT use an agent?" is a favorite senior-interview question. You'll answer with data from your own comparison, not a blog opinion.

items.title: Workflows — chains, routing, parallelization
items.concept:
Two words get abused interchangeably; the essay you're reading today fixed the vocabulary. **Workflows** are systems where LLM calls are orchestrated through code paths YOU predefined. **Agents** are systems where the model directs its own process — it decides which tool to call next and when it's done. Both are built from the same unit, the **augmented LLM**: a model call wired to tools, retrieval and memory.

Five workflow patterns cover most production systems:
- **Prompt chaining** — decompose into fixed steps, each LLM call consuming the last one's output, with programmatic gate checks between.
- **Routing** — classify the input, dispatch to a specialised handler with its own prompt.
- **Parallelization** — split into independent sections run concurrently, or run the same task several times and vote.
- **Orchestrator-workers** — one call plans dynamic subtasks, workers execute them, orchestrator synthesises.
- **Evaluator-optimizer** — one call generates, another critiques against criteria, loop until accepted.

The load-bearing idea is what sits BETWEEN the LLM steps: deterministic code. Validate every intermediate output (Pydantic, length checks, enum labels), fail fast with the offending text in the error, log each artifact. That's what makes workflows predictable, debuggable and cheap — every step is separately testable with the Week 7 eval muscle you already have.
items.why: Most shipped "agent" products are workflows wearing a costume. Pattern selection — chain vs router vs orchestrator — is the actual daily design work of an AI engineer, and clients pay for the judgment, not the buzzword.

learn.focus: Read: the intro, 'What are agents?', 'When (and when not) to use agents', 'When and how to use frameworks', then every pattern under 'Building blocks, workflows, and agents' — augmented LLM, prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer, and the 'Agents' section. Stop before the appendices (saved for w8d1b). Note how often it says 'start simple' — that is the thesis, not a disclaimer.

build.task: Build workflow.py: a three-step chain (outline -> draft -> critique-and-revise) for company briefs, plus a router dispatching queries to extract / summarize / answer handlers.
steps: Write a thin llm(prompt) helper over your W4 llm_client — cheap model, temperature 0.2; this file makes many calls.
Chain step 1: outline (max 5 bullets). Gate: at least 3 non-empty bullet lines, else raise StepFailed carrying the offending output.
Chain steps 2-3: draft strictly following the outline; critique listing concrete gaps; revise addressing every critique point.
Router: classify a query into extract | summarize | answer via a structured-output call constrained to exactly those labels (W4 pattern).
Dispatch through a dict of handler functions, each with its own focused prompt.
Run the chain on 2 topics and the router on 6 mixed queries; write every intermediate artifact to out/ so each step is inspectable.
build.hint: Gates between steps are the whole point — a chain without checks is just an expensive way to propagate garbage forward.

items.challenge: Add a parallelization step: run the critique twice concurrently with different critic personas (accuracy hawk, concision hawk), merge both critiques into the revise step, and check with a quick rubric whether the final brief measurably improves.

debugMission.scenario: Your router ran fine on 5 test queries, then a teammate replayed 20 real ones and it crashed. The classifier is the suspect.
debugMission.artifact:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File 'workflow.py', line 41, in route
    return ROUTES[label](query)
KeyError: 'summarisation'

# classifier prompt (v1):
# 'Classify this query as extract, summarize, or answer.
#  Reply with the label only.'

# labels observed over 20 replayed queries:
#   summarize (11)   extract (4)   answer (3)
#   'summarisation' (1)   'Summarize.' (1)
hints: Look at the five distinct label strings that came back. How many match a ROUTES key exactly?
You solved this class of problem in Week 4 — what makes a model's output safe to use as a dict key?
debugMission.solution: The classifier returns free text, and free text drifts: British spelling, trailing punctuation, capitalisation. The dict lookup treats it as an exact enum, so one drifted label is a production KeyError. Fix: constrain the label with structured output (Literal['extract','summarize','answer'] via your W4 schema-enforced pattern) and keep a logged fallback route for anything that still surprises you. General lesson: LLM output is untrusted boundary input — validate it exactly like user input, because that is what it is.

reflection: Which of the five patterns does your current DocQA /ask endpoint already resemble, and what would upgrading it to evaluator-optimizer cost per query?
Where in your chain did deterministic code catch something the LLM step got wrong?
done: Chain produces a revised brief for 2 topics with all intermediate artifacts saved to out/
Gate check demonstrably fires on a forced-thin outline and the error carries the offending text
Router sends 6/6 test queries to the intended handler
You can name all five workflow patterns from memory with a one-line use case each

keyConcepts.def: A single model call wired to tools, retrieval and memory — the building block of both workflows and agents.
Fixed decomposition into sequential LLM steps with programmatic gate checks between them.
Classify an input, then dispatch it to a specialised downstream handler with its own prompt.
A generate-critique-revise loop where one LLM call grades another's output against explicit criteria.

items.title: When NOT to use agents
items.concept:
The decision checklist, condensed from the essay: if you can enumerate the steps in advance, build a **workflow** — full stop. Consider an agent only when ALL of these hold:
- the steps are genuinely unknown or dynamic (the next action depends on what the last one revealed)
- progress is **verifiable** by something other than the model (tests pass, citations resolve, state is checkable)
- the cost of extra tokens and latency is acceptable for the task's value
- the blast radius is controllable (sandbox, approval gates, caps)

Autonomy has a price list. **Latency**: many serial model calls where a chain makes three. **Spend**: the transcript is resent every step, so cost compounds. **Unpredictability**: a different path every run means your p95 is a guess. **Debugging pain**: no fixed code path to breakpoint — you debug transcripts, not stack traces.

Anthropic's advice is to escalate complexity only when it measurably buys outcome quality: single call -> chain -> workflow -> agent, with evals at each rung. Corollary for consultants: "we used an agent" is a cost centre, not a selling point.
items.why: Saying no to an agent — with reasons — is a senior signal. Interviewers and clients both probe for it, and the checklist gives you a defensible, repeatable answer.

learn.focus: Re-read 'When (and when not) to use agents', then read Appendix 1 'Agents in practice' (customer support, coding agents) — for each, extract WHY the domain suits agents: open-ended steps plus a hard verifier. Skim 'When and how to use frameworks' if you skipped it yesterday. 10-12 minutes.

build.task: Score the six scenarios below as AGENT, WORKFLOW, or WORKFLOW + HUMAN GATE, each with a one-line justification, then reveal the expert answers in-app and grade yourself.
steps: Read each scenario; decide in under 2 minutes each — first instinct, then test the instinct against the four-condition checklist.
For each, write the verdict plus one line naming the DECIDING property: step predictability, verifiability, blast radius, or cost.
Reveal the expert answers; score yourself out of 6.
For every miss, write one sentence on which property you misjudged — that sentence is the lesson.
build.hint: The deciding question is rarely 'could an agent do this?' It is 'what do unknown steps buy here, and who pays when the run varies?'
build.code:
SCENARIOS
1. Invoice intake: 10,000 supplier PDFs a month must land in a fixed
   12-field schema; finance reconciles totals weekly and rejects bad rows.
2. Support inbox: tag each ticket as billing / bug / how-to and draft a
   reply from the matching template for a human to send.
3. 'Make CI green': a 40k-line repo with a failing test suite; nobody
   knows which files need changing; CI is the referee.
4. Nightly ops digest: pull yesterday's numbers from three internal
   APIs, summarise, post to the team channel at 07:00.
5. Due diligence: given a target company and a 500-document data room,
   gather evidence, follow leads across documents, produce a sourced memo.
6. Refunds: approve or reject requests up to 500 GBP using the policy
   document and the customer's order history.

items.expert:
1. WORKFLOW. Steps are fully known (extract -> validate -> file) and output is verifiable against a fixed schema plus weekly reconciliation. An agent adds run-to-run variance exactly where finance wants none. A chain with a validation gate and a human queue for rejects is cheaper, faster and auditable. Deciding property: step predictability.

2. WORKFLOW (routing). Classify-then-dispatch is the routing pattern verbatim; templates keep outputs predictable and easy to eval. A misroute is cheap and shows up in your eval set. Autonomy buys nothing here. Deciding property: step predictability.

3. AGENT. The defining pair is present: the step sequence is genuinely unknown (which files? what edits?) AND progress is machine-verifiable — CI passes or it does not. This is why coding agents are the flagship case in the essay's appendix. Run it with a sandbox, max-steps and a cost cap. Deciding property: verifiability of dynamic steps.

4. WORKFLOW. The same steps run every night; a failure should page a human, not trigger improvisation. Today's debug mission shows the failure mode of agentifying this: a run that silently skips a source and pads the gap with plausible numbers. Deciding property: step predictability (and auditability).

5. AGENT — or orchestrator-workers if you want more structure. Follow-the-evidence means the next query depends on what the last document revealed; you cannot enumerate that in advance. Verification comes from citations resolving back to the data room. Cap tool calls and spend; a sensible hybrid runs a workflow first pass (index + standard checklist) and hands only open threads to the agent. Deciding property: dynamic steps with citation-verifiable output.

6. WORKFLOW + HUMAN GATE. Consequential, irreversible and adversarial-adjacent (people game refund bots). Deterministic policy rules decide the clear cases; ambiguous ones go to a person with the evidence pre-assembled. Model autonomy over money fails the blast-radius test no matter how accurate it looks in testing. Deciding property: blast radius.
items.challenge: Write scenario 7 from your own current job — a real process you know intimately — and score it with the same rigour. That one becomes your go-to interview answer.

debugMission.scenario: A team 'agentified' scenario 4 (the nightly digest). It mostly works. Compare these two consecutive runs and find the defect that determinism would have made impossible.
debugMission.artifact:
# nightly_report agent -- tool traces, same config both nights
run 2025-09-04:
  get_metrics(source='sales') -> ok
  get_metrics(source='ops') -> ok
  get_metrics(source='finance') -> ok
  compose_digest() -> post_to_channel()   [6 calls, 48s]
run 2025-09-05:
  get_metrics(source='sales') -> ok
  compose_digest() -> post_to_channel()   [3 calls, 21s]
  posted text includes: 'Ops incidents: 3 (stable)' and
  'Finance: costs flat vs yesterday'
# ops API was never called on 09-05; actual incident count was 11
hints: Diff the tool sequences. What did the 09-05 run skip, and what appeared in the digest anyway?
Nothing errored. Is 'no error' the same as 'correct' when the model chooses its own steps?
debugMission.solution: On 09-05 the model simply chose not to call two of the three sources — nothing failed, so nothing alerted — then filled the digest's ops and finance sections with plausible invented numbers. With known steps, an agent's freedom is pure downside: variance where variance is a defect. The fix is deterministic: a fixed chain that calls all three sources, fails loudly if any call errors, and only then composes. General lesson: when you can write the steps down, write them down — reserve model autonomy for tasks where you can't.

reflection: Which of the four agent preconditions does your own daily work most often fail — and does that match where you were tempted to reach for an agent?
done: All 6 scenarios scored with one-line justifications BEFORE revealing the expert answers
Self-score out of 6 recorded; every miss annotated with the misjudged property
You can recite the four agent preconditions without notes

keyConcepts.def: Use an agent only when steps are unknown/dynamic, progress is externally verifiable, cost is acceptable and blast radius is controlled.
The latency, compounding token spend, unpredictability and debugging pain you pay for letting the model direct its own process.

items.title: An agent in ~50 lines
items.concept:
An agent is a while-loop around the tool-use dance you already know from Week 5. Send messages + tool schemas; if stop_reason is 'tool_use', execute every tool_use block, append the assistant turn and then a user turn of tool_result blocks, and go round again; if it's 'end_turn', the text blocks are your answer. Add a max_steps guard and a printed trace, and that is the whole thing — everything else agents do (state, gates, evals) bolts onto this loop.

Two mechanical rules cause most beginner crashes. First, ORDER: the assistant message containing tool_use must be appended before the user message containing tool_result, and the ids must match. Second, PARALLEL calls: one response may contain several tool_use blocks — all their tool_results go in ONE following user message.

Your three tools — list_dir, read_file, search_text — operate on a sandbox corpus directory and nothing else. Resolve every path with os.path.realpath and refuse anything outside the sandbox root; return the refusal as a normal tool_result string, not an exception, so the model can recover. This is a safety habit, not paranoia — Week 10 shows you what happens to people who skip it.

One design choice in the starter code repays attention: assistant content blocks are normalised to plain dicts with model_dump() at append time. That keeps the whole transcript JSON-native, which makes tomorrow's save/resume work trivial.
items.why: Framework users ship agents they cannot debug. Owning a 40-line loop means every production question — why did it loop, what did it cost, where did it stop — is answerable by reading code you wrote.

learn.focus: Read: 'How tool use works' (the request/response flow diagram), 'Handling tool use and tool result content blocks', and the section on parallel tool use / multiple tools. Note where stop_reason appears and what values it takes. Skip: fine-grained tool streaming and the token-efficient tool use notes — not needed today.

build.task: Build agent.py (the loop below) plus tools.py, and run a research agent that answers questions over your Week 6 sandbox corpus with file citations, printing the full trace.
steps: Create sandbox_corpus/ and copy in 10-12 small .md/.txt files from your W6 corpus (or split a PDF's extracted text into topic files).
tools.py: TOOLS = three JSON schemas (list_dir, read_file, search_text) with descriptions written like docs — they are the model's only manual.
tools.py: run_tool(name, args) dispatcher; every path goes through a resolve() that realpaths and rejects anything outside sandbox_corpus with a polite refusal string.
Type agent.py from the reference below yourself — no pasting; you need finger-memory of the loop.
Run 3 questions of rising difficulty; read the printed traces end to end and note each decision the model made.
Cap tool_result content at a few thousand characters and log when truncation happens.
build.hint: Write tool descriptions like you'd write docs for a junior colleague: what it does, what args mean, what it returns, when to prefer it over the others.
build.code:
# agent.py -- the whole loop
import json
import anthropic
from tools import TOOLS, run_tool

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
SYSTEM = ('You are a research agent over a small document corpus. '
  'Use the tools to gather evidence before answering. '
  'Cite files for every claim, like [meridian_finances.md].')

def run_agent(question, max_steps=15):
  messages = [{'role': 'user', 'content': question}]
  for step in range(max_steps):
    resp = client.messages.create(
      model='claude-sonnet-4-5', max_tokens=1024,
      system=SYSTEM, tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
    blocks = [b.model_dump() for b in resp.content]
    messages.append({'role': 'assistant', 'content': blocks})
    if resp.stop_reason != 'tool_use':
      text = ''.join(b['text'] for b in blocks if b['type'] == 'text')
      return text, messages
    results = []
    for b in blocks:
      if b['type'] != 'tool_use':
        continue
      print('step', step, '::', b['name'], json.dumps(b['input']))
      try:
        out = run_tool(b['name'], b['input'])   # sandbox enforced inside
      except Exception as exc:
        out = 'TOOL_ERROR: ' + repr(exc)
      results.append({'type': 'tool_result', 'tool_use_id': b['id'],
                      'content': str(out)[:6000]})
    messages.append({'role': 'user', 'content': results})
  return 'Stopped: max_steps reached without a final answer.', messages

if __name__ == '__main__':
  answer, transcript = run_agent('Who founded Meridian, and when?')
  print('\n=== ANSWER ===\n' + answer)

items.challenge: Add a --verbose flag that also prints each tool_result (truncated to 200 chars) and per-step usage from resp.usage — you are one evening away from a trace viewer.

debugMission.scenario: Your first run dies on step 1 with a 400 from the API. The loop looks right to you. The traceback says otherwise.
debugMission.artifact:
anthropic.BadRequestError: Error code: 400 -
{'type': 'error', 'error': {'type': 'invalid_request_error',
 'message': 'messages.1.content.0: unexpected tool_use_id found in
 tool_result blocks: toolu_01Xh2. Each tool_result block must have a
 corresponding tool_use block in the previous message.'}}

# the loop variant that produced it:
#   if resp.stop_reason == 'tool_use':
#     results = execute_all(resp.content)
#     messages.append({'role': 'user', 'content': results})   # <-- only this
hints: Count the messages the API received: user question, then... what came immediately before the tool_result message?
The error names 'the previous message'. What must that previous message contain for a tool_result to be legal?
debugMission.solution: The code executed the tools but never appended the assistant message containing the tool_use blocks, so the tool_result turn arrived with no matching tool_use before it — an immediate 400. Fix: append the assistant turn (resp.content, normalised to dicts) BEFORE the user turn of tool_results, ids intact. General lesson: the transcript is a strict protocol, not a chat log — assistant tool_use and user tool_result alternate in matched pairs, and the API validates the pairing.

reflection: Read one full trace aloud: at which step did the model switch from exploring (list/search) to exploiting (read)? Would you have made the same calls?
What would your loop do today if the model called a tool name that does not exist — and is that behaviour you chose or inherited?
done: Agent answers 3/3 corpus questions with file citations
Full trace prints tool name + args for every step
Path traversal attempt (read_file with '../') returns a refusal string, not file contents and not a crash
You can write the loop's control flow on paper from memory

keyConcepts.def: while not done: call model with transcript + tools; execute tool_use blocks; append matched tool_results; stop on end_turn or a guard.
The API field that tells your loop why generation ended — 'tool_use' means execute-and-continue, 'end_turn' means the answer is ready.
Restricting tool side effects to a dedicated directory or namespace, enforced in code (realpath checks), never by trusting the model.

items.title: Debug mission — the infinite loop
items.concept:
Agents fail as systems, so you debug them as systems: not 'which line is wrong' but 'which incentive is wrong'. The commonest systemic failure is the re-read loop — the model calls the same tool with the same args, gets the same result, and tries again, because nothing in the transcript tells it that repetition is futile and nothing in the instructions licenses giving up.

Today you get a real trace of one. The layered fix mirrors the guards from the quiz: max_steps bounds the damage (it already saved you money here); repeated-call detection turns the N-th identical call into information ('you already read this; the content has not changed'); and a termination instruction ('if the corpus does not contain the answer, say so and stop') makes honest failure a legal move. Note the shape: you rarely fix an agent by patching code alone — you fix the system of code + instructions + tool results together.
items.why: The loop is the failure mode you WILL hit in production first; every framework postmortem features it. Diagnosing it from a trace is a hireable skill.
items.challenge: Add loop detection that triggers on the SECOND identical call but allows legitimately repeated calls with different args — write one test for each case.

debugMission.scenario: A user asked your research agent for a figure the corpus does not contain. The run burned 15 steps and 44k tokens before max_steps killed it. Diagnose from the trace, then implement fixes.
hints: The tool executed perfectly every time. So why does the model keep calling it — what NEW information did steps 4-14 add to the transcript?
The corpus genuinely lacks FY2025. Does anything in the system prompt tell the model what to do when the answer does not exist?
Three layers: bound the run, break the repetition, license honest failure. Which code and which prose implements each?
debugMission.solution: Root cause is systemic: the answer does not exist, the instructions demand cited answers and never mention giving up, and each identical tool_result adds zero new information — so retrying stays the model's best-looking move. Fixes, layered: (1) keep max_steps — it capped the bill; (2) detect repeats by hashing tool name + args and, on a repeat, return 'you already called read_file with these arguments; the result has not changed — do not call it again' instead of re-executing; (3) add to the system prompt: 'If the corpus does not contain the answer, state that plainly, citing where you looked, and stop.' Re-run: the fixed agent answers in ~4 steps that FY2025 is not in the corpus, citing meridian_finances.md as covering only FY2023-24. General lesson: agents fail as systems — the fix spans guards, tool-result content and instructions, not a single line.

reflection: Which of the three fixes would ALONE have prevented the 44k-token bill, and which would alone have produced a useful answer? Why do you want both?
done: Reproduced the loop (or replayed the trace) and written the root cause in two sentences
All three fixes implemented: repeat detection, termination instruction, max_steps retained
Re-run on the same question ends within 5 steps with an honest cited 'not in corpus' answer

keyConcepts.def: Hashing tool name + args to catch identical calls and convert re-execution into corrective guidance for the model.
Explicit system-prompt permission to stop and report failure honestly, removing the incentive to loop.

items.title: Agent state and resumability
items.concept:
Your agent already has a database and you built it on Monday: the **transcript**. Every decision, every tool call, every result lives in that messages list, in order. There is no hidden state — which means persisting the agent is just json.dump(messages), and resuming it is just loading the list and re-entering the loop. Keep the transcript JSON-native (the model_dump() normalisation from w8d2a) and this stays a five-line problem.

Save after every step, atomically: write runs/<id>.tmp then os.replace onto runs/<id>.json. A half-written state file is worse than none, because you will resume from it at 2am and spend an hour blaming the model.

Resuming has one sharp edge. A run killed between the model call and the tool execution leaves a trailing assistant turn whose tool_use blocks have no matching tool_result — and the API rejects that transcript outright. You either drop the trailing assistant turn (cheap: one wasted model call) or synthesise tool_results for it by re-executing. Drop it unless the tools are expensive; today's debug mission is what happens if you do neither.

**Context budget** is the other long-run tax. Step N resends everything from steps 0..N-1, so a 20-step run over chunky file reads can push six figures of input tokens. Trim the CONTENT of old tool_results — never the blocks themselves, never the ids, never assistant reasoning — leaving a marker that says the full text is re-readable. Decisions are small and load-bearing; tool output is bulky and re-fetchable. That asymmetry is the whole trimming policy.

A **scratchpad** tool (note / read_notes, written to a run-scoped file) gives the model somewhere durable to put findings, so 'what did I learn in step 3' survives trimming, restarts and even a fresh transcript. It is memory you can read, diff and eval — unlike anything living implicitly in the context window.
items.why: Long-running agents die: rate limits, timeouts, a deploy, a laptop lid. Resumability turns a lost 40-step run into a 4-step continuation, and the context budget is what stops a working agent becoming an unaffordable one.

build.task: Add state.py to your agent: atomic save after every step, resume-by-run-id with transcript repair, tool_result trimming, and a scratchpad note tool — then kill a run mid-task and resume it.
steps: Write save(run_id, question, messages, step) using the tmp-then-os.replace pattern; call it at the end of every loop iteration.
Add run_agent(question, run_id=None, resume=False): on resume, load the transcript, run repair() on it, and continue from the saved step count.
Implement repair(): drop a trailing assistant turn that contains tool_use blocks, because its tool_results never happened.
Add budget(): for all but the last 3 exchanges, truncate tool_result content over 800 chars and append a trimmed marker; assert every tool_use id still has its tool_result.
Add a note(text) tool writing to runs/<id>/notes.md plus read_notes(); tell the model in the system prompt to record findings there before long reads.
Run a 10-step question, Ctrl-C it around step 5, resume, and diff the final answer against an uninterrupted run of the same question.
build.hint: Test the ugly case deliberately: kill the process DURING a tool call, not between steps. That is the state your repair() exists for, and it is the only one that produces a 400.

items.challenge: Make trimming measurable rather than hopeful: log input tokens per step for a 15-step run with and without budget(), plot the two curves, and check the answers still match. If trimming changed an answer, your cap is too aggressive or you trimmed something that was not re-fetchable.

debugMission.scenario: You killed a run during a slow search_text call and resumed it. The resume dies instantly with a 400, before a single new tool runs.
debugMission.artifact:

anthropic.BadRequestError: Error code: 400 -
{'type': 'error', 'error': {'type': 'invalid_request_error',
