build.hint: Resist the urge to promise a headcount number. Say what the machine takes off the team's plate, in documents per month at what accuracy, and let the client decide what that means for their staffing - that boundary is also where the engagement stays defensible.

items.challenge: Write the one-line answer to 'so can you get us to 99.9%?' that is honest, does not lose the deal, and points at the confidence-threshold design.
reflection: How much faster were you than Case 1, and which section still consumes disproportionate time?
Across all five cases, which section is reliably your weakest - and what one artifact would fix it?
done: All 8 sections attempted inside the timebox before the expert reveal
ROI shown as visible arithmetic with a range and the two dominant sensitivities named
Confidence-based routing, the peak freeze and the rate-limited integration all addressed
Self-scores recorded, cross-case trend reviewed, remaining gaps logged to the revision queue

keyConcepts.def: Sending extractions to straight-through, review-queue or manual handling by field-level confidence instead of promising a single accuracy number.
Stating the two assumptions a cost or ROI model is most sensitive to, so the client can challenge the model instead of the messenger.

items.title: Mock interview marathon
items.concept:
Three rounds, sixty minutes, all of them spoken aloud to an empty room. The full scripts are in the expert panel: a 15-minute recruiter and hiring-manager screen, a 25-minute technical deep-dive on the capstone, and a 20-minute system design redux. Read a question, answer it out loud at real speed, move on. No pausing to look things up, no restarting an answer you dislike.

**Speaking is the skill being trained.** You have written every one of these answers already; you have said almost none of them. The first time you hear yourself explain tenant isolation is going to be either in this room or in front of a hiring manager, and one of those is cheaper.

**Round two is where offers are won and lost.** Deep-dive questions on your own project are the fairest round in the industry and the one candidates prepare least: the interviewer picks a claim from your README and pulls. Every number you put in that metrics table is a legitimate thread. If 'cost per query is about two cents' cannot be broken down into where the two cents goes, do not have it in the README.

**Record one answer.** Use your phone, pick the capstone architecture walkthrough, and listen back afterwards. It is genuinely unpleasant and it is the highest-value ninety seconds of the week: you will hear filler openings ('so, basically, um, the way it works is'), the twenty seconds before your first substantive sentence, and the answer that quietly stopped answering the question. Note three specific fixes.

Score each round with a simple bar: did you answer the question that was asked, in under two minutes, with at least one concrete number or artifact? Anything that fails the bar goes to the revision queue as a rehearsal item.
items.why: Interviews are performed, not submitted. Fluency under mild pressure is a separable skill from competence, and it is trainable in exactly one way: repetition out loud with a clock running.

build.task: Run the three scripted mock rounds aloud against a clock, record one answer and listen back, then log rehearsal items for everything that missed the bar.
steps: Set up: the scripts from the expert panel on screen, timer running, phone ready to record, nobody around to make you self-conscious
Round 1 (15 min): recruiter and hiring-manager screen, roughly 90 seconds per answer, spoken at real interview pace
Round 2 (25 min): capstone deep-dive - answer every follow-up as if the interviewer had your README open, because they do
Round 3 (20 min): system design redux, on paper, including the three curveball follow-ups at the end of the script
Record the capstone architecture walkthrough once, listen back immediately, and write down three specific fixes
Mark each answer pass or fail against the bar (answered the question, under two minutes, one concrete number or artifact) and log failures as rehearsal items
build.hint: If you cannot fill 90 seconds on 'tell me about yourself', that is not a personality problem - it is a missing script. Write four sentences: where you come from, what you have built recently, what you are targeting, why this company.

items.expert:
MOCK SCRIPTS — read each question aloud, answer aloud, no notes. Interviewer intent and failure tells are given so you can score yourself.

**ROUND 1 — RECRUITER AND HIRING-MANAGER SCREEN (15 minutes, about 90 seconds each)**
1. 'Walk me through your background and what you are looking for.' Tests: signal density and target clarity. Tell: a chronological life story instead of four sentences ending in what you want next.
2. 'Tell me about something you built recently that you are proud of.' Tests: whether the project is real. Tell: adjectives instead of numbers.
3. 'Why AI engineering, and why now?' Tests: coherence of the switch. Tell: enthusiasm about the field with nothing about what you have done in it.
4. 'What is the hardest technical problem you have solved in the last six months?' Tests: depth and honesty. Tell: choosing a problem that was hard to type rather than hard to think about.
5. 'Tell me about a time something you built failed or was wrong.' Tests: whether you notice failure and what you changed. Tell: a disguised humblebrag, or blaming a library.
6. 'What are you looking for in your next role, and what would make you say no?' Tests: seriousness. Tell: 'I am open to anything.'

**ROUND 2 — TECHNICAL DEEP-DIVE ON THE CAPSTONE (25 minutes, answer as if they have your README open)**
1. 'Give me the architecture in two minutes.' Then: 'why is ingestion asynchronous?'
2. 'Why hybrid retrieval rather than pure vector search - and what did it buy you, in numbers?'
3. 'How do you know it works? What is in your evaluation set, how big is it, and who wrote the expected answers?'
4. 'You use an LLM as a judge. How do you know the judge is right?' Follow-up: 'what biases does it have?'
5. 'Your README says roughly two cents per query. Break that down for me.' Follow-up: 'halve it without hurting answer quality - what do you try first, and how would you prove it worked?'
6. 'Prove to me that tenant A cannot read tenant B documents. What is the test?'
7. 'The model provider starts returning 429s and then 500s for ten minutes. What does a user see?'
8. 'Show me where it is weakest.' Tests: whether you can criticise your own system before they do.
9. 'What was the hardest bug you hit, and how did you find it?'
10. 'If you started again on Monday, what would you do differently?'
Scoring for this round: 2 if you answered with a number or a file you could open, 1 if you answered qualitatively, 0 if you hedged. Any 0 on questions 2, 3 or 5 means the README is currently over-claiming.

**ROUND 3 — SYSTEM DESIGN REDUX (20 minutes, on paper, aloud)**
Prompt: 'Design an internal question-answering system for a 5,000-person company over 2 million documents across a wiki, a document store and a ticketing system. Answers must cite sources. Content changes daily. Answers should come back in a few seconds and finance is watching the bill.'
Work it in the same budget as yesterday: requirements and numbers, API and data model, architecture, failure modes, evaluation and cost, tradeoffs.
Curveballs, one every few minutes near the end - these are where the round is actually scored:
- 'Finance says the monthly bill has to halve. What goes?'
- 'One department is export-controlled: their documents must never appear in anyone else results. Change your design.'
- 'A document is deleted for legal reasons. What happens to the index, and to an answer that was cached yesterday?'
- 'Your retrieval quality drops one Tuesday and nobody knows why. How do you find out?'
A strong answer to a curveball starts by naming what it breaks in the design you just drew, then proposes the change and its cost. Rebuilding the whole design from scratch reads as panic.

**THE BAR (score every answer)** - answered the question asked, finished inside two minutes, contained at least one concrete number, name or artifact. Below the bar goes to the revision queue as a rehearsal item, not a reading item.
items.challenge: Do round two again the next morning, cold, and time your architecture answer: two minutes is the target and most people run four.
reflection: Listening back to the recording, how many seconds passed before your first substantive sentence?
Which deep-dive question exposed a README claim you cannot fully defend - and are you fixing the claim or the system?
done: All three rounds completed aloud against a clock
One answer recorded, listened back, and three specific fixes written down
Every answer marked pass or fail against the bar
Failed answers logged to the revision queue as rehearsal items

keyConcepts.def: The interview where every claim in your README is a legitimate thread to pull - which is why claims must be defensible line by line.
Naming what a new constraint breaks in your existing design, then changing the smallest part - rather than redesigning from scratch.

items.title: Final competency assessment
items.concept:
The app's assessment covers twelve areas, one per phase of the last twelve weeks: production Python; testing and version control; APIs and backend; LLM fundamentals; tool calling and agents; embeddings and vector search; RAG systems; evaluation; databases, queues and system design; reliability and security; deployment and operations; consulting and communication. Each area holds five to seven can-you statements.

**The evidence rule makes this worth doing.** For every check you mark as met, name the artifact in one line: repository and file, a commit, an eval run, a case score, a ticket you resolved. No artifact means the check is not met - not 'partially met', not 'in principle'. This single rule is what separates an assessment that improves your next month from one that flatters you for an afternoon.

**Verdicts follow the evidence, not the feeling.** Per area: 80% or more of checks met with evidence reads interview-ready; 50 to 79% reads needs-improvement; below 50% reads major-gaps. Expect an uneven picture. Someone who built and evaluated a RAG system for twelve weeks and touched agents for one is supposed to score unevenly, and the honest shape is more useful than a flat wall of green.

**Both directions of dishonesty cost you.** Inflation gets exposed in the deep-dive round, where 'I have used tool calling' meets 'walk me through your retry logic when the model calls the same tool twice'. Deflation is quieter and just as expensive: it sends you back to relearn things you can already do while the applications you should be sending sit unsent.

**The next-30-days plan** takes your weakest areas - the major-gaps first, then needs-improvement - and caps the list at three, ordered by how much your target roles actually care. Each prescription is timeboxed and produces an artifact, because 'revise agents' is not a plan and 'ship a two-tool agent with retries and a trace log by day 10' is. The plan runs alongside applications; it never becomes a reason to delay them.
items.why: You are about to spend a month applying and interviewing. Where you spend the parallel study hours should be decided by evidence about your actual gaps, not by whichever topic feels most uncomfortable this week.

build.task: Complete the 12-area assessment with an artifact named against every met check, accept the generated next-30-days plan, and schedule it.
steps: Open the assessment with your repositories, eval outputs, cost ledgers and case scores available - you will need to open them, not remember them
Work area by area; for each check either name the artifact in one line or mark it unmet, with no third option
Record the verdict per area from the thresholds (80% interview-ready, 50-79% needs-improvement, below 50% major-gaps)
Re-read your three highest-scoring areas and challenge one check in each: could you do it cold, tomorrow, without notes?
Generate the next-30-days plan, then edit each prescription until it names a deliverable artifact and a date
Put the plan in your calendar as fixed blocks and cap it at three areas; everything else waits for the next cycle
build.hint: If naming the artifact takes more than about thirty seconds, the check is unmet. Recall speed is a fair proxy for whether the skill is available under interview conditions.

items.challenge: Write the two-sentence honest summary of where you stand for a mentor who will check it against your repositories - specific enough to be wrong.
reflection: Which area did you want to score higher than the evidence supported, and what were you about to count as evidence that was not?
If a hiring manager independently scored these twelve areas from your public artifacts alone, where would their score differ most from yours?
done: All 12 areas assessed with an artifact named beside every met check
Verdict recorded per area using the stated thresholds
Next-30-days plan generated, edited so each prescription names a deliverable and a date, and capped at three areas
Plan blocks scheduled in the calendar alongside, not instead of, applications

keyConcepts.def: A skill counts as met only if you can name the artifact that proves it: repository, commit, eval run or case score.
Scoring yourself on familiarity rather than demonstrated evidence - exposed reliably in deep-dive interview rounds.

items.title: Retrospective and apply strategy
items.concept:
Forty minutes, three deliverables: a short retrospective, three interview stories, and an application cadence you will actually follow. Then the roadmap stops and the practice does not.

**The retrospective is two lists, not an essay.** What compounded: the project skeleton from Week 1 that every later repository reused, tests that let you refactor without fear, evals that turned opinions about retrieval into measurements, the debug habit of reproducing before theorising. What you would redo: name three specific things, because those are your honest answers to 'what would you do differently' in the deep-dive round.

**Three stories, rehearsed, cover most behavioural questions.** The shipped-system story (the capstone: constraint, decision, measured outcome). The measured-improvement story (a number that moved because you measured it - baseline, change, delta, what you learned). The failure story (something that broke, how you found it, what you changed so the class of bug cannot recur). Structure each as situation, constraint, decision, measured outcome - four beats, ninety seconds, no preamble.

**Application cadence beats application volume, but only just.** A workable shape: eight to ten targeted applications per week in two fixed blocks, five referral or conversation asks per week, and a tracking sheet with role, company, date, channel, what you tailored and the outcome. The tailoring rule keeps it sustainable: rewrite only the headline, the first CV bullet and one project line to mirror the top three requirements in the advert. Fully generic applications waste the send; forty-five-minute bespoke ones waste the week.

**Read the funnel like an engineer.** Under roughly one reply in ten after thirty applications means the CV or the targeting is the problem, not the market - fix the input rather than increasing the volume. Screens that never convert to technical rounds mean your stories need work. Technical rounds that never convert mean go back to yesterday's scripts.

**Maintenance mode** keeps twelve weeks from decaying: twenty minutes of revision-queue flashcards most days, one Interview Mode stack per week, one small build or deploy per fortnight so the shipping muscle stays alive. Triage the queue today - delete anything you have re-explained correctly twice, keep what is still uncomfortable, and archive the rest so the queue stays short enough to actually open.
items.why: The roadmap ends here; the job search does not. A cadence you can sustain for eight weeks and a queue you will actually open are worth more than any final burst of study.

build.task: Write the retrospective, draft and rehearse the three interview stories, and set up the application cadence plan with its tracking sheet and maintenance routine.
steps: Retrospective: two short lists - what compounded, and three things you would redo - written in one page or less
Draft the three stories in the four-beat structure, then say each aloud once and cut everything before the first substantive sentence
Build the tracking sheet with columns: date, company, role, channel, tailoring note, outcome, next action
Fix the cadence in your calendar: two application blocks per week, a weekly funnel review, five referral or conversation asks per week
Write your tailoring rule at the top of the sheet as a hard limit on time per application, so future-you cannot negotiate with it
Triage the revision queue: delete what you have re-explained twice, keep the uncomfortable items, and set the twenty-minute daily and weekly-stack maintenance routine
build.hint: Pick the target-role shortlist before the first application block: roughly fifteen companies you would genuinely join. Targeted rejection teaches you something; scattergun rejection teaches you nothing.

items.challenge: Send one application and one referral ask today, before closing the app - the cadence starts now or it starts never.
reflection: Which of the three stories is weakest, and is that a story problem or a project problem?
What is the smallest weekly commitment you would still keep in a bad week - and is that what you just scheduled?
done: Retrospective written: what compounded plus three things you would redo
Three interview stories drafted in four beats and each said aloud once
Tracking sheet created and cadence blocks scheduled with the tailoring rule written down
Revision queue triaged and the maintenance routine scheduled
One application and one referral ask sent

keyConcepts.def: Situation, constraint, decision, measured outcome - a ninety-second structure that answers most behavioural questions.
A fixed limit on what you customise per application - headline, first bullet, one project line - so cadence survives contact with reality.
Diagnosing a job search by conversion rates between stages instead of by total applications sent.

questions.q: In your capstone, a user uploads a 300-page PDF. What happens, and why is it built that way?
options: The upload request parses, chunks, embeds and indexes the document, then returns the chunk count
The request stores the file, enqueues an ingestion job and returns a job id; a worker chunks, embeds and indexes, and status is polled
The document is embedded lazily on the first question that needs it, to avoid wasted embedding cost
The file is indexed by a nightly batch so that ingestion never competes with query traffic
questions.explain: Ingestion takes minutes and would blow request timeouts and tie up API workers. Enqueue, return a job id, and let a worker do the slow work - the same pattern as any long-running upload pipeline.

questions.q: Your /ask costs about $0.021 per query: $0.0004 to embed the question, $0.0009 for local reranking, and $0.0197 for generation over roughly 6,000 context tokens plus 400 output tokens. An interviewer asks you to halve it. What do you try first?
options: Move to a cheaper embedding model
Cache reranker scores between queries
Cut retrieved context - fewer or tighter chunks after reranking - and re-run the eval set to check quality held
Downgrade the vector database tier
questions.explain: Generation input tokens dominate by a factor of about twenty, so context size is the only lever that matters here. The second half of the answer is what scores: any cut must be re-measured against the gold set before you keep it.

questions.q: In the 8-section case method, which section must come before Architecture?
options: Risks
Go / no-go and approach
POC plan
Evaluation and rollout
questions.explain: The order is Discovery, Assumptions, Go / no-go and approach, Architecture, Risks, Cost estimate, POC plan, Evaluation and rollout. Drawing an architecture before you have chosen and justified an approach produces a solution looking for a problem.

questions.q: A CV bullet reads: 'Improved RAG accuracy by 40% using advanced retrieval techniques.' What is the honesty problem?
options: It uses the word RAG, which non-technical recruiters will not recognise
Percentages are always weaker than absolute numbers on a CV
It names no metric, no baseline and no dataset, so it cannot survive 'tell me more' - and 'advanced techniques' hides which change did the work
It is too short to convey twelve weeks of effort
questions.explain: The honesty rule is that every bullet survives a follow-up. Replace it with something you can defend: recall@5 from 0.58 to 0.87 on a 40-case gold set after adding hybrid retrieval and cross-encoder reranking.

questions.q: Your assessment scores evaluation as interview-ready with evidence, and agents as major-gaps. How should the next-30-days plan be built, and what makes a prescription good rather than useless?
questions.answer: Build it from the evidence-scored weakest areas, not from what feels uncomfortable: take the major-gaps areas first, cap the plan at about three areas, and weight by what your target roles actually require. A good prescription is timeboxed and produces a named artifact with a date - 'ship a two-tool agent with retry handling and a trace log by day 10' - rather than 'revise agents'. The plan runs in parallel with applications and never becomes a reason to postpone them.

questions.q: You are 25 minutes into a 40-minute case and Architecture is only half written, with Risks, Cost, POC and Evaluation untouched. What do you do, and why?
questions.answer: Leave Architecture where it is and produce at least a skeleton of every remaining section before the bell. Scoring is per section, so four empty sections cost far more than one section that is merely adequate. The later sections - risks with named controls, a costed range, a POC with kill criteria, an evaluation and rollout plan - are also where consultants differentiate themselves from engineers, so they are the last thing to sacrifice. Timebox each section from the start and treat the clock as part of the exercise.
